stem: A 56-year-old woman sustains a neck injury during a road traffic incident. On arrival at the hospital she complains of neck pain and undergoes cervical spine x-rays.
prompt: On the lateral cervical XR what is the most reliable sign of injury?
explanation:
The atlantodental interval is measured from the posterior aspect of the anterior arch of C1 to the anterior aspect of the dens.

Normal in adults is <3mm

Normal in children is <5mm

The gap increases due to anterior translocation of the atlas. This often simultaneously causes the posterior arch of C1 to become anterior displaced with respect to the spinolaminar line.

There are a number of non-traumatic causes of an increased atlantodental interval.

The prevertebral space is also important to appreciate on the lateral cervical spine view. Enlargement of the prevertebral soft tissue is a secondary sign of a bony injury. Normal measurements are given below.

<7mm at C2

<5mm at C3+4

<22mm at C6 (14mm in children)

Cervical spine trauma

On the lateral cervical XR which of the following is abnormal?

Pre-odontoid space 4mm

Prevertebral soft tissue 10mm at C6

Prevertebral soft tissue 3mm at C3

Prevertebral soft tissue 5mm at C2

Prevertebral soft tissue 6mm at C4

stem: You are reviewing the shoulder x-ray of a 20-year-old man and notice the scapula is abnormal.
prompt: Which of the following is NOT a feature of Sprengel shoulder? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Sprengel shoulder

This condition can occur in isolation as well as part of Klippel-Feil syndrome. It is (like Klippel-Feil syndrome) also often associated with renal anomalies. Sprengel shoulder is a congenital abnormality where the scapula (usually, but not exclusively, unilateral) is attached to the cervical vertebra either by a fibrous or osseous connection, and therefore fails to descend into the normal position. The result is elevation and medial rotation of the scapula, which is usually hypoplastic. The condition can be readily appreciated on a plain film although cross-sectional imaging is useful to plan surgical correction if required. If present, the osseous connection between the scapula and the spine is termed an omovertebral bar.

Klippel-Feil syndrome (different from Klippel-Trenaunay-Weber syndrome: port-wine stains, localised hypertrophy and venous malformations)

Klippel-Feil syndrome is predominantly a segmentation anomaly which arises during foetal development and leads to cervical fusion of two or more vertebral bodies. C2-3 are most commonly involved, accounting for around half of cases. Thereafter C5-6 accounts for a further third and the remainder are made up from fusions at other levels. There are a multitude of associated features, the predominant ones of which include:

Renal abnormalities (of which a third have unilateral renal agenesis) - ⅔

Scoliosis >20o - ½

Sprengel shoulder - ⅓

Deafness (sensorineural) - ⅓

Cervical ribs - ⅕

The renal anomalies seen include agenesis or dysgenesis, ectopic location, and duplication.

Yet further features of this condition, all present in under 20% of cases include:

Odontoid dysplasia

Hemivertebrae / butterfly vertebrae

Syringomyelia / diastomatomyelia

Ear anomalies (microtia, deformed ossicles etc)

Congenital heart disease (ASD or coarctation)

stem: A 65-year-old lady complains to her GP of ongoing burning pains in her hand and wrist following a fall 6 months previously. At the time she was found to have fractured her ulnar styloid process and wore a plaster cast for 6 weeks. She is otherwise well. On examination her hand is oedematous with some dystrophic nail changes. She undergoes an x-ray and nuclear medicine scan. The GP suspects a diagnosis of complex regional pain syndrome.
prompt: Which of the following combination of findings would be most likely?
explanation:
Complex regional pain syndrome also known as Sudeck dystrophy

Patients develop chronic pain in an area previously affected by an, often disproportionately mild, injury. The pain is said to be burning in nature and symptoms of allodynia (pain with stimuli which would not normally be painful) and hyperalgesia (excessive sensitivity to pain) are also usually described. By contrast, reduced sensation is not normally found. On x-ray there is juxta-articular osteopenia with sub-periosteal bone resorption but preservation of the joint spaces. Soft tissue swelling can also be seen. Nuclear medicine tests may show either increased flow with increased uptake on the delayed blood pool images or (less commonly) decreased flow with decreased uptake on the delayed blood pool images.

topic: Acute rupture of the anterior cruciate ligament
stem: Which of the following is NOT a secondary sign of an acute rupture of the anterior cruciate ligament?
prompt: Select one answer only.
options: Bony contusion to the lateral femoral condyle
Bony contusion to the posterolateral tibia
Buckling of the posterior cruciate ligament
explanation:
The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) is particularly vulnerable to clip injuries and pivot shift injuries. Secondary signs of an ACL tear include:

Anterior translation of the tibia to >5mm

Bowing of the posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) to <105o

So-called ‘uncovering’ of the lateral meniscus where there is posterior displacement of the posterior horn of the lateral meniscus by at least 3.5mm

Lateral compartment contusions (if pivot shift or clip injury mechanism)

Anterior contusions (if hyperextension mechanism)

Although the medial collateral ligament can also be ruptured during a pivot shift or clip type injury, it is not considered as a secondary sign of ACL rupture.

Clip injury and pivot shift injury

These two injuries are very similar. Both involve valgus stress on a flexed knee (such as a tackle to the knee during sports). A pivot shift injury also requires external rotation of the tibia. The three main structures most at risk during these injuries are:

Anterior cruciate ligament (especially in a pivot shift injury)

Medial collateral ligament (especially in a clip injury)

Medial meniscus (remember that the medial meniscus is attached to the medial collateral ligament)

If all three are present together it is referred to as the O’Donoghue triad. Since O’Donoghue defined this triad however, it has been discovered that lateral meniscal tears are actually more common with this type of injury than medial meniscus ones.

Bony contusions occur at the side of impact because the proximal tibia and distal femur impact on one another thus:

Lateral tibial plateau (posterolateral in pivot shift injury)

Lateral femoral condyle

stem: A 34-year-old man suffers a knee injury while on a skiing holiday. He visits a local hospital and has x-rays taken of his knee. No fracture is found. Once back home he undergoes an MRI scan when the pain fails to resolve. There is a tear of the anterior cruciate ligament and bony contusions seen at the lateral femoral condyle and lateral tibial plateau.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
In this question, the answer comes down to either a pivot shift or a clip injury. The two are very similar. The involvement of the ACL makes pivot shift the more likely of the two.

Bony contusions

Bruising to the bone can be detected around 2 days following an injury but may not resolve for many months thereafter. With regards knee injuries, it is often possible to discern the mechanism of injury from the pattern of bruising seen. The contusions follow fluid on MRI scans i.e. low in signal on T1 and high on T2 (and STIR). STIR is used to suppress the fat of the bone marrow thereby making the fluid stand out more.

Clip injury and pivot shift injury

These two injuries are very similar. Both involve valgus stress on a flexed knee (such as a tackle to the knee during sports). A pivot shift injury also requires external rotation of the tibia. The three main structures most at risk during these injuries are:

Anterior cruciate ligament (especially in a pivot shift injury)

Medial collateral ligament (especially in a clip injury)

Medial meniscus (remember that the medial meniscus is attached to the medial collateral ligament)

If all three are present together it is referred to as the O’Donoghue triad. Since O’Donoghue defined this triad however, it has been discovered that lateral meniscal tears are actually more common with this type of injury than medial meniscus ones.

Bony contusions occur at the side of impact because the proximal tibia and distal femur impact on one another thus:

Lateral tibial plateau (posterolateral in pivot shift injury)

Lateral femoral condyle

Transient lateral patella dislocation injury

When the patella dislocates laterally, its medial facet can impact onto the anterolateral corner of the lateral femoral condyle. Both areas become damaged and contusions can be seen on MRI. Often though, the patella reduces spontaneously and thus the exact mechanism of injury must be inferred from the imaging findings.

Joint effusion

Osteochondral injuries to the anterolateral femoral condyle and medial patella facet

Sprain or disruption to the medial retinaculum

Hyperextension injury

These occur often following excessively forceful kicking. There will be bony contusions at the anterior aspect of the tibial plateau and femoral condyles. Either of the anterior or posterior cruciate ligaments may also be involved.

Dashboard injury

As the name would suggest, this injury is usually stained by impact of the knee against the dashboard of a car during a road traffic incident. Force applied to the anterior aspect of the tibia when the knee is flexed leads to:

Osteochondral injury or fracture to the anterior aspect of the tibia

Posterior cruciate ligament rupture/sprain

stem: You are reviewing the x-ray of an 88-year-old man's lumbar spine. He is known to have a large abdominal aortic aneurysm which has been deemed non-operable.
prompt: Which of the following findings is most in-keeping with this diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Anterior vertebral scalloping

There are a number of specific differential diagnoses which can lead to this finding. In each case the image should be interrogated carefully to look for further clues as to the underlying diagnosis. Scalloping is a chronic process whereby mechanical pressure on the bone causes remodelling.

stem: You are reviewing the radiographs of a 40-year-old marathon runner who has been experiencing worsening hip pains over the last few months. There is over-coverage of the left femoral head by the acetabulum.
prompt: Which of the following regarding femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) is INCORRECT? Selec ONE answer only.
options: Acetebular retroversion is seen with pincer-type FAI
More patients have mixed type FAI than either cam or pincer-type
Patients with cam-type FAI are usually younger than those with pincer-type FAI
Protrusio acetabuli predisposes to cam-type FAI
explanation:
Please note that the question asks which answer is INCORRECT.

Femoroacetabular impingement (FAI)

Mixed type - >80% of patients have components of both cam-type and pincer-type FAI.

Cam type - a cam is an engineering term for an oval/egg shaped component with a hole through the middle of the wider end. In cam type FAI the femoral head takes on a 'cam' shaped appearance due to bony overgrowth at the superior aspect of the femoral neck. This abnormal bony contour impinges against the anterosuperior aspect of the acetabulum during movement. The condition occurs more frequently in men and tends to affect men in their 30s. Certain conditions can predispose to cam-type FAI, including SUFE, DDH and Perthes disease. Some patients with cam-type FAI exhibit femoral retroversion.

Pincer type - here bony protuberance of the anterosuperior acetabulum causes over-coverage of the femoral head and impingement against the femoral neck. Protrusio acetabuli predisposes to pincer-type FAI. The relationship of the overgrown anterior acetabular rim to the posterior acetabular rim in pincer-type FAI is called acetabular retroversion since it causes the femoral neck to twist posteriorly. Patients usually stand with their toes pointing outwards as a consequence. The condition is more common in women and a patient is typically aged around 40.

stem: You review an MRI scan of a 50-year-old patient with carpal tunnel syndrome.
prompt: Which of the following nerve passes through the carpal tunnel? Select ONE answer only.
options: The deep branch of the radial nerve
explanation:
The carpal tunnel contains a total of nine flexor tendons (but not the muscles themselves), surrounded by a synovial sheath, and the median nerve.

The tendons contained within the carpal tunnel are:

Flexor digitorum profundus (four tendons)

Flexor digitorum superficialis (four tendons)

Flexor pollicis longus (one tendon)

stem: A 76-year-old office clerk is taken by ambulance to A+E having fallen over and found himself unable to get up. He has severe pain in his left hip and a pelvic x-ray shows an extracapsular fracture through the left femoral neck. The A+E SHO also notices that the trabeculae of the proximal femur are very coarse and sclerotic. Similarly she realises that in the pelvis the left superior pubic ramus is expanded and appears coarsely sclerotic.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Paget disease

Paget disease is seldom found in patients below the age of 50 but is one of the more common musculoskeletal abnormalities thereafter. It consists of polyostotic, asymmetric disordered bone remodelling where intensive osteoclastic activity leads to multiple lytic lesions before osteoblastic activity results in the formation of sclerotic bone. A variety of imaging findings can be seen with x-ray.

Lytic phase: During the lytic phase, radiolucency with a ‘flame’ or ‘blade of grass’ shape extends along the diaphysis and osteoporosis circumscripta (large lucent areas of skull) can be found in the skull.

Mixed phase: lytic and sclerotic phenomena

Sclerotic phase: densely sclerotic bone such as the classical ‘ivory vertebra’ can be found.

Clinically it can be an incidental asymptomatic diagnosis or can present as all or any of:

Elevated ALP with a normal calcium and phosphate

A pathological fracture – although it may be sclerotic, the bone structure is disordered and therefore weaker than normal bone.

Cranial nerve palsies – due to compression at neural foramina

Enlarging head / hat size – due to widening of the diploic spaces (referred to as the Tam O’Shanter sign, whereby the skull takes on the appearance of a the Scottish hat called the Tam O’Shanter)

High output cardiac failure – this is a rare presentation caused by markedly increased bony perfusion

Pain – in the absence of a fracture, it is usually not a painful condition per se but can co-exist with other conditions such as osteoarthritis which may be the cause of the patient’s pain

Radiologically the hallmarks are bony expansion with coarsening of the trabeculae and cortices. On a bone scan active lesions will show increased uptake due to their increased blood flow.

Sarcomatous degeneration of the affected sites into either an osteosarcoma, malignant fibrous histiocytoma or chondrosarcoma carries a poor prognosis and careful study should be made of any known lesions at each imaging opportunity. New soft tissue component formation or new lysis of previously sclerotic bone should raise suspicion.

Mastocytosis

This disease is also caused by clonal proliferation of a particular cell type, however in this case it is of mast cells. Clinically patients may experience symptoms linked to histamine release from the mast cells such as flushing, sweating, diarrhoea and abdominal pains but only around a quarter of patients complain of bony pains. The skeleton can be affected by either focal lesions (usually in the spine) or with diffusely increased density. Other features such as hepatosplenomegaly, and lymph node enlargement (retroperitoneal, mesenteric, periportal) may be present too.

Erdheim-Chester disease

Infiltration of the appendicular skeleton by histiocytes leads to fibrosis and sclerosis which can appear striking on an x-ray. The condition is very similar to Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis (LCH) and both conditions have been reported across a broad range of patient ages. Usually however LCH presents at around the age of 5-10 whereas ECD peaks in incidence at around 55 years of age. Both diseases are caused by clonal proliferations of one or more lines of histiocytes and there are different cellular markers which can help distinguish between the two diseases pathologically. There is considerable overlap in the clinical and radiological features of both diseases.

Clinically patients with ECD present with all or any of the usual histiocytosis triad of diabetes insipidus, exophthalmos and bone pain. Of these, the most prominent feature is usually bony pain.

X-rays show sclerosis in the metadiaphyseal regions in a bilateral symmetrical pattern but with sparing of the epiphyses. Corticomedullary differentiation becomes blurred and there are also multiple areas of lucency indicating the presence of lytic lesions too.

Metastases

Sclerotic metastases are typical with prostate and breast cancers among others. This should always be considered as a pertinent differential diagnosis however there are not other features in this question to suggest it is correct in this case.

Sclerotic metastases:

Prostate (most common)

Breast (mixed lytic and sclerotic)

Transitional Cell Carcinoma

Lymphoma

Mucinous adenocarcinomas (colon, gastric, ovary)

Medulloblastoma

Neuroblastoma

Carcinoid

stem: You are reviewing the scans of a patient who is being followed up in the diabetes clinic. The x-ray is normal, but an MRI scan shows an ulcer overlying the fifth metatarsophalangeal joint. There is adjacent oedema in the soft tissues of the foot and a joint effusion at the MTPJ but normal T1 signal in the bones.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
This is slightly controversial since the absence of T1 marrow changes suggests that this patient actually has osteitis (if at all) rather than osteomyelitis (see below), however the location of the soft tissue changes being adjacent to a fifth MTP ulcer and the paucity of other joint involvement are strong pointers to an infective aetiology over Charcot arthropathy.

Differentiating between osteomyelitis and Charcot arthropathy

There are a number of complications of diabetes which are important to correctly diagnose, the better to guide treatment. Sometimes imaging can help although often there is overlap between the features. Osteomyelitis in a diabetic foot should definitely be suspected where there are marrow changes adjacent to an area of broken skin with soft tissue inflammatory changes in continuity with both the affected bone and the broken skin. Frank fluid collections (as opposed to either effusions or soft tissue oedema) also suggest infection over Charcot arthropathy. High T2 signal in the bone marrow is very sensitive for osteomyelitis and there should be a corresponding loss of normal high T1 signal too. If the T1 signal is normal, technically the finding may be of osteitis as opposed to osteomyelitis.

Changes can be seen on MRI prior to radiographic changes becoming apparent. Effusions are a prominent feature, and may be significant in size. Soft tissue oedema is also seen. Usually Charcot arthropathy affects multiple joints at once, and has a predilection for the mid-foot joints whereas osteomyelitis is more likely to affect an isolated joint, or be contiguous in nature from the index pathogen admission point; thus, the presence of an ulcer with adjacent inflammatory changes is far more suggestive of an infective process than a neuropathic one such as Charcot arthropathy.

Charcot joint also known as neuropathic osteoarthropathy

In patients with advanced diabetes mellitus, Charcot arthropathy is usually seen in the midfoot or ankle joints. Although only a small number of Charcot joints affect the shoulder most of those caused by a syrinx do. A syrinx is also a more common cause of Charcot joints than either multiple sclerosis or Hansen disease (leprosy).

Causes of Charcot joints

Diabetes mellitus

Syringomyelia

Hansen disease (leprosy)

Poliomyelitis

Neurosyphilis

Multiple sclerosis

Whatever the underlying cause, compromise to the sensory nerves supplying the relevant joint prevent the normal protective mechanisms and as such minor trauma does not have sufficient an environment to heal correctly. This is particularly pertinent to weight-bearing joints. Loss of sympathetic control of the same area is also thought to play a part.

The joints can take either an atrophic pattern, a heterotropic pattern or a mixed pattern.

The radiological findings can be summarised as the 5Ds, namely:

Destruction

Dislocation

Density (due to heterotrophic new bone formation and sclerosis)

Disorganisation

Debris

Atrophic

Heterotrophic

More common

Less common

Destruction predominates

Fragmentation and debris formation predominates

Little sclerosis

Much sclerosis

Complex regional pain syndrome (also known as Sudeck dystrophy)

Patients develop chronic pain in an area previously affected by an, often disproportionately mild, injury. The pain is said to be burning in nature and symptoms of allodynia (pain with stimuli which would not normally be painful) and hyperalgesia (excessive sensitivity to pain) are also usually described. By contrast, reduced sensation is not normally found. On x-ray there is juxta-articular osteopenia with sub-periosteal bone resorption but preservation of the joint spaces. Soft tissue swelling can also be seen. Nuclear medicine tests may show either increased flow with increased uptake on the delayed blood pool images or (less commonly) decreased flow with decreased uptake on the delayed blood pool images.

stem: Erosive OA
prompt: Which of the following would be a typical finding of joint involvement for Erosive OA? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Erosive osteoarthritis

This is an inflammatory version of osteoarthritis with a strong female preponderance. The pattern of involvement is that of standard osteoarthritis (distal interphalangeal joints) but the features have an inflammatory component with prominent erosions, particularly of the middle of the distal end of the middle phalanges leading to a classical gull-wing appearance. As with osteoarthritis, osteophytes and subchondral cyst formation is also found.

stem: A 34-year-old man suffers a knee injury while on a heavily activity based holiday. He undergoes x-rays at a local hospital which show no fractures. On returning home he is referred to an orthopaedic surgeon by his GP when his pain fails to resolve. An MRI is arranged which shows a hyperextension injury.
prompt: What findings on MRI would be most consistent with this?
options: High STIR signal to the anterior aspect of the fibula with an associated posterior cruciate ligament tear
High T2 signal to the anterior aspect of the lateral femoral condyle and lateral tibial plateau with an anterior cruciate ligament and medial collateral ligament tear
High signal on STIR to the lateral femoral condyle and posterolateral tibial plateau with an associated tear of the anterior cruciate ligament tear
High signal on T2 and STIR to the anterior aspect of the tibia with an associated anterior cruciate ligament tear
High signal on T2 to the lateral femoral condyle and medial patella facet with an associated tear of the medial retinaculum
explanation:
Bony contusions

Bruising to the bone can be detected around 2 days following an injury but may not resolve for many months thereafter. With regards knee injuries, it is often possible to discern the mechanism of injury from the pattern of bruising seen. The contusions follow fluid on MRI scans i.e. low in signal on T1 and high on T2 (and STIR). STIR is used to suppress the fat of the bone marrow thereby making the fluid stand out more.

Hyperextension injury - High signal on T2 and STIR to the anterior aspect of the tibia with an associated anterior cruciate ligament tear

These occur often following excessively forceful kicking. There will be bony contusions at the anterior aspect of the tibial plateau and femoral condyles. Either of the anterior or posterior cruciate ligaments may also be involved.

Transient lateral patella dislocation injury - High signal on T2 to the lateral femoral condyle and medial patella facet with an associated tear of the medial retinaculum

When the patella dislocates laterally, its medial facet can impact onto the anterolateral corner of the lateral femoral condyle. Both areas become damaged and contusions can be seen on MRI. Often though, the patella reduces spontaneously and thus the exact mechanism of injury must be inferred from the imaging findings.

Joint effusion

Osteochondral injuries to the anterolateral femoral condyle and medial patella facet

Sprain or disruption to the medial retinaculum

Clip injury and pivot shift injury

- High signal on STIR to the lateral femoral condyle and posterolateral tibial plateau with an associated tear of the anterior cruciate ligament tear (Pivot shift)

- High T2 signal to the anterior aspect of the lateral femoral condyle and lateral tibial plateau with an anterior cruciate ligament and medial collateral ligament tear (Clip injury)

These two injuries are very similar. Both involve valgus stress on a flexed knee (such as a tackle to the knee during sports). A pivot shift injury also requires external rotation of the tibia. The three main structures most at risk during these injuries are:

Anterior cruciate ligament (especially in a pivot shift injury)

Medial collateral ligament (especially in a clip injury)

Medial meniscus (remember that the medial meniscus is attached to the medial collateral ligament)

If all three are present together it is referred to as the O’Donoghue triad. Since O’Donoghue defined this triad however, it has been discovered that lateral meniscal tears are actually more common with this type of injury than medial meniscus ones.

Bony contusions occur at the side of impact because the proximal tibia and distal femur impact on one another thus:

Lateral tibial plateau (posterolateral in pivot shift injury)

Lateral femoral condyle

Dashboard injury - High STIR signal to the anterior aspect of the tibia with an associated posterior cruciate ligament tear

As the name would suggest, this injury is usually stained by impact of the knee against the dashboard of a car during a road traffic incident. Force applied to the anterior aspect of the tibia when the knee is flexed leads to:

Osteochondral injury or fracture to the anterior aspect of the tibia

Posterior cruciate ligament rupture/sprain

stem: A 34-year-old man presents to his GP with worsening back pain and stiffness. Plain radiographs show some slight sclerosis of the sacroiliac joints bilaterally with small vertebral syndesmophytes in the lumbar spine. He is referred to an orthopaedic consultant who is concerned he may have ankylosing spondylitis and requests an MRI scan.
prompt: Which sequence would be best to confirm the diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
options: T1 fat sat and STIR, coronal SIJs and sagittal spine
T1 fat sat and T2, sagittal SIJs and axial spine
T1 fat sat pre and post contrast and STIR, coronal SIJs and sagittal spine
T1 fat sat pre and post contrast and T2, axial SIJs and sagittal spine
T2 fat sat and STIR, axial SIJs and coronal spine
explanation:
T1 fat sat - useful for visualisation of bony erosions and new bone formation

T1 fat sat post contrast - useful for detecting bone marrow abnormalities (but so is STIR, so contrast is not an absolute requirement for imaging ankylosing spondylitis).

STIR - useful for detecting bone marrow abnormalities in the SIJs and spine

T2 fat sat - useful for detecting oedema

Coronal SIJ - ideally this should be taken parallel to the long axis of the sacrum, the better to view the SIJs, both SIJs can be seen on each image for comparison.

Axial SIJ - ideally this should be at 90 degrees to the modified coronal plane and is used to evaluate the ligamentous portion of the SIJs.

Axial spine - useful if co-existing disc herniation present but not ordinarily included otherwise

Sagittal spine - useful to evaluate facet and costovertebral joints

Ankylosing spondylitis

This disease usually presents in early adulthood with gradual onset of back pain. There is a male preponderance, though it can affect women too. The vast majority (>90%) of patients are HLA-B27 positive. Radiologically the late features are classical with:

Bilateral symmetrical sacroiliitis

Enthesopathy - calcified tendon insertion sites

Bamboo spine - vertebral syndesmophytes, particularly in the thoracolumbar spine

Dagger sign - spinous process fusion

Erosion, then fusion at the symphysis pubis, costochondral, costovertebral and sternoclavicular joints

Thoracic manifestations: upper lobe pulmonary fibrosis, pericarditis, aortic root dilatation

Early features are far more subtle and require a higher index of suspicion

Enthesopathy - high signal on MRI at tendon insertion sites

Romanus lesions - triangular shaped oedema at the corners of vertebral bodies

Andersson lesions - bony oedema in the vertebral bodies adjacent to the disks.

Oedema in the sacroiliac joints.

Patients with advanced ankylosing spondylitis are at increased risk of pathological fractures due to fusion. These can be pelvic fractures following a simple fall, or chance fractures of the spine (involving all three columns - in ankylosing spondylitis, these fractures are also sometimes termed chalk-stick or carrot fractures).

stem: A 23-year-old man has AP and lateral radiographs of the right ankle after twisting it whilst playing football. There is no fracture seen, however a central, triangular radiolucent area is seen on the lateral projection in the calcaneus. It is well defined with a narrow zone of transition and there is some high density centrally.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Intraosseus lipoma

Calcification within the center of this lesion is a key feature which differentiates it from other lesions of plain film. Fat density on CT or MRI would also be a key differentiator.

Geode

This is a subchondral cyst associated with osteoarthritis which should have communication with the joint space and be present in an older patient.

Pseudo-cyst of calcaneus

This is a variation of the normal trabecular pattern centrally within the calcaneus. Will not have a crisp edge for this reason. Persistence of thin trabeculae and a visible nutrient foramen are supporting features.

Unicameral bone cyst

This is a well-defined lesion with thick sclerotic edges and potentially a multiloculated appearance. Absence of calcification within the lesion is a key differentiator from intraosseous lipoma, although if fractured, a fallen fragment sign can be seen.

Chondroblastoma

The calcaneus, like the patella, is an epiphyseal equivalent, so any epiphyseal lesions should be considered a possibility in this bone. They usually arise eccentrically in the epiphysis, are lobuated with a thin sclerotic margin.

stem: A 43-year-old man presents with a painful palpable lump on the sole of his foot. Ultrasound demonstrates a 3cm well-defined, fusiform hyporeflective area arising from the plantar fascia.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
This is the classical description of a plantar fibroma. On MRI they are characteristically iso/ slightly low in signal on both T1 and T2 weighted sequences compared with normal muscle signal, and show variable contrast enhancement.

A foreign body would be a small echogenic structure. Melanoma metastasis would be unlikely to cause a fusiform swelling and metastasis to the plantar fascia would be unlikely. Osteochondroma and osteophytes would also be hyperechoic due to the bone/ soft tissue interface.

stem: A 40-year-old woman presents with an uncomfortable swelling at the back of her right knee. On examination you palpate a round, smooth, fluctuant mass within the popliteal fossa. An ultrasound scan confirms that she has a Baker's cyst.
prompt: Which of the following is the most lateral structure contained within the popliteal fossa? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
The popliteal fossa is a diamond shaped depression situated at the back of the knee joint. It acts as the main conduit for the neurovascular structures entering and leaving the leg.

The borders of the popliteal fossa are:

Superomedial border: semimembranosus

Superolateral border: biceps femoris

Inferomedial border: medial head of gastrocnemius

Inferolateral border: lateral head of gastrocnemius and plantaris

The roof of the popliteal fossa is formed by (from superficial to deep):

Skin

Superficial fascia

Deep (popliteal) fascia

stem: You are reviewing a trauma series of a 21-year-old man. There is diffuse bony sclerosis on all of the images. The fingers of his hands are short and stubby. On the skull images the cranial sutures are wide and you can see that there is frontal bossing but the mandible is very small.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Pyknodysostosis

This disorder is inherited in an autosomal recessive fashion and causes diffuse bony sclerosis. Patients are of short stature and often have a typical facies; there is usually frontal bossing despite delayed closure of the cranial sutures, small mandibular size and beaking of the nose. Additionally patients have short stubby fingers, the nails of which may be hypoplastic. It can be difficult to tell pyknodysostosis from osteopetrosis however the medullary cavity is still discernible in the case of pyknodysostosis. Patients with osteopetrosis also do not tend to suffer from short stature or mandibular involvement.

Osteopetrosis

This is a disease of abnormal osteoclastic activity which leads to thick, sclerotic bone throughout the skeleton. Although appearing very solid on an x-ray, the bone is very disorganised structurally and consequently very brittle. Patients may experience numerous fractures throughout their lives. There is an autosomal dominant form which does not impede life expectancy but the autosomal recessive form carries are poorer prognosis with death due to complications of bone marrow failure (infections, leukaemia or haemorrhage) before adulthood.

On x-ray there is a generalised increase in bone density and films should be carefully evaluated for the presence of a pathological fracture. A bone-within-a-bone appearance is typical of the autosomal dominant form and there may be alternating lines of sclerosis and lucency in the phalanges.

Osteopetrosis

Image sourced from WikipediaCourtesy of Stevenfruitsmaak CC BY-SA 2.0

Osteopoikilosis

This benign condition leads to multiple small oval bone islands forming around the skeleton. Purportedly, once the epiphyses have fused the number remains static. They can show mildly increased uptake on a nuclear medicine bone scan. Whereas a bone island may exist in isolation or near isolation, the finding of multiple such lesions suggests the diagnosis of osteopoikilosis.

Image sourced from WikipediaCourtesy of Hellerhoff CC BY-SA 3.0

Osteopathia striata

This disease is more similar to osteopoikilosis than the other bony dysplasias. It is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion, but can arise sporadically too. It causes striking longitudinal striations in the metaphyseal regions of the long bones but patients are generally asymptomatic and it is usually therefore an incidental finding. The appearance is said to resemble stalks of celery.

Melorrheostosis

This dysplasia gives a classical appearance said to resemble the dripping of solid candle wax along a bone. The name comes from greek words meaning 'flowing' and 'limb'. It can be asymptomatic but if there is encroachment on nerves or joints patients may present with pain and movement limitations. Uniquely for a dysplasia, it can cross from one bone to the next across a joint, sometimes causing fusion in the process. On imaging the affected 'dripping' areas are seen as slcerotic areas within the affected bones. It usually only affects one limb of the patient but changes can be seen in more than one bone of that limb (i.e. monomelic but polyostotic).

stem: A 57-year-old lady presents with pain and instability in her wrist. Radiographs demonstrate widening of the scapholunate angle and an increased capitolunate angle. The orthopaedic surgeon reviewing the images recognises this as dorsal intercalated segmental instability (DISI).
prompt: Injury to which ligament is most likely to have resulted in this pathology? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Scapholunate

Injury to the scapholunate ligaments results in SLAC and DISI (which is more common than VISI).

Lunotriquetral

Injury to this ligament causes midcarpal dislocation (similar to lunate dislocation and also associate with triquetral fractures). Injury to this ligament also results in VISI.

Dorsal Radiolunate

Lunate dislocation occurs secondary to a dorsal radiolunate injury.

Capitolunate

Injury to this ligament is associated with perilunate dislocation.

stem: A 58-year-old lady undergoes an MRI of her spine. The T6 vertebra returns high signal on both T1 and T2.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Vertebral haemangioma

These lesions are extremely common and should be very familiar to all candidates. They can occur anywhere but commonly arise in the vertebrae. They have a typical appearance of vertical trabeculae which give a ‘corduroy’ appearance when viewed in sagittal or coronal planes but a honeycomb or polka-dot appearance when viewed in the axial plane. On MRI they return high signal on both T1 and T2 sequences.

Metastatic malignant melanoma

This is the exception that proves the rule. Apart from metastatic malignant melanoma, all other skeletal lesions which return high signal on T1 are benign. The melanin pigment has paramagnetic effects and leads to high T1 signal. On top of this melanoma metastases have a high propensity to haemorrhage which can also produce high T1 signals. T2 signal tends to be low though.

stem: You are performing an ultrasound scan on a 47-year-old man who has a suspected rotator cuff tear. You are trying to see the long head of biceps tendon.
prompt: How should you position the patient's arm to see this tendon best?
options: Arm held posteriorly with elbow flexed
Elbow fixed at 90 degrees, hand supinated
Forced internal rotation with hand in the small of the back
explanation:
There are a number of different manoeuvers which can greatly improve visibility of the rotator cuff muscles and tendons when performing a shoulder ultrasound. The basic principle revolves around attempting to straighten each tendon out.

Image sourced from WikipediaCourtesy of Anamotography CC BY-SA 2.1 jp

The long head of biceps is usually relatively easy to find and requires less manipulation to image optimally however in theory it is best imaged with the elbow flexed and hand pointing towards the contralateral knee with the palm facing upwards.

Subscapularis

External rotation and adduction - with palm up and flexed elbow, fix the elbow to the side of the patient and rotate the humerus externally by swinging the hand outwards.

The subscapularis attaches to the lesser tuberosity and this manouvre rotates the lesser tuberosity away from the body, stretching the tendon out as it does so.

Supraspinatus

There are two positions which can be used to see the supraspinatus tendon.

Forced internal rotation - Place the patients hand in the small of their back

Flex the elbow and direct the arm posteriorly by placing the patients hand on their ipsilateral back pocket

The supraspinatus attaches to the greater tuberosity and both these manoeuvers cause internal rotation to a greater or lesser extent whilst the posterior placement of the arm stretches the tendon out further.

Subacromial impingement test

As the supraspinatus passes between the acromion and coracoid processes it can experience impingement. By abducting the arm in internal rotation the supraspinatus muscle can be observed as it moves within this space.

Infraspinatus and teres minor

Place the patients hand anteriorly on their contralateral shoulder. This internally rotates the humerus and extends both infraspinatus and teres minor which sit below the spine of the scapula.

Both muscles can also be imaged in the same position as for the long head of biceps tendon.

stem: A 32-year-old man jumps into a pool head first and sustained neck pain but climbed out independently. He soon developed hemiplegia and was admitted to A&E and underwent a CT scan which showed low attenuation in the left basal ganglia.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The scenario describes traumatic carotid artery dissection (cervical segment) which should be considered for any sort of trauma, however minor (even a long telephone call) to the neck. In the scenario given the patient is well initially but goes on to suffer a cerebral infarction secondary to carotid artery dissection.  Of note in the question the patient is able to climb out of the pool immediately and independently which would be highly unlikely following a spinal cord injury. Similarly an embolic infarction presenting in this manner (highly unlikely but theoretically possible) would also present acutely at the time of the event. Traumatic cerebral contusion may well lead to delayed presentation with headache and confusion and post traumatic contusional injuries would be more likely to affect the temporal lobes (or other areas adjacent to bone) than the basal ganglia. A c-spine fracture is the reflex answer whenever swimming pools are involved in an exam setting but would not give rise to the imaging findings described.

stem: A 67-year-old overweight man presents with lower back pain. On examination he has weakness on his left side of hip extension and extension of his big toe. His GP thinks he may have a problem with an intervertebral disc.
prompt: At which level is this most likely to be?
explanation:
This is a straightforward anatomy question. In the cervical spine the nerve roots exit above their named vertebral body; thus at the level of C4/5 it is the C5 which will be exiting. This is unlike the lumbar spine where the nerve root exits below its named vertebral body and is explained by the presence of 8 cervical nerve roots with only 7 cervical vertebra.

There is also the concept of the exiting nerve root and the descending nerve root. This applies in particular to disc bulges/protrusions/extrusions and is more pertinent in the lumbar spine. The exiting nerve root at a given level will be one less than the descending nerve root. (ie at L2/3 the exiting nerve will be L2 and the descending nerve will be L3). Central disc pathology affects the descending nerve whereas paramedian or foraminal disc pathology may affect the exiting nerve.

stem: A 35-year-old runner complains of pain in the lateral aspect of his foot. Plain radiographs demonstrate a sclerotic band with periosteal reaction in his proximal 3rd metatarsal. The Emergency department doctor identifies this as a stress fracture. She reassures the patient that this has a low risk of complicated healing.
prompt: Which of the following stress fracture sites has a high risk of complicated fracture healing? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
The following stress fractures are at high risk of complicated healing:

Femoral neck

Transverse patellar fracture

Anterior tibial fracture

5th metatarsal

Talus

Navicular

Longitudinal fractures are at low risk of complicated healing. The calcaneus is the most frequently fractured tarsal bone, with stress fractures usually occurring perpendicular to the trabecular lines.

topic: Differentiating between an AVM and an AVF
stem: A 60-year-old man with progressive bilateral leg weakness presents to his GP. He is referred for an urgent MRI which shows multiple tortuous tubes with signal voids on the posterior aspect of the cauda equina on both T1 and T2. Subtle bumps along the surface of the cord are seen and the conus appears expanded with high signal on T2.
prompt: Which of the following will help differentiate between an AVM and an AVF?
options: The presence or absence of a clear nidus
Venous drainage in the arterial phase during angiography
explanation:
A nidus is the tangled knot of vessels at the centre of an AV malformation. A fistlous vessel is a single (can be tortuous) vessel which is an abnormal connection between arterial and venous flow (an AVF).

Subarachnoid haemorrhage is actually reasonably rare in AVF although it can happen. A history of trauma would point towards the lesion being an AVF and is therefore a potentially viable answer for this question too however on balance the presence or absence of a nidus is more definitive. Logically, although a history of trauma may be given and can be seen to be related in population demographic terms, this is less certain for individual cases whereas a nidus is an unequivocal finding.

stem: Concerning Erosive OA:
prompt: Which of the following would be a typical finding of joint involvement for Erosive OA?
explanation:
Erosive osteoarthritis

This is an inflammatory version of osteoarthritis with a strong female preponderance. The pattern of involvement is that of standard osteoarthritis (distal interphalangeal joints) but the features have an inflammatory component with prominent erosions, particularly of the middle of the distal end of the middle phalanges leading to a classical gull-wing appearance. As with osteoarthritis, osteophytes and subchondral cyst formation is also found.

stem: A 27-year-old woman presents to the emergency department after injuring her ankle during a rugby match. Radiographs demonstrate a vertical fracture through the medial malleolus with an associated avulsion fracture of the fibula.
prompt: What mechanism of injury is most likely to have resulted in this injury? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
The Lauge-Hansen classification is a lesser used, but highly useful classification for ankle fractures. It describes the mechanics of the injury in better detail than the Weber classification.

Supination-adduction

Fibula avulsion and vertical medial malleolus fracture.

Pronation-external rotation

Transverse medial malleolus fracture (or deltoid disruption) and spiral fibula fracture.

Supination-external rotation

Most common type of ankle fracture resulting in a low fibula fracture and usually no syndesmotic injury. In severe injuries can eventually result in medial malleolus fracture or deltoid injury.

Pronation-Abduction

Transverse medial malleolus fracture and high transverse fibula fracture.

stem: A 35-year-old female was found unconscious in her room following a house fire. She was admitted to the ICU where her neurological status improved. She was, however, noted to be in acute renal failure. Three days later she started complaining about muscular pain in the back and both lower limbs. Unenhanced thoracic CT showed asymmetric thickening of the left paravertebral musculature. MRI demonstrated STIR high signal intensity of the corresponding muscle groups with patchy heterogeneity within. She had complete recovery after 2 weeks.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Rhabdomyolysis

The diagnosis of rhabdomyolysis after carbon monoxide poisoning was suggested by the clinical history, deranged renal functions, imaging findings, and the typical distribution of the affected muscles.

Paraspinal musculature and lower extremities are the most frequently affected regions. Muscular swelling due to oedema is the most characteristic feature. In severe cases, muscle ischemia may develop leading to frank myonecrosis which demonstrated heterogeneous signal intensity keeping with necrotic areas.

Elevation of the Creatine Kinase (CK) serum level is the most sensitive parameter. Most characteristic complications include acute kidney failure, cardiac arrhythmias, and compartment syndrome.

Rhabdomyolysis is usually self-limiting and resolves within days to weeks with conservative treatment with an associated decrease in the CK serum level.

Pyomyositis

This is a pyogenic infection of the muscles, which is frequently preceded by a trauma that serves as the first source of infection. Early-stage muscular oedema and rhabdomyolysis may be indistinguishable. Nonetheless, isolated muscle involvement is more common in pyomyositis patients. Local pain and fever are more prominent, and the patient's clinical status will deteriorate unless appropriate antibiotic therapy is administered.

Necrotizing fasciitis

This is a rapidly progressing soft tissue infection that mostly spreads along the fascial planes. Patients typically have a history of penetrating trauma. Gas formation, fascial thickening, lack of enhancement, and rapid progression are the key features of this disease.

Inflammatory myopathy

Radiologic findings in early-stage rhabdomyolysis may be identical. However, depending on the underlying autoimmune illness, the affected muscle distribution and clinical symptoms will differ.

Diabetes induced myonecrosis

Clinical history is the key finding for differential diagnosis since this condition typically occurs in patients with a known history of poorly controlled diabetes, associated with other complications such as neuropathy, nephropathy, and retinopathy.

stem: A 94-year-old lady who underwent a wide local excision for the management of her breast cancer presents with back pain and undergoes an MRI scan. The T6 vertebra is fractured and collapsed.
prompt: Which of the following is would make a pathological fracture more likely than an osteoporotic one?
options: Bowing of the posterior cortex of the vertebral body
Fluid adjacent to the end plate
High T1 and isointense T2 signal of the bone marrow
explanation:
There are a number of features which can help differentiate between an osteoporotic vertebral collapse and a metastatic one.

Favours osteoporosis

Favours metastases

Retropulsed bony fragments

Convex posterior cortex

Fluid adjacent to the fractured end plates

Associated soft tissue masses

Multiple compression fractures

Other metastases without compression fractures

Sparing of the marrow signal

Marrow signal abnormalities

Involvement of the posterior elements of the spine

Bone marrow on MRI

Normal bone marrow

High (fatty)

Intermediate

Very high and homogenous

Intermediate (initially high due to oedema)

Haemangioma

High

High

Low but enhances with Gadolinium

High (fluid)

Low

Metastases

Normally metastatic deposits in the spine lead to low T1 signal and high T2 signal. There should be no signal drop out on fat saturated sequences in contrast to marrow reconversion where although red marrow will experience far less signal dropout than yellow marrow, there will still be some loss in signal owing to the fat content of both types of marrow.

Sclerotic or blastic metastases return little signal on either T1 or T2 weighted sequences. These include prostate, breast or TCC metastases among others.

Breast cancer can cause lytic or sclerotic metastases or a mixed picture.

Lytic metastases are more likely than sclerotic metastases to enhance with contrast. Similarly on DWI imaging, whereas lytic metastases will usually appear hyperintense, sclerotic metastases return little signal since they contain little water.

If there is a diffuse abnormality of the bone marrow it can be difficult to identify but normal bone marrow should not be lower in signal intensity than the muscle on T1 weighted sequences.

stem: A 52-year-old man complains of a painful lump in his left foot. He undergoes an MRI scan which shows a 32mm lesion which you suspect to be a Morton neuroma.
prompt: What are most likely signal characteristics of this lesion? Select ONE answer only.
options: High signal on T1, T2 and STIR
High signal on T1, low signal on T2 and STIR
Low signal on T1 and T2, high signal on STIR
Low signal on T1, T2 and STIR
Low signal on T1, high signal on T2 and STIR
explanation:
Morton neuroma

Fibrosis surrounding a plantar digital nerve leads to a hard lump developing in the sole of the foot. Patients complain of a painful lump which feels a bit like walking on a hot lump of gravel. On an MRI scan they are often slightly disguised by their low or isointensity to muscle on T1 weighted sequences and hypointensity on T2 weighted sequences. Curiously for a fibrotic process, they do usually enhance with gadolinium. On ultrasound the classic appearance of a hypoechoic mass situated between but slightly proximal to the metatarsal heads should be sufficient to make the diagnosis. Most are found in the third metatarsal space. The Mulder sign can be performed clinically or with ultrasound and involves eliciting pain and a clicking sound when the metatarsal heads are squeezed together while applying pressure on the dorsum of the foot over the neuroma, or scanning the sole of the foot.

It is said that Morton neuromas are larger and easier to visualise with MRI when the patient is prone, i.e. the foot is slightly plantar-flexed. On ultrasound this translates to a straightforward prone position or one where the patient is sitting on the side of the couch with their feet slightly plantar flexed. One theory is that any physical tension through the metatarsal joints (more likely on supine positioning) causes the neuroma to be pulled up in-between the metatarsal heads.

stem: A 24-year-old woman sustains a direct facial injury during a cricket match. She is brought to the Emergency Department with extensive facial and orbital injuries and undergoes a CT scan for further evaluation.
prompt: Which of the following is most specific for a globe rupture? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Globe rupture

This injury obviously has the propensity to cause significant long-term morbidity to the patient. Straightforward cases, as seen on a trauma CT, will show significant morphological change to the normal shape of the globe with a large overall reduction in globe volume. In the case of a penetrating mechanism of injury, the presence of a foreign body within the posterior chamber is also diagnostic of a globe rupture. Similarly, the presence of intra-ocular gas also implies a globe rupture.

A more subtle sign of globe rupture paradoxically includes an increase to the depth of the anterior chamber due to posterior displacement of the lens occurring in the context of a posterior segment rupture and subsequent loss of pressure there.

A coloboma is a focal defect in the posterior aspect of the globe with outpouching which can be quite striking in size. This is a congenital defect though, not a post-traumatic one. The finding can be unilateral or bilateral with the latter more suggestive of a syndromic association.

A staphyloma is a broader based defect in the globe, which can be located anywhere. It occurs due to degenerative thinning of the sclera and is seen as a smooth contour irregularity on cross-sectional imaging.

stem: A 56-year-old woman sustains a neck injury during a road traffic incident. On arrival at the hospital she complains of neck pain and undergoes cervical spine x-rays.
prompt: On the lateral cervical XR which of the following could be abnormal? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
The atlantodental interval is measured from the posterior aspect of the anterior arch of C1 to the anterior aspect of the dens.

Normal in adults is <3mm

Normal in children is <5mm

The gap increases due to anterior translocation of the atlas. This often simultaneously causes the posterior arch of C1 to become anterior displaced with respect to the spinolaminar line.

There are a number of non-traumatic causes of an increased atlantodental interval.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

The prevertebral space is also important to appreciate on the lateral cervical spine view. Enlargement of the prevertebral soft tissue is a secondary sign of a bony injury. Normal measurements are given below.

<7mm at C2

<5mm at C3+4

<22mm at C6 (14mm in children)

Between C4 and C5 there can be some variation if the x-ray is taken during different phases of swallowing.

stem: A 50-year-old man falls playing football and injures his left knee. He is brought to the Emergency Department by his friends and an X-ray is performed. The x-ray shows a patella fracture but also widening of the intercondylar notch.
prompt: What is the LEAST likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Please note that the question asks for the LEAST likely diagnosis.

Widening of the intercondylar notch is a specific sign which has a relatively narrow differential diagnosis.

JIA/RA

Psoriatic arthropathy

Haemophilia

TB

SAPHO (Synovitis, acne, palmoplantar pustulosis, hyperostosis, osteitis)

This disease is thought to be a variant of psoriatic arthropathy. The cutaneous manifestations may not be apparent at diagnosis (like psoriatic arthropathy) but hyperostosis and osteolysis and ankylosis of the sternoclavicular joint is absolutely typical. On a nuclear medicine bone scan, bilateral uptake in the sternoclavicular joints and manubrium is called a ‘bull’s head’ sign. About a third of patients also have spinal disease with paravertebral ossifications and osteosclerosis. Unilateral sacroiliitis may also occur. Appearances can be quite striking on CT. In the knees, ankles and small joints of the hands there may be inflammation of the joints with juxta-articular osteoporosis.

stem: A 32-year-old Jewish man receives a chest radiograph for insurance purposes. The x-ray is performed by a trainee radiographer and the field of view is left too large. There is a serpiginous area of calcification within the left humeral head and the splenic outline is abnormal. Splenomegaly is confirmed on subsequent clinical examination.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Gaucher disease

This lysosomal storage disease is usually inherited in an autosomal recessive fashion and is around 100 times more common in Ashkenazi Jews than it is in the rest of the population. There is accumulation of glycolipid in macrophage lysosomes. The infantile form is universally lethal before 24 months of age but the adult form may be asymptomatic at diagnosis and is typically diagnosed in young adulthood if not earlier. Hepatosplenomegaly is common and co-existent with thrombocytopaenia and anaemia secondary to bone marrow failure. Osteonecrosis occurs in the femoral or humeral heads leaving serpiginous sclerotic areas or a bone-within-bone appearance. Modelling deformities such as the Erlenmeyer flask deformity (Flared metaphysis + diaphyseal thinning) also occur and are considered characteristic.

Differential diagnosis for the Erlenmeyer flask deformity

Marrow infiltration

Gaucher disease

Thalassaemia

Sickle Cell disease

Dysplasia

Fibrous dysplasia

Osteopetrosis

Achondroplasia

Ollier disease

Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI)

A defect on either chromosome 7 or 17 leads to abnormal type 1 collagen. Most cases are inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion. An adult with OI is most likely to have either type I or type IV. On imaging there is diffuse undermineralisation of the skeleton and (sometimes extreme) cortical thinning. Once a child with OP has become mobile the soft bones become bowed under the weight of the body. The pressure of the femoral heads on the soft acetabulae leads to acetabular protrusion. Basilar invagination results from pressure of the cervical spine on the base of the skull. Insufficiency fracture of the vertebral bodies lead to a biconcave appearance. OI is a differential diagnosis for multiple wormian bones which persist to adulthood.

Type

Inheritance

Clinical features

I

AD

Most common form. Normal life expectancy. Presents aged 2-6. Blue sclera, joint laxity, deafness.

II

Often stillborn or perinatal death due to pulmonary hypoplasia.

III

Progressively deforming, fractures at birth in most cases.

IV

Variable severity. Usually shorter in statue, by adulthood, than normal. Normal colour sclera. Usually normal hearing.

These are a constellation of lysosomal storage disorders which, with the exception of Hunter syndrome (X-linked) are inherited in an autosomal recessive fashion. Mental retardation is common (except in Morquio syndrome). Short, thick fingers with pointing at the proximal end of the metacarpals is classical. Hypoplastic lumbar vertebra is also common, in some cases this extends to vertebra plana, in others there is characteristic ‘beaking’ either of the inferior end plate or centrally.

stem: A 55-year-old man complains to his GP of pain in both wrists. On examination his GP notices a salmon-pink patch of skin on his forearm. There is some silver coloured scale overlying the patch. Bilateral x-rays of the wrist are requested which show soft tissue swelling to the second and third digits with marginal erosions and periosteal new bone formation. You suspect he may have psoriatic arthropathy.
prompt: Which of the following regarding this condition is correct? Select ONE answer only.
options: Affects around 10% of patients with psoriasis
The presence of the rash is essential for diagnosis
explanation:
Psoriatic arthropathy

Around a fifth of patients with psoriasis develop arthropathy and it is also possible to suffer from psoriatic arthropathy in the absence of the typical psoriatic cutaneous plaques.

Importantly, on x-ray there are findings of both erosive changes in addition to productive changes with periosteal new bone formation. The combination of the two contrives to leave a ‘pencil-in-cup’ appearance. The joints can appear fluffy due to the exuberance of new bone formation.

The differential diagnosis for periosteal reactions in the presence of an arthropathy is relatively narrow and very specific:

Psoriatic arthropathy

Juvenile rheumatoid arthritis

Reiter syndrome

Infective arthritis

Although often classified as a distal arthropathy, preferring the DIPs to the MCPs, psoriatic arthropathy does also affect the spine and SI joints frequently. ‘Sausage digits’ is a term used to describe the diffuse soft tissue swelling which can affect the fingers and toes. Osteoporosis does occur but is a feature of later disease.

>65yrs

stem: Which of the following most accurately describes a Tarlov cyst?
prompt: Select one answer only.
options: Ballooning of the dural sac resulting in posterior vertebral scalloping and herniation into the nerve root sleeves
Hyperdense on CT causing vertebral body scalloping, dumbbell widening of the neural exit foramina
Neural tube defect with protrusion of membranes through bony defect in vertebral column
Simple cystic structure closely related to the exiting S2 nerve root. Widened sacral foramina with bony scalloping
Uncomplicated cystic formation connected to the facet joint containing synovial fluid
explanation:
A Tarlov cyst

A tarlov cyst is the name given to dilatation of the posterior nerve root sheath. They follow CSF on all sequences and can cause significant bony scalloping.

A synovial cyst – ‘Uncomplicated cystic formation connected to the facet joint containing synovial fluid’

Synovial cysts relate to the joint rather than the nerve. They tend to be seen in cases where the facet joints are already degenerate.

Dural ectasia – ‘Ballooning of the dural sac resulting in posterior vertebral scalloping and herniation into the nerve root sleeves’

This is an interesting alternative diagnosis however usually occurs over more than one vertebral level. It can be associated with tarlov cysts.

Nerve sheath tumour – ‘Hyperdense on CT causing vertebral body scalloping, dumbbell widening of the neural exit foramina’.  For example: a schwannoma.

Meningocoele – ‘Neural tube defect with protrusion of membranes through bony defect in vertebral column’

stem: You are reviewing the x-ray of a 38-year-old man's lumbar spine. There are concavities to the anterior surface of the vertebral bodies affecting L3 and L4.
prompt: Which of the following is NOT a likely cause of this finding? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Please note that the question asks which answer is NOT a cause.

Anterior vertebral scalloping

There are a number of specific differential diagnoses which can lead to this finding. In each case the image should be interrogated carefully to look for further clues as to the underlying diagnosis. Scalloping is a chronic process whereby mechanical pressure on the bone causes remodelling.

stem: Concerning Pseudogout:
prompt: Which of the following would be a typical finding of joint involvement for Pseudogout?
explanation:
Calcium pyrophosphate dehydrate disease (CPPD) also known as pseudogout

CPPD can present in an acute or subacute fashion but is also seen as a chronic cause of joint inflammation. It may be misdiagnosed as simple osteoarthritis owing to its often bilateral and symmetrical distribution but there are also a couple of areas of the body which can be affected in particular, and which would be unusual for isolated degenerative changes.

The patellofemoral joint – joint space loss here can be extremely striking with almost complete preservation of the joint space at the medial and lateral compartments of the knee

Triangular fibrocartilaginous complex of the wrist – calcification

Radiocarpal joint – degenerative changes without involvement of the DIPs and PIPs

stem: A 65 -year-old man with a history of chronic arthritis presented with a recent fall. His routine blood investigations were unremarkable with normal renal function. Axial CT image at the level of the atlantoaxial joint demonstrated multiple bony erosions and periarticular cloud like soft tissue high-density areas. Sagittal CT demonstrated punched out overhanging margins with normal alignment at the atlantoaxial joint, unremarkable facet joints and disc spaces.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Gout

This crystal arthropathy presents as juxta-articular well-defined erosions with overhanging edges mainly involving the lumbar spine followed by cervical and thoracic. Tophi are seen as soft tissue nodules with associated calcification. Joint space is preserved early in the disease with no associated osteopenia. Spine involvement in gout is rare and is almost always seen in the presence of peripheral joint involvement.

Amyloid arthropathy

Amyloid arthropathy of the spine occurs due to extracellular deposition of amyloid. It is frequently seen in patients with chronic renal failure on dialysis and rarely in patients with primary amyloidosis. It may show aggressive osteolytic vertebral bony destruction with soft tissue involvement that could be seen as dense soft tissue deposits. It predominately involves the thoracic spine followed by the cervical spine. In the vignette above, the patient did not have a history of renal failure.

Vertebral osteomyelitis

Vertebral osteomyelitis is common in IV drug users and HIV patients. Vertebral osteomyelitis is best seen on MRI with inflammatory oedema starting at the disc followed by end plates involvement with enhancement after gadolinium administration. CT is less sensitive in osteomyelitis; however, it has an advantage in assessing cortical bone abnormalities and detecting pathological calcification. In the vignette above, the bony changes are limited to the atlantoaxial joint with no involvement of the discs and endplates. Also, the patient did not present with a clinical history suggestive of osteomyelitis.

Degenerative joint disease

Cervical spine degenerative osteoarthritis is extremely common in the elderly population over the age of 55. It manifests as disc space narrowing, osteophyte formation, spondylolytic ridging, uncovertebral spurring, and facet joint arthropathy. In this case, the arthritic changes did not result in disc space narrowing or facet arthropathy commonly seen in degenerative osteoarthritis.

Rheumatoid Arthritis

Rheumatoid arthritis is an inflammatory arthritis with chronic synovitis resulting in osseous erosions, pannus formation, periarticular osteopenia, ligament laxity, and instability. When it affects the spine, it is most commonly at the atlantoaxial region. Frequently, this results in anterior atlantoaxial subluxation or less commonly in a lateral or posterior atlantoaxial subluxation. Another less common finding is superior migration of the odontoid peg. In this case, there was no subluxation of the atlantoaxial joint.

stem: A 42-year-old builder presents with pain and instability in his wrist. He recalls falling awkwardly whilst carrying heavy materials at work several years ago, since when his wrist has never been the same. Plain radiographs demonstrated  no fractures at that time. New films now show there is a widened scapholunate distance with a scapholunate angle of 20 degrees.
prompt: What is the best description of this abnormality? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Volar Intercalated Segment Instability (VISI)

This occurs in the setting of carpal instability when there is narrowing of the scapholunate angle to less than 30 degrees. Scapholunate widening is also found in VISI.

Scaphoid Non-Union Advanced collapse (SNAC)

This occurs following a scaphoid fracture. It is similar to SLAC but there is a normal scapholunate distance, with a scaphoid fracture. Like SLAC, there is radioscaphoid degenerative change, followed by proximal migration of the capitate and eventually dorsal intercalated instability.

Scaphoid-lunate advanced collapse (SLAC)

This occurs following injury to the scapholunate ligament or secondary to CPPD. It is similar to SNAC but there is scapholunate widening, rather than a scaphoid fracture. Radioscaphoid degenerative changes are an early feature, followed by proximal migration of the capitate and eventually dorsal intercalated instability.

Avascular necrosis (AVN) of the scaphoid

This is usually secondary to a proximal fracture. The most reliable sign is low T1 signal in the scaphoid.

Midcarpal dislocation

This occurs in association with triquetral fracture and is very similar to lunate dislocation.

stem: A 40-year-old woman presents with an uncomfortable swelling at the back of her right knee. On examination you palpate a round, smooth, fluctuant mass within the popliteal fossa. An ultrasound scan confirms that she has a Baker's cyst.
prompt: Which of the following is the most medial structure contained within the popliteal fossa? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
The popliteal fossa is a diamond shaped depression situated at the back of the knee joint. It acts as the main conduit for the neurovascular structures entering and leaving the leg.

The borders of the popliteal fossa are:

Superomedial border: semimembranosus

Superolateral border: biceps femoris

Inferomedial border: medial head of gastrocnemius

Inferolateral border: lateral head of gastrocnemius and plantaris

The roof of the popliteal fossa is formed by (from superficial to deep):

Skin

Superficial fascia

Deep (popliteal) fascia

The floor of the popliteal fossa is formed by:

Popliteal surface of the femur

Capsule of the knee joint

Fascia covering the popliteus muscle

The contents of the popliteal fossa (from medial to lateral) are:

Popliteal artery

Popliteal vein

Tibial nerve

Common peroneal nerve

The tibial and common peroneal nerves are the most superficial of the contents of the popliteal fossa. The deepest structure is the popliteal artery. The small saphenous vein pierces the deep fascia to enter the popliteal fossa. The popliteal lymph nodes surround the vessels.

The popliteal fossa and its contents, with the popliteal lymph nodes in blue (from Gray’s Anatomy)

stem: A 56-year-old office clerk presents with pains in both knees. There is no history of trauma. X-rays show bilateral sclerotic foci on both sides of the knee joint. On direct questioning he has also noticed symptoms of polyuria and polydipsia in the last few months.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Erdheim-Chester disease

Infiltration of the appendicular skeleton by histiocytes leads to fibrosis and sclerosis which can appear striking on an x-ray. The condition is very similar to Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis (LCH) and both conditions have been reported across a broad range of patient ages. Usually however LCH presents at around the age of 5-10 whereas ECD peaks in incidence at around 55 years of age. Both diseases are caused by clonal proliferations of one or more lines of histiocytes and there are different cellular markers which can help distinguish between the two diseases pathologically. There is considerable overlap in the clinical and radiological features of both diseases.

Clinically patients with ECD present with all or any of the usual histiocytosis triad of diabetes insipidus, exophthalmos and bone pain. Of these, the most prominent feature is usually bony pain.

X-rays show sclerosis in the metadiaphyseal regions in a bilateral symmetrical pattern but with sparing of the epiphyses. Corticomedullary differentiation becomes blurred and there are also multiple areas of lucency indicating the presence of lytic lesions too.

Mastocytosis

This disease is also caused by clonal proliferation of a particular cell type however in this case it is of mast cells. Clinically patients may experience symptoms linked to histamine release from the mast cells such as flushing, sweating, diarrhoea and abdominal pains but only around a quarter of patients complain of bony pains. The skeleton can be affected by either focal lesions (usually in the spine) or with diffusely increased density. Other features such as hepatosplenomegaly, and lymph node enlargement (retroperitoneal, mesenteric, periportal) may be present too.

Metastases

Sclerotic metastases are typical with prostate and breast cancers among others. This should always be considered as a pertinent differential diagnosis however there are not other features in this question to suggest it is correct in this case.

Sclerotic metastases:

Prostate (most common)

Breast (mixed lytic and sclerotic)

Transitional Cell Carcinoma

Lymphoma

Mucinous adenocarcinomas (colon, gastric, ovary)

Medulloblastoma

Neuroblastoma

Carcinoid

Paget disease

Paget disease is seldom found in patients below the age of 50 but is one of the more common musculoskeletal abnormalities thereafter. It consists of polyostotic, asymmetric disordered bone remodelling where intensive osteoclastic activity leads to multiple lytic lesions before osteoblastic activity results in the formation of sclerotic bone. A variety of imaging findings can be seen with x-ray.

Lytic phase: During the lytic phase, radiolucency with a ‘flame’ or ‘blade of grass’ shape extends along the diaphysis and osteoporosis circumscripta (large lucent areas of skull) can be found in the skull.

Mixed phase: lytic and sclerotic phenomena

Sclerotic phase: densely sclerotic bone such as the classical ‘ivory vertebra’ can be found.

Clinically it can be an incidental asymptomatic diagnosis or can present as all or any of:

Elevated ALP with a normal calcium and phosphate

A pathological fracture – although it may be sclerotic, the bone structure is disordered and therefore weaker than normal bone.

Cranial nerve palsies – due to compression at neural foramina

Enlarging head / hat size – due to widening of the diploic spaces (referred to as the Tam O’Shanter sign, whereby the skull takes on the appearance of a the Scottish hat called the Tam O’Shanter)

High output cardiac failure – this is a rare presentation caused by markedly increased bony perfusion

Pain – in the absence of a fracture, it is usually not a painful condition per se but can co-exist with other conditions such as osteoarthritis which may be the cause of the patient’s pain

Radiologically the hallmarks are bony expansion with coarsening of the trabeculae and cortices. On a bone scan active lesions will show increased uptake due to their increased blood flow.

Sarcomatous degeneration of the affected sites into either an osteosarcoma, malignant fibrous histiocytoma or chondrosarcoma carries a poor prognosis and careful study should be made of any known lesions at each imaging opportunity. New soft tissue component formation or new lysis of previously sclerotic bone should raise suspicion.
