stem: You are reviewing the images of a patient with sacroiliitis known to have an inflammatory arthritis.
prompt: Which of the following is NOT a differential diagnosis for sacroiliitis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Please note that the question asks which answer is NOT a differential diagnosis.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

Psoriatic arthropathy

Around a fifth of patients with psoriasis develop arthropathy and it is also possible to suffer from psoriatic arthropathy in the absence of the typical psoriatic cutaneous plaques. Around 80% of patients are HLA-B27 positive.

Importantly, on x-ray there are findings of both erosive changes in addition to productive changes with periosteal new bone formation. The combination of the two contrives to leave a ‘pencil-in-cup’ appearance. The joints can appear fluffy due to the exuberance of new bone formation.

The differential diagnosis for periosteal reactions in the presence of an arthropathy is relatively narrow and very specific:

Psoriatic arthropathy

Juvenile rheumatoid arthritis

Reiter syndrome

Infective arthropathy

Although often classified as a distal arthropathy, preferring the DIPs to the MCPs, psoriatic arthropathy does also affect the spine and SI joints frequently. ‘Sausage digits’ is a term used to describe the diffuse soft tissue swelling which can affect the fingers and toes. Osteoporosis does occur but is a feature of later disease.

Seronegative arthritides - These are negative for Rheumatoid factor but have a strong association with HLA-B27 positivity.

Ankylosing spondylitis - 95%

Enteropathic arthropathy - 90%

Psoriatic arthritis - 80%

Chronic reactive arthritis - 70%

Ankylosing spondylitis

This disease usually presents in early adulthood with gradual onset of back pain. There is a male preponderance, though it can affect women too. The vast majority (>90%) of patients are HLA-B27 positive. Radiologically the late features are classical with:

Bilateral symmetrical sacroiliitis

Enthesopathy - calcified tendon insertion sites

Bamboo spine - vertebral syndesmophytes, particularly in the thoracolumbar spine

Dagger sign - spinous process fusion

Erosion, then fusion at the symphysis pubis, costochondral, costovertebral and sternoclavicular joints

Thoracic manifestations: upper lobe pulmonary fibrosis, pericarditis, aortic root dilatation

Early features are far more subtle and require a higher index of suspicion.

Enthesopathy - high signal on MRI at tendon insertion sites

Romanus lesions - triangular shaped oedema at the corners of vertebral bodies

Andersson lesions - bony oedema in the vertebral bodies adjacent to the disks.

Oedema in the sacroiliac joints.

Patients with advanced ankylosing spondylitis are at increased risk of pathological fractures due to fusion. These can be pelvic fractures following a simple fall, or chance fractures of the spine (involving all three columns - in ankylosing spondylitis, these fractures are also sometimes termed chalk-stick or carrot fractures).

Chronic reactive arthritis

This disease is said to present as a triad of arthritis, conjunctivitis/uveitis and urethritis/cervicitis (Can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree) however in reality only around a third of patients present with all three symptoms. Patients are usually aged 16-60 years. It has a reasonably strong male predominance but does occur in women. It can occur following infection with chlamydia, but also with gastrointestinal infections such as salmonella, shigella, campylobacter and yersinia. Most (>2/3rds) of patients are HLA-B27 positive.

Bilateral asymmetrical sacroiliitis

Paravertebral ossification - similar to syndesmophytes but in theory are seen separately from the disc, bridging around it. Most commonly in the thoracolumbar spine.

Enthesopathy - particularly at achilles tendon insertion, interspinous ligaments, and pelvic ligaments.

Enteropathic arthropathy

This occurs in a subsect of patients with inflammatory or infective bowel disease. Roughly 10-20% of patients with Crohn’s or ulcerative colitis suffer from enteropathic arthropathy. Like chronic reactive arthropathy, it can also occur in the context of salmonella, shigella and yersinia infections. Appearances are very similar to those of ankylosing spondylitis; the two can be very difficult to separate radiologically.

Bilateral symmetrical sacroillitis

Enthesopathy

Vertebral syndesmophytes

Fusion of spinous processes

Juvenile idiopathic arthritis

This condition used to be termed juvenile rheumatoid arthritis. It is a cluster of similar conditions affecting patients under the age of 16.

The affected joints show:

Effusions

Erosions

Cartilage destruction

Epiphyseal overgrowth secondary to reactive hyperaemia occurs owing to the immature nature of the skeleton. Premature physeal closure can result in limb length discrepancies in adulthood.

Large joints are typically affected first and the small joints of the hands and feet are affected later on.

stem: You are reporting an x-ray of a 35-year-old man which shows a lucent lesion in the tibia. It is metaphyseal but extends into the epiphysis and is eccentrically placed within the bone. There is some expansion but no periosteal reaction.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Giant Cell Tumour also known as osteoclastoma

These are benign bony tumours arising from within bone. They can cause bony expansion from within but not bony scalloping from without. Since they always occur in the mature skeleton they are seldom found in children or adolescent patients although the peak age group is still young; 30s. Typically they occur around the knee but can be found anywhere in the skeleton. They are seen on x-ray as expansile lytic lesions with the words ‘soap bubble’ often used to describe them in literature. On MRI they usually return low signal on both T1 and T2, in contrast to many of the potential differential diagnoses which would otherwise return high signal on one or the other.

Four criteria of GCT (according to Clyde A. Helms)

After epiphyseal closure

Abuts articular surface

Well defined, non-sclerotic margin

Eccentric location

Intraosseous lipoma

These benign lesions can present with pain but around a third of cases are diagnosed incidentally. The classic location for them is the calcaneum but they do occur all around the body. On x-ray they appear as a lucent bone lesion with a thin cortex and no periosteal reaction. Some show dystrophic calcifications. On MRI signal characteristics follow fat with high signal on T1 and signal loss on fat suppression sequences. The presence of granulation tissue can give high signal and calcifications, if present, will return low signal. On CT the fat within the lesion will show low/negative Hounsfield units.

Image sourced from WikipediaCourtesy of Hellerhoff CC BY-SA 3.0

Enchondroma

As the name suggests, this is a cartilage forming tumour showing ground-glass matrix and ring or arc calcifications (as with all cartilage forming tumours). Patients are typically young (10-30 years) and the lesions are typically found in the hands (although they can form anywhere in the body. In the hands they are unusual to be found in the terminal phalanges). They are thought to derive from ongoing growth of small foci of cartilage which have become displaced from the growth plate. They can expand the cortex but, unless presenting as a fracture, should be painless and therefore are often an incidental diagnosis. Although they are benign tumours, malignant degeneration to a chondrosarcoma can occur.

Title - an Enchondroma with a pathological fracture

Image sourced from WikipediaCourtesy of Hellerhoff CC BY-SA 3.0

Malignant fibrous histiocytoma (MFH) - this is now known as undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma

A soft-tissue MFH is the most common subtype of MFHs and the most common malignant primary soft tissue tumour in the over 50s age bracket. It usually presents as a painless soft tissue mass which enlarges over a matter of months. They can be large at the time of diagnosis measuring tens of centimetres. On x-ray they appear as a partly calcified soft tissue mass. Cortical erosion of the underlying bone is an important diagnostic feature.

Osteoid osteoma

These are small benign tumours but which can be quite symptomatic, classically with pain relieved by aspirin. The majority form in the diaphyses of long bones but the posterior elements of the spine is another classic location.

The radiolucent nidus and symptoms of night pain in a young patient point to either an osteoid osteoma or an osteoblastoma. The final diagnosis comes down to size: <1.5 cm is definitely an osteoid osteoma, and >2 cm is definitely an osteoblastoma. There is a nasty grey area somewhere between the two sizes.

On x-ray the radiolucent nidus may not be fully appreciated, and the abnormality which is picked up will be the consequential sclerotic solid periosteal reaction. In the spine there may be a painful scoliosis concave towards the lesion as a result of adjacent muscular spasm. CT is used to confirm the diagnosis as the nidus is readily appreciable.

Image sourced from WikipediaCourtesy of Hellerhoff CC BY-SA 3.0

stem: A 25-year-old man complains of worsening night pain to his GP. He undergoes lumbar spine xrays on which a sclerotic abnormality is picked up for which he has a CT scan. There is a 1cm lesion in posterior element L2 which, on close inspection, reveals a radiolucent nidus.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The radiolucent nidus and symptoms of night pain in a young patient point to either an osteoid osteoma or an osteoblastoma. The final diagnosis comes down to size. <1.5cm is definitely an osteoid osteoma, and >2cm is definitely an osteoblastoma. There is a nasty grey area somewhere between the two sizes. The posterior elements of the spine are a classic location for osteoid osteomas.

Aneurysmal bone cysts – these are non-aggressive lesions demonstrating cystic ‘soap-bubble’ expansion. They can be primary lesions or secondary to GCTs, osteoblastomas, chondroblastomas and many others. On MRI fluid-fluid levels can be seen.

Paget disease – coarse trabeculae with cortical thickening are the radiographic features classically described in Paget disease. It is a disease of abnormal bony remodelling. Despite the impressive coarseness and thickening the bone is abnormal bone and therefore fragile, conferring a fracture risk under normal stressors It would be an unusual finding in a patient of this age.

Langerhans cell histiocytosis – There are a number of skeletal entities typically associated with LCH, in particular with the more benign version, eosinophilic granuloma. These include vertebra plana, and punched out lytic skull lesions.

stem: A 22-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of lower back pain. She has also noticed pain in her left sternoclavicular joint. She undergoes x-rays of her shoulder which shows that the joint space is well preserved but there is bony expansion and ankylosis. A subsequent MRI scan is reported as showing new bone formation with oedema and synovitis at the sternoclavicular joint. There is no discernible collection. She goes on to have a nuclear medicine scan which shows uptake in both sternoclavicular joints. Old x-rays of her pelvis show left sided sclerosis of the sacroiliac joint.
prompt: Which of the following is NOT typical for SAPHO? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Please note the question asks which of the answers is NOT a feature of SAPHO.

Salmon-pink cutaneous patches with a silver scale is the classic description for psoriasis. Although the two conditions are thought to be related, the cutaneous manifestations of SAPHO (if present) are acne and pustulosis.

SAPHO (Synovitis, acne, palmoplantar pustulosis, hyperostosis, osteitis)

This disease is thought to be a variant of psoriatic arthropathy. The cutaneous manifestations may not be apparent at diagnosis (like psoriatic arthropathy) but hyperostosis and osteolysis and ankylosis of the sternoclavicular joint is absolutely typical. On a nuclear medicine bone scan, bilateral uptake in the sternoclavicular joints and manubrium is called a ‘bull’s head’ sign. About a third of patients also have spinal disease with paravertebral ossifications and osteosclerosis. Unilateral sacroiliitis may also occur. Appearances can be quite striking on CT. In the knees, ankles and small joints of the hands there may be inflammation of the joints with juxta-articular osteoporosis.

stem: Pseudogout
prompt: Which of the following would be a typical finding of joint involvement for pseudogout? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Calcium pyrophosphate dehydrate disease (CPPD) also known as pseudogout

CPPD can present in an acute or subacute fashion but is also seen as a chronic cause of joint inflammation. It may be misdiagnosed as simple osteoarthritis owing to its often bilateral and symmetrical distribution but there are also a couple of areas of the body which can be affected in particular, and which would be unusual for isolated degenerative changes.

The patellofemoral joint – joint space loss here can be extremely striking with almost complete preservation of the joint space at the medial and lateral compartments of the knee

Triangular fibrocartilaginous complex of the wrist – calcification

Radiocarpal joint – degenerative changes without involvement of the DIPs and PIPs

stem: A 16-year-old undergoes an x-ray of his right knee which shows a small effusion despite a normal joint space. The intercondylar notch is widened. He goes on to have an MRI. On the MRI there is nodular thickening of the synovium in the suprapatellar space which returns low signal on both T1 and T2 weighted sequences.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Haemophilic arthropathy

The larger joints are most at risk for this disease, and the knee is particularly classical. On an x-ray there may only be a joint effusion in early disease but erosions and subchondral cysts develop. In particular there may be widening of the intercondylar notch (for which there is a differential diagnosis of: JIA/RA, Psoriatic arthropathy, TB and haemophilia) due to pannus formation. Also classical is epiphyseal overgrowth secondary to hyperaemia.

On an MRI there may well be nodular deposits on the synovium however the presence of blood degradation products renders these very low in signal on all sequences with blooming artefact present on gradient echo sequences or similar. If a haemarthrosis is present, the signal of the fluid will change depending on the chronicity of the event.

A haemophilic pseudotumour occurs in around 1-2% of patients with haemophilia. The presence of blood degradation products leads to a wide variety of intralesional signal patterns. The lesions are usually surrounded by a low signal haemosiderin rim though. Lesions can arise within bone (intra-osseous) or in soft tissues (usually muscular). Growth and pressure effects on adjacent bone can cause scalloping.

PVNS - Pigmented villonodular synovitis

The classic joint to be affected by PVNS is the knee but it can also occur at other large joints. Usually only one joint is affected in each patient. On x-ray the only sign may be a large joint effusion. Large subchondral cysts can also be seen. On MRI however, the appearances are characteristic. Haemorrhagic proliferation of the synovium in a frond-like fashion gives rise to the classic low signal 'feathery' sea-anemone-like finding. On susceptibility weighted sequences there is blooming artefact owing to the presence of haemosiderin. Patients are usually middle-aged and treatment is with synovectomy although there is a high rate of recurrence.

If the patient is male, the usual differential diagnosis for PVNS is of haemophilic arthropathy owing to the presence of blood products there too. PVNS appears as a differential diagnosis for subarticular lucent bone lesions due to the formation of large subchondral cysts.

Lipoma arborescens

This condition can affect children or adults and is thought to be a reaction to chronic inflammation of the synovium leading to extensive fatty infiltration of the synovium. It is almost always the knee which is affected. Plain radiographs will show only an effusion, which may be large, but on MRI there is frond-like or nodular synovial proliferation which returns fat-signal according to the different sequences used. The signal should be high on T1 and T2 but suppress on fat-saturated sequences. Post-contrast the synovium itself will enhance. Treatment is by synovectomy.

Rheumatoid arthritis

A joint effusion and synovial thickening (which would avidly enhance post-contrast) is a worthy description for rheumatoid arthritis however the high-fatty signal of the synovium is not a feature of rheumatoid arthritis. As the condition develops, patients with rheumatoid arthritis exhibit erosive changes with cartilage loss, bony erosions and marrow oedema.

stem: You review an MRI scan of a 50-year-old patient with carpal tunnel syndrome.
prompt: Which of the following tendons passes through the carpal tunnel? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
The carpal tunnel contains a total of nine flexor tendons (but not the muscles themselves), surrounded by a synovial sheath, and the median nerve. The tendons contained within the carpal tunnel are:

Flexor digitorum profundus (four tendons)

Flexor digitorum superficialis (four tendons)

Flexor pollicis longus (one tendon)

The eight tendons of the flexor digitorum profundus and superficialis are surrounded by a single synovial sheath, whereas the tendon of flexor pollicis longus is surrounded by its own synovial sheath. These sheaths allow free movement of the tendons.

The tendon of flexor carpi radialis does not pass through the carpal tunnel, but is instead located within the flexor retinaculum itself.

stem: A 43-year-old woman is seen in A+E after falling on her outstretched hand. The lateral wrist radiograph clearly shows a bony fragment at the dorsum of the hand.
prompt: A fracture of which bone is most likely? Select ONE answer only.
explanation: A bony fragment at the dorsum of the wrist is likely to be either from the triquetrum or the hamate. Triquetrum is not provided as a potential choice in this question, so the correct answer has to be hamate. On a radiograph, hamate will lie more superiorly and is far less common than a triquetrum fracture. Of the carpal bones, the scaphoid is most frequently fractured, followed by the triquetrum.

stem: An 85-year-old man undergoes a total hip replacement. Two years later he is found to have an aseptic lymphocyte-dominated vasculitis associated lesion (ALVAL).
prompt: With which kind of prosthesis is this condition associated?
explanation:
Aseptic lymphocyte-dominated vasculitis associated lesion (ALVAL)

This is a relatively new phenomenon which has been found to result from metal on metal implants. As a consequence of this discovery, the use of such implants has been curtailed to specific circumstances. The condition arises when nanoparticles of the metal are created within the joint by the two surfaces rubbing against one another. The nanoparticles are ingested by macrophages but are toxic to them. The appearance on an MRI is akin to a sterile inflammatory lesion, also referred to as a pseudotumour. Most commonly these appear in a posterior location to the joint.

stem: A 43-year-old man weight lifter presents with unilateral calf pain. When this fails to resolve with simple analgesia blood tests are taken which show an elevated creatinine kinase. He undergoes an MRI scan. The MRI shows enlargement of the calf muscles with high T2 signal. The muscle fibres and architecture is preserved.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The preservation of the muscular fibres and architecture helps confirm this diagnosis.

Hypertrophy related to exercise should be bilateral and approximately symmetrical.

The elevation of the creatinine kinase simply confirms that there is an acute muscular process going on where muscle cells are being damaged, thereby releasing their creatinine kinase into the blood.

There are a number of causes of myositis and further information would have to be provided to progress the diagnosis. One of the roles of MRI in cases where more than one muscle is involved, is to indicate the best muscle group to biopsy for diagnosis. Those with active inflammation, including enhancement post-contrast, are most likely to yield diagnostic tissue.

stem: A 43-year-old man presents with pain and instability in his wrist. Radiographs demonstrate disruption to the arcs of Gilula. The orthopaedic surgeon reviewing the images recognises this as a midcarpal dislocation.
prompt: Injury to which ligament is most likely to have resulted in this pathology? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
The carpal arcs or Gilula arcs are lines drawn on DP view of the wrist to demonstrate the normal alignment of the carpal bones.

Lunotriquetral

Injury to this ligament causes midcarpal dislocation (similar to lunate dislocation and also associated with triquetral fractures).

Injury to this ligament can also result in VISI.

Scapholunate

Injury to the scapholunate ligaments results in SLAC and DISI (which is more common than VISI).

Dorsal Radiolunate

Lunate dislocation occurs secondary to a dorsal radiolunate injury.

Capitolunate

Injury to this ligament is associated with perilunate dislocation.

stem: You are reviewing the x-rays of a 38-year-old man. His skull x-ray shows the paranasal sinuses to be enlarged, as is the sella. There is hyperostosis to the inner table of the skull. He has also had other x-rays taken.
prompt: Which of the following would fit with a diagnosis of acromegaly? Select ONE answer only.
options: Hook-like osteophytes on the second and third metacarpal heads
explanation:
Acromegaly

Excess circulating growth hormone can be caused either by a pituitary adenoma (>90%) or hyperplasia of the anterior pituitary. If this occurs prior to skeletal maturation it leads to gigantism in children. Thereafter there are a number of skeletal manifestations. Some of the most widely known are prognathism and spade-like hands.

Famously, the actor Richard Kiel who played Jaws in the James Bond films ‘Moonraker’ and ‘The Spy Who Loved Me’ had acromegaly.

Other important characteristics to look for are as follows:

Enlargement of the paranasal sinuses – 75%

Posterior vertebral scalloping – 30%

Widening of the terminal tufts

Heel pad thickness >25mm

Premature osteoarthritis

Enlargement and erosion of the sella

Hyperostosis of the inner table of the skull

stem: A 56-year-old woman presents with neck discomfort with pain and weakness in her arms and hands. She undergoes an MRI of her cervical spine for further assessment. The C4/C5 vertebral disc is seen to extrude posteriorly and effaces the exiting nerve root.
prompt: Which nerve root is most likely to be affected? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
In the cervical spine the nerve roots exit at the spinal cord without needing to traverse (as in the lumbar spine). The exiting nerve root takes the name of the vertebra BELOW the affected disc. A disc protrusion at C3/4 will affect the C4 nerve root. This allows for the extra nerve root at C8 before reaching the thoracic spine. In the thoracic spine the affected level takes its name from the vertebral body ABOVE that level.

In the lumbar spine the exiting nerve root is usually compressed in the neural foramen, whereas the traversing nerve root is compressed usually in the lateral recess. Far lateral bulges affect the exiting nerve root (takes its name from the vertebral body ABOVE that level). Paracentral bulges affect the traversing nerve root (takes its name from the vertebral body BELOW that level).

Image © Medical Exam Prep

stem: TFCC tear
prompt: Where should the contrast be injected?
explanation:
The TFCC - the triangular fibrocartilage complex

There are five components to the TFCC.

TFC - triangular fibrocartilage

Dorsal and volar radiolunar ligaments

Ulnolunate and ulnotriquetral ligamemts

Meniscus

Extensor carpi ulnaris tendon

Leakage of contrast from the radiocarpal compartment into the distal radioulnar compartment confirms the presence of a tear.

stem: You are reviewing the images of a patient with sacroiliitis known to have an inflammatory arthritis.
prompt: Which of the following diagnoses is correctly associated with its usual pattern of sacroiliitis? Select ONE answer only.
options: Bilateral asymmetrical sacroiliitis in ankylosing spondylitis
Bilateral asymmetrical sacroiliitis in enteropathic arthropathy
Bilateral asymmetrical sacroiliitis in psoriatic arthropathy
Bilateral symmetrical sacroiliitis in chronic reactive arthritis
Bilateral symmetrical sacroiliitis in infective arthropathy
explanation:
Sacroiliitis in psoriatic arthropathy can be bilateral symmetrical or bilateral asymmetrical though the latter is more common.

Psoriatic arthropathy

Around a fifth of patients with psoriasis develop arthropathy and it is also possible to suffer from psoriatic arthropathy in the absence of the typical psoriatic cutaneous plaques. Around 80% of patients are HLA-B27 positive.

Importantly, on x-ray there are findings of both erosive changes in addition to productive changes with periosteal new bone formation. The combination of the two contrives to leave a ‘pencil-in-cup’ appearance. The joints can appear fluffy due to the exuberance of new bone formation.

The differential diagnosis for periosteal reactions in the presence of an arthropathy is relatively narrow and very specific:

Psoriatic arthropathy

Juvenile rheumatoid arthritis

Reiter syndrome

Infective arthropathy

Although often classified as a distal arthropathy, preferring the DIPs to the MCPs, psoriatic arthropathy does also affect the spine and SI joints frequently. ‘Sausage digits’ is a term used to describe the diffuse soft tissue swelling which can affect the fingers and toes. Osteoporosis does occur but is a feature of later disease.

Seronegative arthritides - These are negative for Rheumatoid factor but have a strong association with HLA-B27 positivity.

Ankylosing spondylitis - 95%

Enteropathic arthropathy - 90%

Psoriatic arthritis - 80%

Chronic reactive arthritis - 70%

Ankylosing spondylitis

This disease usually presents in early adulthood with gradual onset of back pain. There is a male preponderance, though it can affect women too. The vast majority (>90%) of patients are HLA-B27 positive. Radiologically the late features are classical with:

Bilateral symmetrical sacroiliitis

Enthesopathy - calcified tendon insertion sites

Bamboo spine - vertebral syndesmophytes, particularly in the thoracolumbar spine

Dagger sign - spinous process fusion

Erosion, then fusion at the symphysis pubis, costochondral, costovertebral and sternoclavicular joints

Thoracic manifestations: upper lobe pulmonary fibrosis, pericarditis, aortic root dilatation

Early features are far more subtle and require a higher index of suspicion.

Enthesopathy - high signal on MRI at tendon insertion sites

Romanus lesions - triangular shaped oedema at the corners of vertebral bodies

Andersson lesions - bony oedema in the vertebral bodies adjacent to the disks.

Oedema in the sacroiliac joints.

Patients with advanced ankylosing spondylitis are at increased risk of pathological fractures due to fusion. These can be pelvic fractures following a simple fall, or chance fractures of the spine (involving all three columns - in ankylosing spondylitis, these fractures are also sometimes termed chalk-stick or carrot fractures).

Chronic reactive arthritis

This disease is said to present as a triad of arthritis, conjunctivitis/uveitis and urethritis/cervicitis (Can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree) however in reality only around a third of patients present with all three symptoms. Patients are usually aged 16-60 years. It has a reasonably strong male predominance but does occur in women. It can occur following infection with chlamydia, but also with gastrointestinal infections such as salmonella, shigella, campylobacter and yersinia. Most (>2/3rds) of patients are HLA-B27 positive.

Bilateral asymmetrical sacroiliitis

Paravertebral ossification - similar to syndesmophytes but in theory are seen separately from the disc, bridging around it. Most commonly in the thoracolumbar spine.

Enthesopathy - particularly at achilles tendon insertion, interspinous ligaments, and pelvic ligaments.

Enteropathic arthropathy

This occurs in a subsect of patients with inflammatory or infective bowel disease. Roughly 10-20% of patients with Crohn’s or ulcerative colitis suffer from enteropathic arthropathy. Like chronic reactive arthropathy, it can also occur in the context of salmonella, shigella and yersinia infections. Appearances are very similar to those of ankylosing spondylitis; the two can be very difficult to separate radiologically.

Bilateral symmetrical sacroillitis

Enthesopathy

Vertebral syndesmophytes

Fusion of spinous processes

Juvenile idiopathic arthritis

This condition used to be termed juvenile rheumatoid arthritis. It is a cluster of similar conditions affecting patients under the age of 16.

The affected joints show:

Effusions

Erosions

Cartilage destruction

Epiphyseal overgrowth secondary to reactive hyperaemia occurs owing to the immature nature of the skeleton. Premature physeal closure can result in limb length discrepancies in adulthood.

Large joints are typically affected first and the small joints of the hands and feet are affected later on.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

stem: A 56-year-old man undergoes a routine arthrogram of his shoulder. He subsequently develops symptoms which lead you to believe he has developed post-procedure arthralgia.
prompt: Which of the following regarding this condition is correct? Select ONE answer only.
options: Symptoms are worst at around 12 hours post procedure
Symptoms start at around half an hour post procedure
The main symptoms are redness and swelling
The pain is caused by a septic joint
The subacromial bursa normally communicates with the joint
explanation:
Post-arthroscopy arthralgia causes pain that begins at four hours and reaches a peak at 12 hours post-procedure. The pain is caused by a sterile chemical synovitis to the joint. A septic joint should always be considered where intervention has taken place however would manifest more insidiously over the course of the ensuing days.

The subacromial bursa should not communicate with the joint. If the patient has suffered a rotator cuff tear (particularly supraspinatus) or has undergone prior surgery then a communication may be present.

stem: You are reviewing the radiographs of a 40-year-old marathon runner who has been experiencing worsening hip pains over the last few months. There is overcoverage of the left femoral head by the acetabulum and you suspect she has pincer-type femoroacetabular impingement.
prompt: Which of the following is most likely to be seen with this abnormality?
explanation:
Femoroacetabular impingement (FAI)

Mixed type - >80% of patients have components of both cam-type and pincer-type FAI.

Cam type - a cam is an engineering term for an oval/egg shaped component with a hole through the middle of the wider end. In cam type FAI the femoral head takes on a 'cam' shaped appearance due to bony overgrowth at the superior aspect of the femoral neck. This abnormal bony contour impinges against the anterosuperior aspect of the acetabulum during movement. The condition occurs more frequently in men and tends to affect men in their 30s. Certain conditions can predispose to cam-type FAI, including SUFE, DDH and Perthes disease. Some patients with cam-type FAI exhibit femoral retroversion.

Pincer type - here bony protruberance of the anterosuperior acetabulum causes overcoverage of the femoral head and impingement against the femoral neck. Protrusio acetabuli predisposes to pincer-type FAI. The relationship of the overgrown anterior acetabular rim to the posterior acetabular rim in pincer-type FAI is called acetabular retroversion since it causes the femoral neck to twist posteriorly. Patients usually stand with their toes pointing outwards as a consequence. The condition is more common in women and a patient is typically aged around 40.

stem: A 24-year-old man undergoes a lumbar spine x-ray which shows dense sclerosis to the L4 vertebra. The vertebral body height is preserved, and the discs appear unaffected.
prompt: Which SINGLE one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Image © Medical Exam Prep

The ivory vertebra sign denotes dense sclerosis of a solitary vertebra without any change in its size or shape.

Ivory vertebra differential diagnosis

Paediatric

Adult

Lymphoma

Osteosarcoma

Osteoblastoma

Metastatic Ewing sarcoma

Metastatic medulloblastoma

Paget disease

Tuberculous spondylitis

Haemangioma

Prostate/ breast metastatic cancer

stem: A 17-year-old man has AP and lateral radiographs of the right ankle after twisting it whilst playing lacrosse. No fracture is seen, however a radiolucent lesion is seen within the calcaneus on the lateral projection. It has a thin sclerotic edge and calcification within. There is some endosteal scalloping and a subtle periosteal reaction.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Chondroblastoma

The calcaneus, like the patella, is an epiphyseal equivalent, so any epiphyseal lesions should be considered a possibility in this bone. They usually arise eccentrically in the epiphysis, are lobulated with a thin sclerotic margin.

Pseudo-cyst of calcaneus

This is a variation of the normal trabecular pattern centrally within the calcaneus. Will not have a crisp edge for this reason. Persistence of thin trabeculae and a visible nutrient foramen are supporting features.

Unicameral bone cyst

This is a well-defined lesion with thin sclerotic edges and potentially a multiloculated appearance. Absence of calcification within the lesion is a key differentiator from intraosseous lipoma, although if fractured, a fallen fragment sign can be seen.

Intraosseous lipoma

Calcification within the center of this lesion is a key feature which differentiates it from other lesions of plain film. Fat density on CT or MRI would also be a key differentiator. There should not be a periosteal reaction associated with this lesion, even in the presence of an acute fracture.

Geode

This is a subchondral cyst associated with osteoarthritis which should have communication with the joint space and be present in an older patient.

stem: You are reviewing the x-ray of a 38-year-old man's lumbar spine. There are concavities to the posterior surface of the vertebral bodies affecting L3 and L4.
prompt: Which of the following is the most likely cause of this finding? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Posterior vertebral scalloping

There are a number of specific differential diagnoses which can lead to this finding. In each case the image should be interrogated carefully to look for further clues as to the underlying diagnosis. Scalloping is a chronic process whereby mechanical pressure on the bone causes remodelling. In many cases the mechanism of posterior vertebral scalloping is secondary to dural ectasia.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

stem: A 27-year-old woman undergoes an x-ray of her right knee which shows a small effusion despite a normal joint space. She goes on to have an MRI. On the MRI there is nodular thickening of the synovium in the suprapatellar space which returns low signal on both T1 and T2 weighted sequences.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
PVNS - Pigmented villonodular synovitis

PVNS is an old term which has been replaced by Tenosynovial Giant Cell tumour.

TGCTs come in two types, duffuse or localised.

The localised version occurs in the tendon sheaths of the small muscles in the hands or feet (most frequently) and affect a slightly younger cohort of patients than the diffuse type. Patients are in their 30s-40s usually. The presence of fibrosis and/or haemosiderin deposition within these lesions shows as a low signal capsule surrounding a tumour which can have a variable signal, either low, iso or high in intensity as compared to nearby normal skeletal muscle. On post contrast images localised TGCTs tend to enhance avidly.

The diffuse version occurs within larger joints and is altogether a more aggressive lesion. The patients tend to be slightly older 50-60s. These lesions appear as a nodular infiltrative aggressive soft tissue mass extending out from the joint into the adjacent fat. Within the synovium there are characteristic 'sea-anenome' villous projections and low signal within the lesion is again in keeping with haemosiderin deposits, moreso than is usually present in localised TGCTs. Again there is usually also a variety of signal types in addition to the haemosiderin but consistently between lesions there is notable enhancement on post contrast sequences. Blooming on susceptibility weighted sequences confirms haemosiderin deposition

Treatment is with synovectomy although there is a high rate of recurrence.

If the patient is male, the usual differential diagnosis for TGCT is of haemophilic arthropathy owing to the presence of blood products there too. TGCT appears as a differential diagnosis for subarticular lucent bone lesions due to the formation of large subchondral cysts.

Haemophilic arthropathy

Haemophilic arthropathy could also give the appearance described in the vignette however is much much rarer in women than in men.

The larger joints are most at risk for this disease, and the knee is particularly classical. On an xray there may only be a joint effusion in early disease but erosions and subchondral cysts develop. In particular there may be widening of the intercondylar notch (for which there is a differential diagnosis of: JIA/RA, Psoriatic arthropathy, TB and haemophilia) due to pannus formation.  Also classical is epiphyseal overgrowth secondary to hyperaemia.

On an MRI there may well be nodular deposits on the synovium however the presence of blood degradation products renders these very low in signal on all sequences with blooming artefact present on gradient echo sequences or similar. If a haemarthrosis is present, the signal of the fluid will change depending on the chronicity of the event.

A haemophilic pseudotumour occurs in around 1-2% of patients with haemophilia. The presence of blood degradation products leads to a wide variety of intralesional signal patterns. The lesions are usually surrounded by a low signal haemosiderin rim though. Lesions can arise within bone (intra-osseous) or in soft tissues (usually muscular). Growth and pressure effects on adjacent bone can cause scalloping.

Lipoma arborescens

This condition can affect children or adults and is thought to be a reaction to chronic inflammation of the synovium leading to extensive fatty infiltration of the synovium. It is almost always the knee which is affected. Plain radiographs will show only an effusion, which may be large, but on MRI there is frond-like or nodular synovial proliferation which returns fat-signal according to the different sequences used. The signal should be high on T1 and T2 but suppress on fat-saturated sequences. Post-contrast the synovium itself will enhance. Treatment is by synovectomy.

Rheumatoid arthritis

A joint effusion and synovial thickening (which would avidly enhance post-contrast) is a worthy description for rheumatoid arthritis however the high-fatty signal of the synovium is not a feature of rheumatoid arthritis. As the condition develops, patients with rheumatoid arthritis exhibit erosive changes with cartilage loss, bony erosions and marrow oedema.

stem: A 64-year-old lady who underwent a wide local excision for the management of her breast cancer presents with back pain and is found to have metastatic disease in her thoracic vertebra.
prompt: Which of the following is the LEAST likely appearance of the metastases on an MRI scan?
options: High on T1, low on T2
Low on T1, high on T2
Low on T1, low on T2
explanation:
Bone marrow on MRI

T1

T2

Normal bone marrow

High (fatty)

Intermediate

Post-Radiotherapy

Very high and homogenous

Intermediate (initially high due to oedema)

Haemangioma

High

High

Abnormal bone (metastases, myeloma, regeneration)

Low but enhances with Gadolinium

High (fluid)

Blastic metastases (prostate, breast, TCC) and myelofibrosis

Low

Low

Metastases

Normally metastatic deposits in the spine lead to low T1 signal and high T2 signal. There should be no signal drop out on fat saturated sequences in contrast to marrow reconversion where although red marrow will experience far less signal dropout than yellow marrow, there will still be some loss in signal owing to the fat content of both types of marrow.

Sclerotic or blastic metastases return little signal on either T1 or T2 weighted sequences. These include prostate, breast or TCC metastases among others.

Breast cancer can cause lytic or sclerotic metastases or a mixed picture.

Lytic metastases are more likely than sclerotic metastases to enhance with contrast. Similarly on DWI imaging, whereas lytic metastases will usually appear hyperintense, sclerotic metastases return little signal since they contain little water.

If there is a diffuse abnormality of the bone marrow it can be difficult to identify but normal bone marrow should not be lower in signal intensity than the muscle on T1 weighted sequences.

stem: You are reviewing the cervical spine x-rays from a 20-year-old woman. There is an obvious block vertebra affecting the C2 and C3 vertebral bodies.
prompt: Which SINGLE one of the following is a cause of block vertebra?
explanation:
There is a differential diagnosis for block vertebra and although Sprengel shoulder features as a predominant part of Klippel-Feil syndrome, an isolated sprengel shoulder is not a cause of block vertebra.

Differential diagnosis for block vertebra:

Congenital

Klippel-Feil syndrome

Isolated

Arthritides

Rheumatoid arthritis

Ankylosing spondylitis

Miscellaneous

Post-operative

Post-traumatic fusion

Post-Tuberculosis infection

Sprengel shoulder

This condition can occur in isolation as well as part of Klippel-Feil syndrome. It is (like Klippel-Feil syndrome) also often associated with renal anomalies. Sprengel shoulder is a congenital abnormality where the scapula (usually, but not exclusively, unilateral) is attached to the cervical vertebra either by a fibrous or osseous connection, and therefore fails to descend into the normal position. The result is elevation and medial rotation of the scapula, which is usually hypoplastic. The condition can be readily appreciated on a plain film although cross-sectional imaging is useful to plan surgical correction if required. If present, the osseous connection between the scapula and the spine is termed an omovertebral bar.

Klippel-Feil syndrome (different from Klippel-Trenaunay-Weber syndrome: port-wine stains, localised hypertrophy and venous malformations)

Klippel-Feil syndrome is predominantly a segmentation anomaly which arises during foetal development and leads to cervical fusion of two or more vertebral bodies. C2-3 are most commonly involved, accounting for around half of cases. Thereafter C5-6 accounts for a further third and the remainder are made up from fusions at other levels. There are a multitude of associated features, the predominant ones of which include:

Renal abnormalities (of which a third have unilateral renal agenesis) - ⅔

Scoliosis >20o - ½

Sprengel shoulder - ⅓

Deafness (sensorineural) - ⅓

Cervical ribs - ⅕

The renal anomalies seen include agenesis or dysgenesis, ectopic location, and duplication.

Yet further features of this condition, all present in under 20% of cases include:

Odontoid dysplasia

Hemivertebrae / butterfly vertebrae

Syringomyelia / diastomatomyelia

Ear anomalies (microtia, deformed ossicles etc)

Congenital heart disease (ASD or coarctation)

Holt-Oram syndrome

This syndrome is associated with numerous skeletal and cardiac malformations. It is usually evident either antenatally or in the early neonatal period. Cardiac manifestations include either ASD or VSD, tetralogy of Fallot and coarctation. Perhaps most strikingly the condition is often associated with radial ray hypoplasia often meaning the absence of one or both thumbs. An x-ray may show absence or hypoplasia of one or both radii.

stem: A 43-year-old man presents with pain and instability in his wrist. Radiographs demonstrate narrowing of the scapholunate angle and an increased capitolunate angle. The orthopaedic surgeon reviewing the images recognises this as volar intercalated segmental instability (VISI).
prompt: Injury to which ligament is most likely to have resulted in this pathology? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Lunotriquetral

Injury to this ligament results in VISI.

Injury to this ligament also causes midcarpal dislocation (similar to lunate dislocation and also associate with triquetral fractures).

Scapholunate

Injury to the scapholunate ligaments results in SLAC and DISI (which is more common than VISI).

Dorsal Radiolunate

Lunate dislocation occurs secondary to a dorsal radiolunate injury.

Capitolunate

Injury to this ligament is associated with perilunate dislocation.

stem: A 37-year-old female presented with a few-month's history of back pain and paraesthesia in the lower legs bilaterally. She was on psychiatric medications and previously developed a habit of recreational inhalation of a gaseous computer cleaning product. An X-ray of the lumbar spine showed osteophytosis and diffuse osseous sclerosis. An AP pelvis radiograph shows diffuse osseous sclerosis and calcification of the sacrotuberous ligaments bilaterally. Bone scintigraphy demonstrates diffusely increased uptake in the axial and appendicular skeleton predominately with periarticular activity.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Skeletal Fluorosis

Skeletal fluorosis is traditionally noted in the setting of a high concentration of fluoride in groundwater. However, this could also be due to repeated inhalation of fluorocarbons present in aerosolized computer cleaner. Elevated serum and urine fluoride levels as well as bone marrow histopathology is used to make a diagnosis.

The main findings in skeletal fluorosis are diffuse osseous sclerosis, osteophytosis/hypersotosis, and calcification of ligaments, tendons, and interosseous membranes.

Technetium bone scintigraphy will show diffusely increased osseous uptake, particularly in the periarticular regions

Renal osteodystrophy

Renal osteodystrophy occurs in patients with chronic renal disease and secondary hyperparathyroidism. Bone density is diffusely increased, especially in the axial spine where alternating bands of increased density at the endplates and decreased density in the central vertebral bodies leads to the characteristic rugger jersey appearance.

Paget's Disease

Paget's Disease shows more localized areas of cortical thickening and coarsened trabeculae, compared to the diffusely sclerotic bone of skeletal fluorosis.

Bone lymphoma

Bone lymphoma can result in a diffusely sclerotic “ivory vertebra.” This finding is usually isolated to one vertebral body and does not involve posterior elements.

Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH)

Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH) can cause ossification of ligaments and osteophytosis, however bone density will be normal.

stem: A 30-year-old man injures his knee in a road traffic incident. Once life threatening injuries have been ruled out, he is examined carefully by the A+E doctor. He complains of tenderness to his left knee and undergoes x-rays of it. There is a crescentic shaped bony fragment adjacent to the head of the fibula. An injury to the arcuate complex is suspected.
prompt: Involvement of which of the following is LEAST consistent with an injury to the arcuate complex?
explanation:
The arcuate ligament, complex and sign.

The arcuate ligament of the knee is a Y-shaped ligament arising from the fibular styloid process and splitting into a medial limb and a lateral limb. Together with the lateral collateral ligament and lateral joint capsule (different sources of literature also variably include the biceps femoris tendon and fabellofibular ligament), it forms the arcuate complex and is important in stabilising the knee joint.

The arcuate sign is the elliptical shaped avulsed bony fragment adjacent to the fibular styloid process representing an avulsion fracture of the fibular styloid.

The usual mechanism of injury is a direct blow in extension such as a traffic incident whereby a vehicle strikes a standing pedestrian.

Associated cruciate ligament injuries are common with arcuate ligament avulsions. Some literature reports this to be particularly so for the posterior cruciate ligament injuries.

A segond fracture is an avulsion fracture of the lateral aspect of the tibia which gives rise to a bony fragment placed more medially and more anterior than that of an arcuate sign.

stem: A 13-year-old girl complains of pain in her wrist following a fall. An x-ray reveals no fractures but the carpal angle is markedly decreased to around 110o and the proximal carpus is V-shaped. Additionally the distal radio-ulnar joint is dorsally subluxed.
prompt: With which condition is this deformity LEAST likely to be associated?
explanation:
The patient has a Madelung deformity. This arises due to a problem with the development of the ulnar side of the distal end of the radius. The distal radioulnar joint subluxes and the ulna displaces dorsally. Owing to growth failure of the distal radius, by comparison the ulna appears lengthened (Positive ulnar variance). The carpal bones become altered in shape from the norm, in particular the lunate appears triangular. The overall appearance is of a V-shape to the radioulnarcarpal joint with angles of <120o considered characteristic.

The Madelung deformity has a number of different aetiologies (Mnemonic = DIGIT):

D = Dysplastic - Ollier disease, osteochondromatosis, achondroplasia, mucopolysaccharidoses, diaphyseal aclasis

I = Idiopathic

G = Genetic - Autosomal dominant.

50% of patients have bilateral deformities. Most common association is Turner syndrome

I = Infection

T = Post-Traumatic

Diaphyseal aclasis can be associated with a Madelung deformity but patients may have a reverse-Madelung (or pseudo-Madelung) deformity instead. Here there is negative ulnar variance due to excessive overgrowth and bowing of the radius with consequential ulnar deviation at the wrist.

Ulnar variance

Description

Associations

Positive

The ulna is unusually long

Ulnar impaction syndrome

Negative

The ulna is unusually short

Kienboch disease

Image sourced from WikipediaCourtesy of Hellerhoff CC BY-SA 3.0

stem: A 34-year-old man suffers a knee injury while on a skiing holiday. He visits a local hospital and has x-rays taken of his knee. No fracture is found. Once back home he undergoes an MRI scan when the pain fails to resolve. He is told he has a transient patella dislocation injury.
prompt: What findings on MRI would be most consistent with this?
options: High STIR signal to the anterior aspect of the tibia with an associated posterior cruciate ligament tear
High T2 signal to the anterior aspect of the lateral femoral condyle and lateral tibial plateau with an anterior cruciate ligament and medial collateral ligament tea
High signal on STIR to the lateral femoral condyle and posterolateral tibial plateau with an associated tear of the anterior cruciate ligament tear
High signal on T2 and STIR to the anterior aspect of the tibia with an associated anterior cruciate ligament tear
High signal on T2 to the anterolateral femoral condyle and medial patella facet with an associated tear of the medial retinaculum
explanation:
Bony contusions

Bruising to the bone can be detected around 2 days following an injury but may not resolve for many months thereafter. With regards knee injuries, it is often possible to discern the mechanism of injury from the pattern of bruising seen. The contusions follow fluid on MRI scans i.e. low in signal on T1 and high on T2 (and STIR). STIR is used to suppress the fat of the bone marrow thereby making the fluid stand out more.

Transient lateral patella dislocation injury - High signal on T2 to the anterolateral femoral condyle and medial patella facet with an associated tear of the medial retinaculum

When the patella dislocates laterally, its medial facet can impact onto the anterolateral corner of the lateral femoral condyle. Both areas become damaged and contusions can be seen on MRI. Often though, the patella reduces spontaneously and thus the exact mechanism of injury must be inferred from the imaging findings.

Joint effusion

Osteochondral injuries to the anterolateral femoral condyle and medial patella facet

Sprain or disruption to the medial retinaculum

Clip injury and pivot shift injury

- High signal on STIR to the lateral femoral condyle and posterolateral tibial plateau with an associated tear of the anterior cruciate ligament tear (Pivot shift)

- High T2 signal to the anterior aspect of the lateral femoral condyle and lateral tibial plateau with an anterior cruciate ligament and medial collateral ligament tear (Clip injury)

These two injuries are very similar. Both involve valgus stress on a flexed knee (such as a tackle to the knee during sports). A pivot shift injury also requires external rotation of the tibia. The three main structures most at risk during these injuries are:

Anterior cruciate ligament (especially in a pivot shift injury)

Medial collateral ligament (especially in a clip injury)

Medial meniscus (remember that the medial meniscus is attached to the medial collateral ligament)

If all three are present together it is referred to as the O’Donoghue triad. Since O’Donoghue defined this triad however, it has been discovered that lateral meniscal tears are actually more common with this type of injury than medial meniscus ones.

Bony contusions occur at the side of impact because the proximal tibia and distal femur impact on one another thus:

Lateral tibial plateau (posterolateral in pivot shift injury)

Lateral femoral condyle

Hyperextension injury - High signal on T2 and STIR to the anterior aspect of the tibia with an associated anterior cruciate ligament tear

These occur often following excessively forceful kicking. There will be bony contusions at the anterior aspect of the tibial plateau and femoral condyles where they collide with one another. Either of the anterior or posterior cruciate ligaments may also be involved.

Dashboard injury - High STIR signal to the anterior aspect of the tibia with an associated posterior cruciate ligament tear

As the name would suggest, this injury is usually stained by impact of the knee against the dashboard of a car during a road traffic incident. Force applied to the anterior aspect of the tibia when the knee is flexed leads to:

Osteochondral injury or fracture to the anterior aspect of the tibia

Posterior cruciate ligament rupture/sprain

Of these five, the dashboard injury is the only one to injure the posterior cruciate ligament (obviously it can get injured in any number of other ways beyond these five)

stem: A 42-year-old builder presents with pain and instability in his wrist. He recalls falling awkwardly whilst carrying heavy materials at work several years ago, since when his wrist has never been the same. Plain radiographs demonstrate what appears to be an old scaphoid fracture. There is a widened scapholunate distance with a scapholunate angle of 70 degrees.
prompt: What is the best description of this abnormality? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Dorsal Intercalated Segment Instability (DISI)

This occurs in the setting of carpal instability when there is widening of the scapholunate angle to greater than 60 degrees.

Scaphoid Non-Union Advanced collapse (SNAC)

This occurs following a scaphoid fracture. It is similar to SLAC but there is a normal scapholunate distance, with a scaphoid fracture. Like SLAC, there is radioscaphoid degenerative change, followed by proximal migration of the capitate and eventually dorsal intercalated instability.

Scaphoid-lunate advanced collapse (SLAC)

This occurs following injury to the scapholunate ligament or secondary to CPPD. It is similar to SNAC but there is scapholunate widening, rather than a scaphoid fracture. Radioscaphoid degenerative changes are an early feature, followed by proximal migration of the capitate and eventually dorsal intercalated instability.

Avascular necrosis (AVN) of the scaphoid

This is usually secondary to a proximal fracture. The most reliable sign is low T1 signal in the scaphoid.

Midcarpal dislocation

This occurs in association with triquetral fracture and is very similar to lunate dislocation.

stem: You are performing an ultrasound scan on a patient with only one kidney. She has attended with a sign-language interpreter who explains that she also has abnormalities of her heart, neck and left shoulder.
prompt: Which of the following is NOT a feature of Klippel-Feil syndrome? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Please note that the question asks which is NOT a feature of Klippel-Feil syndrome.

A third of cases have sensorineural deafness but bony deformities (and thus conductive deafness) of the middle ear are present in a number of cases too. Congenital ASD is associated with the syndrome, not VSD.

Klippel-Feil syndrome (different from Klippel-Trenaunay-Weber syndrome: port-wine stains, localised hypertrophy and venous malformations)

Klippel-Feil syndrome is predominantly a segmentation anomaly which arises during foetal development and leads to cervical fusion of two or more vertebral bodies. C2-3 are most commonly involved, accounting for around half of cases. Thereafter C5-6 accounts for a further third and the remainder are made up from fusions at other levels. There are a multitude of associated features, the predominant ones of which include:

Renal abnormalities (of which a third have unilateral renal agenesis) - ⅔

Scoliosis >20o - ½

Sprengel shoulder - ⅓

Deafness (sensorineural) - ⅓

Cervical ribs - ⅕

The renal anomalies seen include agenesis or dysgenesis, ectopic location, and duplication.

Yet further features of this condition, all present in under 20% of cases include:

Odontoid dysplasia

Hemivertebrae / butterfly vertebrae

Syringomyelia / diastomatomyelia

Ear anomalies (microtia, deformed ossicles etc)

Congenital heart disease (ASD or coarctation)

Sprengel shoulder

This condition can occur in isolation as well as part of Klippel-Feil syndrome. It is (like Klippel-Feil syndrome) also often associated with renal anomalies. Sprengel shoulder is a congenital abnormality where the scapula (usually, but not exclusively, unilateral) is attached to the cervical vertebra either by a fibrous or osseous connection, and therefore fails to descend into the normal position. The result is elevation and medial rotation of the scapula, which is usually hypoplastic. The condition can be readily appreciated on a plain film although cross-sectional imaging is useful to plan surgical correction if required. If present, the osseous connection between the scapula and the spine is termed an omovertebral bar.

stem: A 24-year-old rugby player twists his knee in a tackle and suffers a meniscal tear. You are asked to review his MRI scan.
prompt: Which SINGLE statement regarding the menisci of the knee is true?
options: Both menisci are attached at both ends to the intercondylar area of the tibia
The lateral meniscus is attached to the joint capsule
The lateral meniscus is attached to the lateral collateral ligament
The lateral meniscus is larger than the medial meniscus
They act to increase friction between the femur and tibia
explanation:
The menisci of the knee are two pads of fibrocartilaginous tissue, which have two main functions:

They deepen the articular surface of the tibia and increase stability of the knee joint

To disperse friction between the femur and tibia, acting as ‘shock absorbers’

Both menisci are C shaped and are attached at both ends to the intercondylar area of the tibia.

The medial meniscus is also fixed to the medial collateral ligament and the joint capsule. As a consequence of this injuries to the medial collateral ligament are often accompanied by a tear of the medial meniscus. The lateral meniscus is smaller and does not have any extra attachments, rendering it fairly mobile.

The head of the tibia from above, showing the menisci and ligament attachments (from Gray’s Anatomy)

stem: A 65-year-old lady complains to her GP of ongoing burning pains in her hand and wrist following a fall 6 months previously. At the time she was found to have fractured her ulnar styloid process and wore a plaster cast for 6 weeks. She is otherwise well. On examination her hand is oedematous with some dystrophic nail changes. She undergoes an x-ray which shows peri-articular patchy osteopenia and subperiosteal bone resorption but the joint spaces are well preserved. The GP suspects a diagnosis of complex regional pain syndrome.
prompt: Which of the following regarding this condition is FALSE? Select ONE answer only.
options: Symptoms develop following an initial URTI
The initial injury is often disproportionately mild
The joint spaces are well preserved
explanation:
Please note that the question asks which answer is FALSE.

Complex regional pain syndrome also known as Sudeck dystrophy

Patients develop chronic pain in an area previously affected by an, often disproportionately mild, injury. The pain is said to be burning in nature and symptoms of allodynia (pain with stimuli which would not normally be painful) and hyperalgesia (excessive sensitivity to pain) are also usually described. By contrast, reduced sensation is not normally found. On x-ray there is juxta-articular osteopenia with sub-periosteal bone resorption but preservation of the joint spaces. Soft tissue swelling can also be seen. Nuclear medicine tests may show either increased flow with increased uptake on the delayed blood pool images or (less commonly) decreased flow with decreased uptake on the delayed blood pool images.

stem: You are reviewing the images of a 21-year-old man who has suffered a wrist fracture following a fall. Aside from the fracture you also notice that all of the bones included in the films appear densely sclerotic. The medullary cavity is not visible on the images. A previous view of his lumbar spine reveals a bone-within-a-bone appearance to the vertebra.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Osteopetrosis

This is a disease of abnormal osteoclastic activity which leads to thick, sclerotic bone throughout the skeleton. Although appearing very solid on an x-ray, the bone is very disorganised structurally and consequently very brittle. Patients may experience numerous fractures throughout their lives. There is an autosomal dominant form which does not impede life expectancy but the autosomal recessive form carries are poorer prognosis with death due to complications of bone marrow failure (infections, leukaemia or haemorrhage) before adulthood.

On x-ray there is a generalised increase in bone density and films should be carefully evaluated for the presence of a pathological fracture. A bone-within-a-bone appearance is typical of the autosomal dominant form and there may be alternating lines of sclerosis and lucency in the phalanges.

Osteopetrosis

Image sourced from WikipediaCourtesy of Stevenfruitsmaak CC BY-SA 2.0

Pyknodysostosis

This disorder is inherited in an autosomal recessive fashion and causes diffuse bony sclerosis. Patients are of short stature and often have a typical facies; there is usually frontal bossing despite delayed closure of the cranial sutures, small mandibular size and beaking of the nose. Additionally patients have short stubby fingers, the nails of which may be hypoplastic. It can be difficult to tell pyknodysostosis from osteopetrosis however the medullary cavity is still discernible in the case of pyknodysostosis. Patients with osteopetrosis also do not tend to suffer from short stature or mandibular involvement.

Osteopoikilosis

This benign condition leads to multiple small oval bone islands forming around the skeleton. Purportedly, once the epiphyses have fused the number remains static. They can show mildly increased uptake on a nuclear medicine bone scan. Whereas a bone island may exist in isolation or near isolation, the finding of multiple such lesions suggests the diagnosis of osteopoikilosis.

Image sourced from WikipediaCourtesy of Hellerhoff CC BY-SA 3.0

Osteopathia striata

This disease is more similar to osteopoikilosis than the other bony dysplasias. It is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion, but can arise sporadically too. It causes striking longitudinal striations in the metaphyseal regions of the long bones but patients are generally asymptomatic and it is usually therefore an incidental finding. The appearance is said to resemble stalks of celery.

Melorrheostosis

This dysplasia gives a classical appearance said to resemble the dripping of solid candle wax along a bone. The name comes from greek words meaning 'flowing' and 'limb'. It can be asymptomatic but if there is encroachment on nerves or joints patients may present with pain and movement limitations. Uniquely for a dysplasia, it can cross from one bone to the next across a joint, sometimes causing fusion in the process. On imaging the affected 'dripping' areas are seen as slcerotic areas within the affected bones. It usually only affects one limb of the patient but changes can be seen in more than one bone of that limb (i.e. monomelic but polyostotic).

stem: You review the scans of a trauma patient with a suspected spinal cord injury.
prompt: Which of following segmental nerve roots is NOT correctly matched with its corresponding myotome? Select ONE answer only.
options: L5 – Ankle and big toe dorsiflexors
explanation:
The key myotomes are:

C5 – Deltoid

C6 – Wrist extensors

C7 – Elbow extensors

C8 – Finger flexors to middle finger (flexor digitorum profundus)

T1 – Small finger abductors (abductor digiti minimi)

L2 – Hip flexors (Iliopsoas)

L3, L4 – Knee extensors

L4, L5 & S1 – Knee flexion

L5 – Ankle and big toe dorsiflexors

S1 – Ankle plantar flexors

stem: A 32-year-old man presents to his GP with troubling joint pains. He mentions suffering from food poisoning during his recent holiday abroad. On examination there is no rash and his HLA-B27 comes back as positive. His GP requests some x-rays which show bilateral symmetrical sacroiliitis.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Seronegative arthritides - These are negative for Rheumatoid factor but have a strong association with HLA-B27 positivity.

Ankylosing spondylitis - 95%

Enteropathic arthropathy - 90%

Psoriatic arthritis - 80%

Chronic reactive arthritis - 70%

Enteropathic arthropathy

This occurs in a subsect of patients with inflammatory or infective bowel disease. Roughly 10-20% of patients with Crohn’s or ulcerative colitis suffer from enteropathic arthropathy. Like chronic reactive arthropathy, it can also occur in the context of salmonella, shigella and yersinia infections. Appearances are very similar to those of ankylosing spondylitis; the two can be very difficult to separate radiologically.

Bilateral symmetrical sacroillitis

Enthesopathy

Vertebral syndesmophytes

Fusion of spinous processes

Chronic reactive arthritis (Reiter syndrome)

This disease is said to present as a triad of arthritis, conjunctivitis/uveitis and urethritis/cervicitis (Can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree) however in reality only around a third of patients present with all three symptoms. Patients are usually aged 16-60 years. It has a reasonably strong male predominance but does occur in women. It can occur following infection with chlamydia, but also with gastrointestinal infections such as salmonella, shigella, campylobacter and yersinia. Most (>2/3rds) of patients are HLA-B27 positive.

Bilateral asymmetrical sacroiliitis

Paravertebral ossification - similar to syndesmophytes but in theory are seen separately from the disc, bridging around it. Most commonly in the thoracolumbar spine.

Enthesopathy - particularly at achilles tendon insertion, interspinous ligaments, and pelvic ligaments.

Psoriatic arthropathy

Around a fifth of patients with psoriasis develop arthropathy and it is also possible to suffer from psoriatic arthropathy in the absence of the typical psoriatic cutaneous plaques. Around 80% of patients are HLA-B27 positive.

Importantly, on x-ray there are findings of both erosive changes in addition to productive changes with periosteal new bone formation. The combination of the two contrives to leave a ‘pencil-in-cup’ appearance. The joints can appear fluffy due to the exuberance of new bone formation.

The differential diagnosis for periosteal reactions in the presence of an arthropathy is relatively narrow and very specific:

Psoriatic arthropathy

Juvenile rheumatoid arthritis

Reiter syndrome

Infective arthropathy

Although often classified as a distal arthropathy, preferring the DIPs to the MCPs, psoriatic arthropathy does also affect the spine and SI joints frequently. ‘Sausage digits’ is a term used to describe the diffuse soft tissue swelling which can affect the fingers and toes. Osteoporosis does occur but is a feature of later disease.

Ankylosing spondylitis

This disease usually presents in early adulthood with gradual onset of back pain. There is a male preponderance, though it can affect women too. The vast majority (>90%) of patients are HLA-B27 positive. Radiologically the late features are classical with:

Bilateral symmetrical sacroiliitis

Enthesopathy - calcified tendon insertion sites

Bamboo spine - vertebral syndesmophytes, particularly in the thoracolumbar spine

Dagger sign - spinous process fusion

Erosion, then fusion at the symphysis pubis, costochondral, costovertebral and sternoclavicular joints

Thoracic manifestations: upper lobe pulmonary fibrosis, pericarditis, aortic root dilatation

Early features are far more subtle and require a higher index of suspicion.

Enthesopathy - high signal on MRI at tendon insertion sites

Romanus lesions - triangular shaped oedema at the corners of vertebral bodies

Andersson lesions - bony oedema in the vertebral bodies adjacent to the disks.

Oedema in the sacroiliac joints.

Patients with advanced ankylosing spondylitis are at increased risk of pathological fractures due to fusion. These can be pelvic fractures following a simple fall, or chance fractures of the spine (involving all three columns - in ankylosing spondylitis, these fractures are also sometimes termed chalk-stick or carrot fractures).

Juvenile idiopathic arthritis

This condition used to be termed juvenile rheumatoid arthritis. It is a cluster of similar conditions affecting patients under the age of 16.

The affected joints show:

Effusions

Erosions

Cartilage destruction

Epiphyseal overgrowth secondary to reactive hyperaemia occurs owing to the immature nature of the skeleton. Premature physeal closure can result in limb length discrepancies in adulthood.

Large joints are typically affected first and the small joints of the hands and feet are affected later on.
