stem: You are reviewing the radiographs of a 40-year-old marathon runner who has been experiencing worsening hip pains over the last few months. There is over-coverage of the left femoral head by the acetabulum and you suspect she has pincer-type femoroacetabular impingement.
prompt: Which of the following is most likely to be seen with this abnormality? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Femoroacetabular impingement (FAI)

Mixed type - >80% of patients have components of both cam-type and pincer-type FAI.

Cam type - a cam is an engineering term for an oval/egg shaped component with a hole through the middle of the wider end. In cam type FAI the femoral head takes on a 'cam' shaped appearance due to bony overgrowth at the superior aspect of the femoral neck. This abnormal bony contour impinges against the anterosuperior aspect of the acetabulum during movement. The condition occurs more frequently in men and tends to affect men in their 30s. Certain conditions can predispose to cam-type FAI, including SUFE, DDH and Perthes disease. Some patients with cam-type FAI exhibit femoral retroversion.

Pincer type - here bony protuberance of the anterosuperior acetabulum causes over-coverage of the femoral head and impingement against the femoral neck. Protrusio acetabuli predisposes to pincer-type FAI. The relationship of the overgrown anterior acetabular rim to the posterior acetabular rim in pincer-type FAI is called acetabular retroversion since it causes the femoral neck to twist posteriorly. Patients usually stand with their toes pointing outwards as a consequence. The condition is more common in women and a patient is typically aged around 40.

stem: A 43-year-old man undergoes lumbar spine radiographs three weeks after slipping and falling on an icy pavement. He has been suffering from lumbar back pain since the fall. The x-rays show mild anterolisthesis of L5 on S1 with normal spinous process alignment.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Spondylolysis

Anterolisthesis of L5 over S1 with normal spinous process alignment is typical for bilateral pars defects, also known as spondylolysis. The pars is the junction of the spinous lamina, pedicle and facet. A bony defect in the pars interarticularis allows separation of the spinous process from the rest of the vertebra, which slips forwards. Patients can be asymptomatic from this or may develop worsening anterolisthesis with consequential nerve root impingement.

On an x-ray the outline of a 'scottie dog' is said to be formed by the posterior elements of the spine. If there is a lucent linear defect in the neck of the scottie dog, a pars defect is present.

stem: A 35-year-old woman visits A+E following a fall. She is otherwise unhurt but has pain and tenderness to her left index finger. An x-ray shows there to be a solitary well circumscribed lucent lesion in the diaphysis of the proximal phalange of the index finger. There is cortical expansion but no associated soft tissue mass is seen.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Enchondroma

As the name suggests, this is a cartilage forming tumour showing ground-glass matrix and ring or arc calcifications (as with all cartilage forming tumours). Patients are typically young (10-30 years) and the lesions are typically found in the hands (although they can form anywhere in the body. In the hands they are unusual to be found in the terminal phalanges). They are thought to derive from ongoing growth of small foci of cartilage which have become displaced from the growth plate. They can expand the cortex but, unless presenting as a fracture, should be painless and therefore are often an incidental diagnosis. Although they are benign tumours, malignant degeneration to a chondrosarcoma can occur.

Chondroblastoma

Largely speaking these tumours only arise in epiphyses or epiphyseal equivalent bones (such as the patella) and are therefore confined, in-terms of age, to children or adolescents. They can present in a fairly indolent fashion with pain, swelling and tenderness preceding diagnosis by weeks, if not months. They typically occur in the long bones, around two thirds are found in the leg and half are found around the knee. On x-ray they appear as a lucent, lobulated lesion with a thin sclerotic margin. Surrounding oedema, if present, can be surprisingly florid, even leading to an overestimation of the extent of the underlying lesion. Calcification associated with the lesion does occur but is better appreciated with CT.

Brodie abscess

The best explanation of these abscesses is of a smouldering osteomyelitis. Most commonly they are caused by staphylococcus aureus (or Salmonella in patients with sickle cell disease) and in children they arise in the metaphyses and the presence of the growth plate acts as a physical barrier hindering spread to the epiphyses. In very young children (<18 months) there are blood vessels traversing the growth plate and thus abscesses can form in both the metaphyses and the epiphyses. In patients where the growth plates have fused, vessel cross the site of the old growth plate and the epiphysis can become infected.

Age

Site of infection

< 18 months

Metaphysis and epiphysis

> 18 months, before fusion of growth plate

Metaphysis

After fusion of growth plate

Epiphysis

On x-ray a lucent lesion with a sclerotic margin should raise the possibility of a Brodie abscess and the presence of a lucent channel extending towards the growth plate is considered pathognomonic. The diagnosis is usually confirmed with MRI where the sclerotic bone returns little signal on T2 weighted sequences but the adjacent inner granulation tissue returns high signal. The combination of the two is referred to as the ‘double-line’ effect. The rim of granulation tissue can enhance with gadolinium but the absence of enhancement does not rule the condition out. Adjacent bone marrow is often oedematous (high on T2, low on T1).

Osteoid osteoma

These are small benign tumours but which can be quite symptomatic, classically with pain relieved by aspirin. The majority form in the diaphyses of long bones but the posterior elements of the spine is another classic location.

The radiolucent nidus and symptoms of night pain in a young patient point to either an osteoid osteoma or an osteoblastoma. The final diagnosis comes down to size: <1.5 cm is definitely an osteoid osteoma, and >2 cm is definitely an osteoblastoma. There is a nasty grey area somewhere between the two sizes.

On x-ray the radiolucent nidus may not be fully appreciated, and the abnormality which is picked up will be the consequential sclerotic solid periosteal reaction. In the spine there may be a painful scoliosis concave towards the lesion as a result of adjacent muscular spasm. CT is used to confirm the diagnosis as the nidus is readily appreciable.

Osteoblastoma

Osteoblastomas are quite rare, even for bone tumours. To all intent and purposes they can be considered as large osteoid osteomas. They occur in slightly older patients than osteoid osteomas but most patients are still under 30-years-old. Around a third arise in the posterior elements of the spine, sometimes giving a painful scoliosis, a further third can be found in the long bones and roughly the remaining third arise in the small bones of the hands and feet.

stem: A 52-year-old man complains of a painful lump in his left foot. He visits his GP who suspects he may have a Morton neuroma and refers him for an ultrasound scan.
prompt: What is the best position for assessing whether the patient has a Morton neuroma?
options: Sitting with feet on the floor
Sitting with feet slightly plantar flexed
Standing on tiptoes with active dorsiflexion
explanation:
Morton neuroma

Fibrosis surrounding a plantar digital nerve leads to a hard lump developing in the sole of the foot. Patients complain of a painful lump which feels a bit like walking on a hot lump of gravel. On an MRI scan they are often slightly disguised by their low or isointensity to muscle on T1 weighted sequences and hypointensity on T2 weighted sequences. Curiously for a fibrotic process, they do usually enhance with gadolinium. On ultrasound the classic appearance of a hypoechoic mass situated between but slightly proximal to the metatarsal heads should be sufficient to make the diagnosis. Most are found in the third metatarsal space. The Mulder sign can be performed clinically or with ultrasound and involves eliciting pain and a clicking sound when the metatarsal heads are squeezed together while applying pressure on the dorsum of the foot over the neuroma, or scanning the sole of the foot.

It is said that Morton neuromas are larger and easier to visualise with MRI when the patient is prone, i.e. the foot is slightly plantar-flexed. On ultrasound this translates to a straightforward prone position or one where the patient is sitting on the side of the couch with their feet slightly plantar flexed. One theory is that any physical tension through the metatarsal joints (more likely on supine positioning) causes the neuroma to be pulled up in-between the metatarsal heads.

stem: A 19-year-old man suffers a severe motorbike accident and is brought into A+E. His initial CT is reported as showing bilateral temporal and frontal hypodensities. The following day his GCS deteriorates and he is taken for a second CT scan.
prompt: What are the likely imaging findings?
options: Crescenteric high attenuation overlying the left cerebral hemisphere
High attenuation in the left sylvian fissure
Lentiform high attenuation underlying the left temporal bone
New high density of previous areas of low density
explanation: The question pertains to the development of haemorrhage within an area of cerebral oedema. This may become more apparent a day or so following the injury. The other answers given describe extradural, subdural, subarachnoid and intraventricular haemorrhages. Cerebral contusions tend to be found in areas of the brain adjacent to bone. The ‘coup’ injury occurs at the site of impact and the ‘contracoup’ injury is found diametrically opposite it.

stem: A 53-year-old man has AP and lateral radiographs of the right ankle after twisting it whilst playing football. There is no fracture seen, however a central, triangular radiolucent area is seen on the lateral projection in the talar dome. It is well defined with a narrow zone of transition and communicates with the joint space.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Geode

This is a subchondral cyst associated with osteoarthritis which should have communication with the joint space and be present in an older patient.

Pseudo-cyst of calcaneus

This is a variation of the normal trabecular pattern centrally within the calcaneus. Will not have a crisp edge for this reason. Persistence of thin trabeculae and a visible nutrient foramen are supporting features.

Unicameral bone cyst

This is a well-defined lesion with thick sclerotic edges and potentially a multiloculated appearance. Absence of calcification within the lesion is a key differentiator from intraosseous lipoma, although if fractured, a fallen fragment sign can be seen.

Intraosseus lipoma

Calcification within the center of this lesion is a key feature which differentiates it from other lesions of plain film. Fat density on CT or MRI would also be a key differentiator.

Chondroblastoma

The calcaneus, like the patella, is an epiphyseal equivalent, so any epiphyseal lesions should be considered a possibility in this bone. They usually arise eccentrically in the epiphysis, are lobuated with a thin sclerotic margin.

stem: A 29-year-old man sprains his right ankle playing football and attends the Emergency Department. An x-ray of the right ankle is performed. There is no evidence of a fracture but the lateral view does demonstrate a well defined radiolucent lesion with a faint sclerotic margin in the calcaneus. The lesion has some calcification centrally.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Intraosseous lipoma

These benign lesions can present with pain but around a third of cases are diagnosed incidentally. The classic location for them is the calcaneum but they do occur all around the body. On x-ray they appear as a lucent bone lesion with a thin cortex and no periosteal reaction. Some show dystrophic calcifications. On MRI signal characteristics follow fat with high signal on T1 and signal loss on fat suppression sequences. The presence of granulation tissue can give high signal and calcifications, if present, will return low signal. On CT the fat within the lesion will show low/negative Hounsfield units.

Enchondroma

As the name suggests, this is a cartilage forming tumour showing ground-glass matrix and ring or arc calcifications (as with all cartilage forming tumours). Patients are typically young (10-30 years) and the lesions are typically found in the hands (although they can form anywhere in the body. In the hands they are unusual to be found in the terminal phalanges). They are thought to derive from ongoing growth of small foci of cartilage which have become displaced from the growth plate. They can expand the cortex but, unless presenting as a fracture, should be painless and therefore are often an incidental diagnosis. Although they are benign tumours, malignant degeneration to a chondrosarcoma can occur.

Unicameral bone cyst also known as simple bone cyst

These benign, asymptomatic lesions are almost always found in children in the metaphyseal region of long bones. They can, however, present with pain from a fracture, in which case the ‘fallen fragment’ sign is almost pathognomonic. This occurs when a small piece of the thin cortex overlying the lesion breaks off and is seen dependant within the cyst. Otherwise on x-ray they appear as a lucent bone lesion with a narrow zone of transition, no periosteal reaction and no soft tissue component. Since they are fluid-filled they return high signal on T2 weighted MRI sequences.

Causes of bone infarction:

Sickle cell disease

Excess corticosteroid

Pancreatitis

Caisson disease ‘The Bends’

Gaucher disease

Leukemia/lymphoma

Medullary osteonecrosis can be secondary to anything leading to vascular compromise and has the propensity to lead to severe loss or architecture and loss of function, not to mention pain, to the patient. It is an important diagnosis to make. On plain film the finding is usually of a lucent area with a sclerotic serpiginous border of granulation tissue. On MRI this serpiginous border returns low signal on T1 and a ‘double-line’ sign on T2 (high signal of granulation tissue surrounded by low signal of sclerosis). Strangely enough, centrally within the infarction the signal retains the characteristics of normal fatty marrow.

stem: You are reviewing the radiographs of a 40-year-old marathon runner who has been experiencing worsening hip pains over the last few months. There is over-coverage of the left femoral head by the acetabulum.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Femoroacetabular impingement (FAI)

Mixed type - >80% of patients have components of both cam-type and pincer-type FAI.

Cam type - a cam is an engineering term for an oval/egg shaped component with a hole through the middle of the wider end. In cam type FAI the femoral head takes on a 'cam' shaped appearance due to bony overgrowth at the superior aspect of the femoral neck. This abnormal bony contour impinges against the anterosuperior aspect of the acetabulum during movement. The condition occurs more frequently in men and tends to affect men in their 30s. Certain conditions can predispose to cam-type FAI, including SUFE, DDH and Perthes disease. Some patients with cam-type FAI exhibit femoral retroversion.

Pincer type - here bony protuberance of the anterosuperior acetabulum causes over-coverage of the femoral head and impingement against the femoral neck. Protrusio acetabuli predisposes to pincer-type FAI. The relationship of the overgrown anterior acetabular rim to the posterior acetabular rim in pincer-type FAI is called acetabular retroversion since it causes the femoral neck to twist posteriorly. Patients usually stand with their toes pointing outwards as a consequence. The condition is more common in women and a patient is typically aged around 40.

stem: An 18-year-old boy dislocates his knee playing sport. His knee is successfully reduced in the A+E. His dorsalis pedis pulse is found to be absent subsequently, but his foot remains pink.
prompt: What is the most likely explanation?
options: Dissection of the anterior tibial artery
explanation: Arterial injury is surprisingly common with knee injuries and the exact mechanism of injury bears equally surprisingly little relation to the vascular injury sustained. The dorsalis pedis artery is a continuation of the anterior tibial artery, itself a distal branch of the popliteal artery. In simplistic terms for the foot to remain pink there ought to be ongoing supply to it which would be via the posterior tibial artery. The branches of the popliteal artery are often referred to as a trifurcation. In reality the anterior tibial artery is usually given off first followed by a bifurcation into the posterior tibial and common peroneal arteries. The exact height where the anterior tibial artery begins is variable. A notably high origin can complicate access to the popliteal artery.

stem: An 8-year-old girl is tackled during a football training session and is unable to weight-bear. An x-ray in A+E shows a medial malleolar fracture but also a lucent expansile bone lesion in distal tibial metaphysis which has thin sclerotic borders. The astute clerking doctor also notices pigmented patches on patients back. She goes on to have a nuclear medicine bone scan on which the lesion is shows high uptake.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
This patient has McCune-Albright syndrome

Fibrous dysplasia

This tends to be a condition of childhood-adolescence. It is otherwise rarely seen in patients older than 30. It is a benign condition caused by abnormal osteoblasts and leading to focal replacement of normal bone with fibrous tissue. Most cases are monostotic but polyostotic cases occur around 20% of the time. Virtually any bone can be affected although the long bones tend to be more frequently affected in the polyostotic form. That said, fibrous dysplasia is also a typical differential diagnosis for a rib or skull lesion.

Classically the appearances on x-ray or CT is described as 'ground glass' in matrix, and situated within the centre of the bone (i.e. medullary), but often causing bony expansion. Since the bone is abnormal there is an increased risk of fractures but unless there is an acute injury there should not be a periosteal reaction.

On a nuclear medicine bone scan the lesions tend to show increased uptake and this is therefore rarely useful in diagnosing this condition.

Aside from pathological fractures, the condition can also occasionally be complicated by secondary degeneration which would be to osteosarcoma and should be suspected if the patient complains of pain and the growth of a soft tissue mass. This occurs more frequently in patients who have previously been exposed to radiation.

There are a number of eponymous or descriptive terms associated with fibrous dysplasia:

Shepherds crook deformity - coxa varus deformity of the proximal femur. This is usually used to describe the effect of fibrous dysplasia on the proximal femur with chronic bowing and remodelling secondary to microfractures, but the same appearance can occur with conditions such as Paget disease or osteogenesis imperfecta, for the same reasons.

Protrusio acetabuli - fibrous dysplasia is one of a number of things which can cause protrusion of the femoral head into the pelvis due to remodelling of the acetabulum.

Leontiasis ossea - facial involvement causing a specific appearance said to resemble that of a lion. Owing to canal stenosis caused by bony expansion patients can exhibit cranial nerve palsies.

Cherubism - facial (maxilla and mandible) involvement causes a specific appearance said to resemble that of a cherub. Owing to canal stenosis caused by bony expansion patients can exhibit cranial nerve palsies. Cherubism is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion.

McCune-Albright syndrome - this almost always only affects girls and consists of a triad of cafe-au-lait spots, precocious puberty (or other endocrine pathology), and polyostotic fibrous dysplasia. The cafe-au-lait pigmentation is often on the back and can commonly be seen to respect the midline.

Mazabraud syndrome - this is a very rare condition. Patients present with polyostotic fibrous dysplasia and soft tissue tumours and are at increased risk of malignant degeneration to osteosarcoma.

Histiocytosis (Langerhans cell histiocytosis - LCH)

There are three separate forms of this disease:

Eosinophilic granuloma (70%) – a limited version confined to the skeleton in children or young adults. Clinically presents as fever, raised WCC and ESR with painful bony lesions. In the skull these have a typical ‘beveled edge’ or ‘hole within a hole’ appearance or can be seen as a ‘button sequestrum’. In the spine it is one of the main causes of vertebra plana.

Hand-Schüller-Christian Disease (20%) – classically a triad of destructive bony lesions, diabetes insipidus and exophthalmos. In a quarter of these patients the lungs are involved with cyst formation and spontaneous pneumothoraces possible. Nodule formation, fibrosis and honeycombing are also seen.

Letterer-Siwe Disease (10%) – a fulminant multi-organ variant affecting very young infants.

There is a strong association with smoking for patients who develop pulmonary features of LCH. Heavy smoking causes an accumulation of Langerhans cells and hence, as with other inspiration-related lung diseases, there is a predilection for the upper zones. The Langerhans cells can collect with other cells and become small granulomas seen as small lung nodules. Despite being a type of fibrotic lung disease the lung volumes can be increased. Small lung cysts form and there is a risk of spontaneous pneumothorax. There is usually sparing of the costophrenic angles which can be a key finding.

Giant Cell Tumour also known as osteoclastoma

These are benign bony tumours arising from within bone. They can cause bony expansion from within but not bony scalloping from without. Since they always occur in the mature skeleton they are seldom found in children or adolescent patients although the peak age group is still young; 30s. Typically they occur around the knee but can be found anywhere in the skeleton. They are seen on x-ray as expansile lytic lesions with the words ‘soap bubble’ often used to describe them in literature. On MRI they usually return low signal on both T1 and T2, in contrast to many of the potential differential diagnoses which would otherwise return high signal on one or the other.

stem: A 23-year-old woman is brought in by ambulance having been involved in a road traffic accident. A FAST scan is performed to check for a haemoperitoneum.
prompt: In which of the following areas is free fluid most likely to be seen if a haemoperitoneum is present? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
A Focussed Assessment with Sonography for Trauma (FAST) scan is a point-of-care ultrasound examination performed at the time of presentation of a trauma patient.

The main aim of a FAST scan is to identify intra-abdominal free fluid (assumed to be haemoperitoneum in the context of trauma). This helps to make decisions about further management.

Sensitivity of FAST scanning is in the region of 90% and specificity of is approximately 95% for detecting intraperitoneal fluid. The sensitivity for detecting solid organ injuries is much lower. It has now largely replaced diagnostic peritoneal lavage as the preferred initial method for assessment of haemoperitoneum.

Four regions are assessed during a standard FAST scan:

Subxiphoid transverse view: assess for pericardial effusion and left lobe liver injuries

Longitudinal view of the right upper quadrant: assess for right liver injuries, right kidney injury and fluid in the hepatorenal recess (Morison’s pouch)

Longitudinal view of the left upper quadrant: assess for splenic injury and left kidney injury

Transverse and longitudinal views of the suprapubic region: assess the bladder and fluid in the pouch of Douglas

An ‘extended FAST’ or ‘eFAST’ may also be performed that looks at the left and right thoracic that helps to assess for the presence of pneumothorax and haemothorax.

The hepatorenal recess is the deepest part of the peritoneal cavity when lying supine. It is therefore the most likely place for fluid to accumulate in a patient lying flat.

Ultrasound scan showing free fluid in the hepatorenal recess

stem: A 24-year-old woman sustains a direct facial injury during a cricket match. She is brought to the Emergency Department with extensive facial and orbital injuries and undergoes a CT scan for further evaluation.
prompt: Which of the following is NOT a sign of globe rupture? Select ONE answer only.
options: An irregular contour to the posterior segment
Focal low density in posterior segment
Increase depth to the anterior chamber
explanation:
Please note that the question asks which is NOT a sign of globe rupture.

A coloboma is a known mimic for globe rupture.

Globe rupture

This injury obviously has the propensity to cause significant long-term morbidity to the patient. Straightforward cases, as seen on a trauma CT, will show significant morphological change to the normal shape of the globe with a large overall reduction in globe volume. In the case of a penetrating mechanism of injury, the presence of a foreign body within the posterior chamber is also diagnostic of a globe rupture. Similarly, the presence of intra-ocular gas also implies a globe rupture.

A more subtle sign of globe rupture paradoxically includes an increase to the depth of the anterior chamber due to posterior displacement of the lens occurring in the context of a posterior segment rupture and subsequent loss of pressure there.

A coloboma is a focal defect in the posterior aspect of the globe with outpouching which can be quite striking in size. This is a congenital defect though, not a post-traumatic one. The finding can be unilateral or bilateral with the latter more suggestive of a syndromic association.

A staphyloma is a broader based defect in the globe, which can be located anywhere. It occurs due to degenerative thinning of the sclera and is seen as a smooth contour irregularity on cross-sectional imaging.

stem: You are reviewing the cervical spine x-rays from a 20-year-old woman. There is an obvious block vertebra affecting the C2 and C3 vertebral bodies.
prompt: Which of the following is a cause of block vertebra?
explanation:
There is a differential diagnosis for block vertebra and although Sprengel shoulder features as a predominant part of Klippel-Feil syndrome, an isolated sprengel shoulder is not a cause of block vertebra.

Differential diagnosis for block vertebra

Congenital

Klippel-Feil

Isolated

Arthritides

Rheumatoid arthritis

Ankylosing spondylitis

Miscllaneous

Post-operative

Post-traumatic fusion

Post-Tuberculosis infection

Sprengel shoulder

This condition can occur in isolation as well as part of Klippel-Feil syndrome. It is (like Klippel-Feil syndrome) also often associated with renal anomalies. Sprengel shoulder is a congenital abnormality where the scapula (usually, but not exclusively, unilateral) is attached to the cervical vertebra either by a fibrous or osseous connection, and therefore fails to descend into the normal position. The result is elevation and medial rotation of the scapula, which is usually hypoplastic. The condition can be readily appreciated on a plain film although cross-sectional imaging is useful to plan surgical correction if required. If present, the osseous connection between the scapula and the spine is termed an omovertebral bar.

Klippel-Feil syndrome

(different from Klippel-Trenaunay-Weber syndrome: port-wine stains, localised hypertrophy and venous malformations)

Klippel-Feil syndrome is predominantly a segmentation anomaly which arises during foetal development and leads to cervical fusion of two or more vertebral bodies. C2-3 are most commonly involved, accounting for around half of cases. Thereafter C5-6 accounts for a further third and the remainder are made up from fusions at other levels. There are a multitude of associated features, the predominant ones of which include:

Main associations and frequency

Renal abnormalities (of which a third have unilateral renal agenesis)

⅔

Scoliosis >20o

½

Sprengel shoulder

⅓

Deafness (Sensorineural)

⅓

Cervical ribs

⅕

The renal anomalies seen include agenesis or dysgenesis, ectopic location, and duplication.

Yet further features of this condition, all present in under 20% of cases include:

Odontoid dysplasia

Hemivertebrae / butterfly vertebrae

Syringomyelia / diastomatomyelia

Ear anomalies (microtia, deformed ossicles etc)

Congenital heart disease (ASD or coarctation)

Holt-Oram syndrome

This syndrome is associated with numerous skeletal and cardiac malformations. It is usually evident either antenatally or in the early neonatal period.

Cardiac manifestations include either ASD or VSD, tetralogy of Fallot and coarctation.

Perhaps most strikingly the condition is often associated with radial ray hypoplasia often meaning the absence of one or both thumbs. An x-ray may show absence or hypoplasia of one or both radii.

stem: A 34-year-old man suffers a knee injury while on a skiing holiday. He visits a local hospital and has x-rays taken of his knee. No fracture is found. Once back home he undergoes an MRI scan when the pain fails to resolve. He is told he has a clip injury.
prompt: What findings on MRI would be most consistent with this?
options: High STIR signal to the anterior aspect of the tibia with an associated posterior cruciate ligament tear
High T2 signal to the anterior aspect of the lateral femoral condyle and lateral tibial plateau with an anterior cruciate ligament and medial collateral ligament tear
High signal on STIR to the lateral femoral condyle and posterolateral tibial plateau with an associated tear of the anterior cruciate ligament tear
High signal on T2 and STIR to the anterior aspect of the tibia with an associated anterior cruciate ligament tear
High signal on T2 to the lateral femoral condyle and medial patella facet with an associated tear of the medial retinaculum
explanation:
Bony contusions

Bruising to the bone can be detected around 2 days following an injury but may not resolve for many months thereafter. With regards knee injuries, it is often possible to discern the mechanism of injury from the pattern of bruising seen. The contusions follow fluid on MRI scans i.e. low in signal on T1 and high on T2 (and STIR). STIR is used to suppress the fat of the bone marrow thereby making the fluid stand out more.

Clip injury and pivot shift injury

- High signal on STIR to the lateral femoral condyle and posterolateral tibial plateau with an associated tear of the anterior cruciate ligament tear (Pivot shift)

- High T2 signal to the anterior aspect of the lateral femoral condyle and lateral tibial plateau with an anterior cruciate ligament and medial collateral ligament tear (Clip injury)

These two injuries are very similar. Both involve valgus stress on a flexed knee (such as a tackle to the knee during sports). A pivot shift injury also requires external rotation of the tibia. The three main structures most at risk during these injuries are:

Anterior cruciate ligament (especially in a pivot shift injury)

Medial collateral ligament (especially in a clip injury)

Medial meniscus (remember that the medial meniscus is attached to the medial collateral ligament)

If all three are present together it is referred to as the O’Donoghue triad. Since O’Donoghue defined this triad however, it has been discovered that lateral meniscal tears are actually more common with this type of injury than medial meniscus ones.

Bony contusions occur at the side of impact because the proximal tibia and distal femur impact on one another thus:

Lateral tibial plateau (posterolateral in pivot shift injury)

Lateral femoral condyle

Transient lateral patella dislocation injury - High signal on T2 to the lateral femoral condyle and medial patella facet with an associated tear of the medial retinaculum

When the patella dislocates laterally, its medial facet can impact onto the anterolateral corner of the lateral femoral condyle. Both areas become damaged and contusions can be seen on MRI. Often though, the patella reduces spontaneously and thus the exact mechanism of injury must be inferred from the imaging findings.

Joint effusion

Osteochondral injuries to the anterolateral femoral condyle and medial patella facet

Sprain or disruption to the medial retinaculum

Hyperextension injury - High signal on T2 and STIR to the anterior aspect of the tibia with an associated anterior cruciate ligament tear

These occur often following excessively forceful kicking. There will be bony contusions at the anterior aspect of the tibial plateau and femoral condyles. Either of the anterior or posterior cruciate ligaments may also be involved.

Dashboard injury - High STIR signal to the anterior aspect of the tibia with an associated posterior cruciate ligament tear

As the name would suggest, this injury is usually stained by impact of the knee against the dashboard of a car during a road traffic incident. Force applied to the anterior aspect of the tibia when the knee is flexed leads to:

Osteochondral injury or fracture to the anterior aspect of the tibia

Posterior cruciate ligament rupture/sprain

stem: A 24-year-old woman presents with reduced sensation in her ring and little fingers. The neurologist suspects cubital tunnel syndrome and requests an MRI scan. This demonstrates a band of intermediate signal tissue isointense to muscle originating at the olecranon and inserting onto the medial epicondyle.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation: Cubital tunnel syndrome is often the result of repetitive valgus stress. Where the ulnar nerve passess under the cubital tunnel retinaculum, this point is known as Osbourne’s band. The question describes an accessory muscle; anconeus epitrochlearis which is the most common accessory muscle to cause ulnar nerve compression and can be surgically removed/ released.

stem: A 40-year-old woman presents with an uncomfortable swelling at the back of her right knee. On examination you palpate a round, smooth, fluctuant mass within the popliteal fossa. An ultrasound scan confirms that she has a Baker's cyst.
prompt: Which of the following muscles forms the superomedial border of the popliteal fossa? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
The popliteal fossa is a diamond shaped depression situated at the back of the knee joint. It acts as the main conduit for the neurovascular structures entering and leaving the leg.

The borders of the popliteal fossa are:

Superomedial border: semimembranosus

Superolateral border: biceps femoris

Inferomedial border: medial head of gastrocnemius

Inferolateral border: lateral head of gastrocnemius and plantaris

The roof of the popliteal fossa is formed by (from superficial to deep):

Skin

Superficial fascia

Deep (popliteal) fascia

The floor of the popliteal fossa is formed by:

Popliteal surface of the femur

Capsule of the knee joint

Fascia covering the popliteus muscle

The contents of the popliteal fossa (from medial to lateral) are:

Popliteal artery

Popliteal vein

Tibial nerve

Common peroneal nerve

The tibial and common peroneal nerves are the most superficial of the contents of the popliteal fossa. The deepest structure is the popliteal artery. The small saphenous vein pierces the deep fascia to enter the popliteal fossa. The popliteal lymph nodes surround the vessels.

The popliteal fossa and its contents, with the popliteal lymph nodes in blue (from Gray’s Anatomy)

stem: A patient cuts his arm on a glass whilst working as a waiter. He experiences some wrist weakness once the initial incision has healed and undergoes an MRI scan for evaluation. There is damage to the palmaris longus muscle as a consequence of the injury.
prompt: Which SINGLE statement regarding the palmaris longus muscle is NOT correct?
options: It arises from the common origin on the medial epicondyle of the humerus
It is a strong flexor of the wrist joint
It is innervated by the median nerve
It is often used in tendon grafts for the wrist
It receives its blood supply from the ulnar artery
explanation:
Palmaris longus is a muscle that lies in the anterior compartment of the forearm. It is absent in approximately 15% of the population but absence of the muscle does not have an effect on grip strength.

It arises from the common origin on the medial epicondyle of the humerus and inserts into the distal half of the flexor retinaculum and into the palmar aponeurosis.

Palmaris longus is innervated by the median nerve and receives its blood supply from the ulnar artery.

Palmaris longus is a weak flexor of the wrist and also acts to tighten the palmar aponeurosis. It is often used in tendon grafts for the wrist because of the length and diameter of the tendon, and because it can be used without producing any functional deformity.

If present it can easily be seen and palpated in the midline by touching the tips of the little finger and thumb together whilst the wrist is in flexion:

stem: An 8-year-old girl is tackled during a football training session and is unable to weight-bear. An x-ray in A+E shows a medial malleolar fracture but also a distal tibial lesion thought to be fibrous dysplasia.
prompt: Which of the following is NOT part of the spectrum of fibrous dysplasia? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Please note that the question asks which answer is NOT related to fibrous dysplasia.

This patient has McCune-Albright syndrome

Fibrous dysplasia

This tends to be a condition of childhood-adolescence. It is otherwise rarely seen in patients older than 30. It is a benign condition caused by abnormal osteoblasts and leading to focal replacement of normal bone with fibrous tissue. Most cases are monostotic but polyostotic cases occur around 20% of the time. Virtually any bone can be affected although the long bones tend to be more frequently affected in the polyostotic form. That said, fibrous dysplasia is also a typical differential diagnosis for a rib or skull lesion.

Classically the appearances on x-ray or CT is described as 'ground glass' in matrix, and situated within the centre of the bone (i.e. medullary), but often causing bony expansion. Since the bone is abnormal there is an increased risk of fractures but unless there is an acute injury there should not be a periosteal reaction.

On a nuclear medicine bone scan the lesions tend to show increased uptake and this is therefore rarely useful in diagnosing this condition.

Aside from pathological fractures, the condition can also occasionally be complicated by secondary degeneration which would be to osteosarcoma and should be suspected if the patient complains of pain and the growth of a soft tissue mass. This occurs more frequently in patients who have previously been exposed to radiation.

There are a number of eponymous or descriptive terms associated with fibrous dysplasia:

Shepherds crook deformity - coxa varus deformity of the proximal femur. This is usually used to describe the effect of fibrous dysplasia on the proximal femur with chronic bowing and remodelling secondary to microfractures, but the same appearance can occur with conditions such as Paget disease or osteogenesis imperfecta, for the same reasons.

Protrusio acetabuli - fibrous dysplasia is one of a number of things which can cause protrusion of the femoral head into the pelvis due to remodelling of the acetabulum.

Leontiasis ossea - facial involvement causing a specific appearance said to resemble that of a lion. Owing to canal stenosis caused by bony expansion patients can exhibit cranial nerve palsies.

Cherubism - facial (maxilla and mandible) involvement causes a specific appearance said to resemble that of a cherub. Owing to canal stenosis caused by bony expansion patients can exhibit cranial nerve palsies. Cherubism is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion.

McCune-Albright syndrome - this almost always only affects girls and consists of a triad of cafe-au-lait spots, precocious puberty (or other endocrine pathology), and polyostotic fibrous dysplasia. The cafe-au-lait pigmentation is often on the back and can commonly be seen to respect the midline.

Mazabraud syndrome - this is a very rare condition. Patients present with polyostotic fibrous dysplasia and soft tissue tumours and are at increased risk of malignant degeneration to osteosarcoma.

Hand-Schüller-Christian Disease is a type of histiocytosis.

stem: A 77-year-old man with a ruptured AAA has an emergency open repair. Post-operatively he develops lower back pain and incontinence. An MRI shows focal high T2 signal in the cord with mild cord swelling.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The anterior spinal artery of Adamkiewicz can be compromised following acute aortic pathology. Ischaemia to the cord gives the symptoms and imaging findings given.

Guillain-Barre syndrome which is an autoimmune mediated ascending flaccid paralysis. Most imaging will be normal in such cases, with the exception of some possible contrast enhancement and thickening to the nerve roots at the cauda equina.

Brown-Sequard syndrome refers to hemisection of the cord causing ipsilateral loss of touch and vibration sense with contralateral loss of pain and temperature sense.

Vitamin B12 deficiency classically gives the appearance of an ‘inverted V’ sign of symmetrical high signal in the dorsal columns.

Thiamine deficiency causes high T2 signal in the thalami, among other features.

stem: A 59-year-old lady undergoes an MRI of her spine. Six months previously she had received radiotherapy to lumbar spine as part of management of breast carcinoma.
prompt: Which of the following is the most likely appearance of the bone marrow?
options: High on T1, high on T2
High on T1, isointense on T2
Isointense on T1, low on T2
Low on T1, low on T2
Very high on T1, isointense on T2
explanation:
Favours osteoporosis

Favours metastases

Retropulsed bony fragments

Convex posterior cortex

Fluid adjacent to the fractured end plates

Associated soft tissue masses

Multiple compression fractures

Other metastases without compression fractures

Sparing of the marrow signal

Marrow signal abnormalities

Involvement of the posterior elements of the spine

Bone marrow on MRI

T1

T2

Normal bone marrow

High (fatty)

Intermediate

Post-Radiotherapy

Very high and homogenous

Intermediate (initially high due to oedema)

Haemangioma

High

High

Abnormal bone (metastases, myeloma, regeneration)

Low but enhances with Gadolinium

High (fluid)

Blastic metastases (prostate, breast, TCC) and myelofibrosis

Low

Metastases

Normally metastatic deposits in the spine lead to low T1 signal and high T2 signal. There should be no signal drop out on fat saturated sequences in contrast to marrow reconversion where although red marrow will experience far less signal dropout than yellow marrow, there will still be some loss in signal owing to the fat content of both types of marrow.

Sclerotic or blastic metastases return little signal on either T1 or T2 weighted sequences. These include prostate, breast or TCC metastases among others.

Breast cancer can cause lytic or sclerotic metastases or a mixed picture.

Lytic metastases are more likely than sclerotic metastases to enhance with contrast. Similarly on DWI imaging, whereas lytic metastases will usually appear hyperintense, sclerotic metastases return little signal since they contain little water.

If there is a diffuse abnormality of the bone marrow it can be difficult to identify but normal bone marrow should not be lower in signal intensity than the muscle on T1 weighted sequences.

stem: A 45-year-old man has acute on chronic left-hand pain and swelling. In addition, he has complained of right elbow swelling for the last five years. Clinical examination revealed swelling surrounding the MCP and IP joints throughout the left hand. The patient had elevated uric acid levels, as well as elevated CRP and ESR levels. A frontal radiograph demonstrates multiple well-circumscribed juxta-articular erosions with over-hanging edges and multiple cloudy soft tissue nodules.
prompt: Considering the diagnosis which of the following modalities is best for disease quantification?
explanation:
The overall tophus burden or volume of uric acid deposition may be calculated for individual lesions, joints, or the entire scanned area. Its ability to quantify tophi without significant user variability makes dual-energy CT an ideal tool for evaluating even small changes in tophus burden, and it may be used to document response to treatment for purposes of daily practice.

Because dual-energy CT may directly depict urate crystal deposition, it is specifically used to evaluate for gout regardless of the patient’s serum urate levels. Thus, dual-energy CT findings may easily confirm a diagnosis of gout in patients with normal serum urate levels or exclude it in patients with hyperuricemia.

Dual-energy CT may depict subclinical urate crystal deposition at other asymptomatic sites that have been included in the imaging field, which helps establish a diagnosis of gout and enables initiation of treatment before irreversible joint damage occurs.

topic: Differentiating between an AVM and an AVF
stem: A 60-year-old man with progressive bilateral leg weakness presents to his GP. He is referred for an urgent MRI which shows multiple tortuous tubes with signal voids on the posterior aspect of the cauda equina on both T1 and T2. Subtle bumps along the surface of the cord are seen and the conus appears expanded with high signal on T2.
prompt: Which of the following will help differentiate between an AVM and an AVF?
options: The presence or absence of a clear nidus
Venous drainage in the arterial phase during angiography
explanation: Subarachnoid haemorrhage is actually reasonably rare in AVF although it can happen. A history of trauma would point towards the lesion being an AVF and is therefore a potentially viable answer for this question too however on balance the presence or absence of a nidus is more definitive. Logically, although a history of trauma may be given and can be seen to be related in population demographic terms, this is less certain for individual cases whereas a nidus is an unequivocal finding.

stem: A 78-year-old lady falls while walking her dog and a fractured neck of femur is suspected. She has a history of stage III node negative breast cancer dating back 15 years. The pelvic x-ray shows multiple small sclerotic foci in the pelvic girdle and both femora, which are subsequently found to have slightly increased uptake on a bone scan.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Osteopoikilosis

This benign condition leads to multiple small oval bone islands forming around the skeleton. It usually looks absolutely characteristic and review of old films would confirm the diagnosis, however it has been (deliberately) poorly described in the question.  Frustrating though this may be, it is reflective of the nature of some of the questions in the exam.

Purportedly, once the epiphyses have fused the number remains static. They can (albeit rarely, such that many sources say ‘never’ happens) show mildly increased uptake on a nuclear medicine bone scan. Whereas a bone island may exist in isolation or near isolation, the finding of multiple such lesions suggests the diagnosis of osteopoikilosis.

Since osteopoikilosis is a condition consisting of multiple bone islands, the answer option of 'bone islands' is also technically correct. Given the choice (arguably unfair though it may be) between these two options, osteopoikilosis is a more specific entity and deemed to be correct in this case.

stem: A 40-year-old amateur rower presents with wrist pain. An MRI reveals high signal within, and increased fluid surrounding the extensor carpi radialis brevis and longus tendons as they cross over the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Intersection syndrome

This is tendonitis at the intersection between the 1st and 2nd compartments (1st compartment- extensor pollicis brevis and abductor pollicis longus, 2nd compartment- extensor carpi radialis brevis and longus). It is classically seen in rowers.

DeQuervains syndrome

This affects the first dorsal compartment (extensor pollicis brevis and abductor pollicis longus) tenosynovitis. It is more common in women.

Rheumatoid arthritis

Multiple flexor tendonitis can precede joint involvement, however tendonitis at the 1st/ 2nd tendon is specific for intersection syndrome.

Early Dupuytren contracture

Commonly occurs in people with alcoholic liver disease. Early Dupuytren is a nodular mass on the on the palmar aspect of the aponeurosis.

stem: A 38-year-old man complains to his GP of ongoing knee pains. An x-ray is requested which shows subchondral sclerosis with cyst formation. There is loss of joint space affecting the patellofemoral compartment only; the medial and lateral compartments of the knee are well preserved. Cartilage calcification is also evident. The man goes on to have an aspiration.
prompt: Which kind of crystals are most likely to be found?
explanation:
Calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate disease (CPPD) also known as pseudogout

CPPD can present in an acute or subacute fashion but is also seen as a chronic cause of joint inflammation. It may be misdiagnosed as simple osteoarthritis owing to its often bilateral and symmetrical distribution but there are also a couple of areas of the body which can be affected in particular, and which would be unusual for isolated degenerative changes.

The patellofemoral joint – joint space loss here can be extremely striking with almost complete preservation of the joint space at the medial and lateral compartments of the knee

Triangular fibrocartilatinous complex of the wrist – calcification

Radiocarpal joints – degenerative changes without involvement of the DIPs and PIPs

Soft tissue calcification is common and chondrocalcinosis is also classical. The formation of unusually large subchondral cysts is often seen and sometimes these can be so large that they are mistaken for giant cell tumours.

Gout

Excess circulating urate levels leads to crystalisation of urate (monosodium urate crystals) within the joint spaces. An acute attack may be precipitated by any acute event such as trauma or surgery as well as a change in diet to include purine containing foods (liver, kidney, game meat, some seafood, alcohol). Historically chronic manifestations of this condition included the development of gouty tophi; white lumpy areas under the skin which could ulcerate and exude a chalky material. These are still seen today but far less so thanks to improved management strategies. Involvement of the first metatarsophalangeal joint is considered classical but involvement of the carpometacarpal joints of the hands is often most debilitating where it occurs. On x-ray the earliest radiological manifestation is a joint effusion. Joint erosions develop on the lateral corners of a joint but contrary to many other erosive processes the base of the ulcers has a sclerotic margin. Juxta-articular osteopenia is not often seen, a feature which acts as a good distinguisher from rheumatoid arthritis, which is thought to be because the attacks come in acute bursts during which time disuse osteopenia does not have the time to develop. Another reasonably specific feature of gouty arthritis is the preservation of the joint space itself until relatively late into the disease.

Crystals

Gout

Pseudogout

Content

Monosodium urate

Calcium pyrophosphate dehydrate

Shape

Needle

Rhomboid

Birefringence

Strongly negative

Weakly positive

stem: You are performing an ultrasound scan on a 54-year-old man who has a suspected rotator cuff tear. You are trying to see the subscapularis tendon.
prompt: How should you position the patient's arm to see this tendon best?
options: Arm held posteriorly with elbow flexed
Forced internal rotation with hand in the small of the back
Internal rotation with hand pointing to the contralateral knee
explanation:
There are a number of different manoeuvers which can greatly improve visibility of the rotator cuff muscles and tendons when performing a shoulder ultrasound. The basic principle revolves around attempting to straighten each tendon out.

Subscapularis

Courtesy of Anamotography CC BY-SA 2.1 jp

External rotation and adduction - with palm up and flexed elbow, fix the elbow to the side of the patient as much as possible and rotate the humerus externally by swinging the hand outwards.

Supraspinatus

There are two positions which can be used to see the supraspinatus tendon.

Forced internal rotation - Place the patients hand in the small of their back

Flex the elbow and direct the arm posteriorly by placing the patients hand on their ipsilateral back pocket

The supraspinatus attaches to the greater tuberosity and both these manoeuvers cause internal rotation to a greater or lesser extent whilst the posterior placement of the arm stretches the tendon out further.

Long head of biceps

The long head of biceps is usually relatively easy to find and requires less manipulation to image optimally however in theory it is best imaged with the elbow flexed and hand pointing towards the contralateral knee with the palm facing upwards.

Subacromial impingement test

As the supraspinatus passes between the acromion and coracoid processes it can experience impingement. By abducting the arm in internal rotation the supraspinatus muscle can be observed as it moves within this space.

Infraspinatus and teres minor

Place the patients hand anteriorly on their contralateral shoulder. This internally rotates the humerus and extends both infraspinatus and teres minor which sit below the spine of the scapula.

Both muscles can also be imaged in the same position as for the long head of biceps tendon.

stem: You are reviewing the MRI of a 64-year-old man. There are multiple lesions in the vertebral bodies which return low signal on T1 and high signal on T2 weighted sequences. In the periphery of the images you also notice hepatosplenomegaly.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Both lymphoma and myelofibrosis can cause hepatosplenomegaly but the bone marrow in myelofibrosis becomes replaced fibrous tissue which returns very little signal on any sequence. In contrast, abnormal bone marrow in a lymphoma patient returns high signal on T2 weighted sequences.

Bone marrow on MRI

T1

T2

Intermediate

Post-Radiotherapy

Intermediate (initially high due to oedema)

Haemangioma

Low but enhances with Gadolinium

High (fluid)

Blastic metastases (prostate, breast, TCC) and myelofibrosis

Low

Low

Age

Marrow

Birth

Largely red marrow with low fat content   → looks like skeletal muscle i.e low on T1

Adolescence

Yellow marrow at the diaphyses      → high on T1

Red marrow with low fat content     → low to iso on T1

Adulthood

Largely yellow marrow throughout    → high on T1

Any residual red marrow has a high fat content → iso to high on T1

Lymphoma

Primary lymphoma of the bone is far rarer than other types of non-Hodgkin lymphoma but has a variety of imaging features. Most commonly on x-ray there will be permeative bony destruction which can be overlooked initially. Lytic lesions with a wide zone of transition may be present but patients can also have sclerotic lesions (an ivory vertebra) or a mixed picture instead. Cortical destruction occurs late on in the disease process. On MRI the affected bone marrow will return low signal on T1 and high signal on T2. (by contrast, normal bone marrow which is high in fat returns high signal on T1 and intermediate signal on T2).

Differential diagnosis for permeative bone destruction:

Lymphoma

Ewing sarcoma

Eosinophilic granuloma

Osteomyelitis

Marrow reconversion

Image © Medical Exam Prep

As children age, the red marrow with which we are born slowly converts to yellow marrow, beginning in the diaphysis and spreading to either end of the bones. By late adolescence this process is almost complete and only a few areas of the skeleton retain red marrow, these include the proximal femora and humeri as well as the flat bones. A small amount of red marrow does persist throughout adulthood but various conditions can cause a re-conversion whereby red marrow once again replaces the yellow marrow. On MRI yellow marrow, which is high in fat content, returns high signal on T1 and intermediate signal on T2. The red marrow that we are born with is isointense to skeletal muscle on all sequences but as we age the fat content of red marrow increases and so the appearance changes. Residual red marrow islands can often be found close to the growth plates. It is best appreciated on fat saturated sequences as it will experience less signal drop out than the yellow marrow.

When haematopoiesis increases the yellow marrow can reconvert back to red marrow. This can occur in a number of different scenarios:

Marrow reconversion

Chronic haemolytic anaemia

Sickle cell disease

Thalassaemia

Increased oxygen demand or decreased oxygen supply

Athletes

High altitudes

Smoking

Iatrogenic

G-CSF

Erythropoietin

On an MRI scan where you should find high T1 signal fatty yellow marrow there will be low T1 signal red marrow which remains reasonably bright on STIR or other fat saturated sequences. The pattern of marrow reconversion is the exact reverse of the initial conversion, so beginning at the ends of the long bones and spreading to the diaphysis.

In the spine in particular, it can be difficult to differentiate between marrow reconversion and. Even red marrow does contain some fat cells and thus should exhibit some signal drop-out on STIR or out of phase images whereas metastatic disease will not lose any signal at all.

Metastases

Normally metastatic deposits in the spine lead to low T1 signal and high T2 signal. There should be no signal drop out on fat saturated sequences in contrast to marrow reconversion where although red marrow will experience far less signal dropout than yellow marrow, there will still be some loss in signal owing to the fat content of both types of marrow.

Sclerotic or blastic metastases return little signal on either T1 or T2 weighted sequences. These include prostate, breast or TCC metastases among others.

Lytic metastases are more likely than sclerotic metastases to enhance with contrast. Similarly on DWI imaging, whereas lytic metastases will usually appear hyperintense, sclerotic metastases return little signal since they contain little water.

Myelofibrosis

In myelofibrosis the bone marrow is gradually replaced by fibrous tissue which contains few water molecules and thus returns little signal on T1 or T2 weighted sequences. It is a haematological condition and concurrent hepatosplenomegaly is common due to the need for extramedullary haematopoiesis. Paraspinal soft tissue masses may also be seen for the same reason. On x-rays or CT there can be a generalised increase in bone density and it is one of the causes of a superscan on nuclear medicine bone scans.

Vertebral haemangioma

These lesions are extremely common and should be very familiar to all candidates. They can occur anywhere but commonly arise in the vertebrae. They have a typical appearance of vertical trabeculae which give a ‘corduroy’ appearance when viewed in sagittal or coronal planes but a honeycomb or polka-dot appearance when viewed in the axial plane. On MRI they return high signal on both T1 and T2 sequences.

stem: You are reviewing the scans of a patient who is being followed up in the diabetes clinic. The x-ray is normal but an MRI scan shows effusions and soft tissue oedema.
prompt: Which of the following suggests a diagnosis of Charcot arthropathy over one of osteomyelitis?
explanation:
Differentiating between osteomyelitis and Charcot arthropathy

There are a number of complications of diabetes which are important to correctly diagnose, the better to guide treatment. Sometimes imaging can help although often there is overlap between the features. Osteomyelitis in a diabetic foot should definitely be suspected where there are marrow changes adjacent to an area of broken skin with soft tissue inflammatory changes in continuity with both the affected bone and the broken skin. Frank fluid collections (as opposed to either effusions or soft tissue oedema) also suggest infection over Charcot arthropathy. High T2 signal in the bone marrow is very sensitive for osteomyelitis and there should be a corresponding loss of normal high T1 signal too. If the T1 signal is normal, technically the finding may be of osteitis as opposed to osteomyelitis.

The earliest radiographic manifestation of Charcot arthropathy is juxta-articular osteoporosis however changes can be seen on MRI prior to radiographic changes becoming apparent. Effusions are a prominent feature, and may be significant in size. Soft tissue oedema is also seen. Usually Charcot arthropathy affects multiple joints at once, and has a predilection for the mid-foot joints whereas osteomyelitis is more likely to affect an isolated joint, or be contiguous in nature from the index pathogen admission point; thus, the presence of an ulcer with adjacent inflammatory changes is far more suggestive of an infective process than a neuropathic one such as Charcot arthropathy.

Charcot joint also known as neuropathic osteoarthropathy

More commonly this condition is seen in the forefoot or ankle joints in patients with advanced diabetes mellitus. Although only a small number of Charcot joints affect the shoulder most of those caused by a syrinx do. A syrinx is also a more common cause of Charcot joints than either multiple sclerosis or Hansen disease (leprosy).

Causes of Charcot joints

Diabetes mellitus

Syringomyelia

Hansen disease (Leprosy)

Poliomyelitis

Neurosyphilis

Multiple sclerosis

Whatever the underlying cause, compromise to the sensory nerves supplying the relevant joint prevent the normal protective mechanisms and as such minor trauma does not have sufficient an environment to heal correctly. This is particularly pertinent to weight-bearing joints. Loss of sympathetic control of the same area is also thought to play a part.

The joints can take either an atrophic pattern, a heterotropic pattern or a mixed pattern.

The radiological findings can be summarised as the 5Ds, namely:

Destruction

Dislocation

Density (due to heterotrophic new bone formation and sclerosis)

Disorganisation

Debris

Atrophic

Heterotrophic

More common

Less common

Destruction predominates

Fragmentation and debris formation predominates

Little sclerosis

Much sclerosis

stem: A 29-year-old man with back pain has an MRI which shows an eccentric lesion expanding spinal cord centred at T4. It is hyperintense on T2 with some enhancement post contrast. The interpedicular distance at this level is widened.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This question pertains to spinal lesions. The characteristics of the lesions listed should all be relatively familiar to the candidate but their features are a little different when considered as spinal lesions. The main other differential diagnosis not given is a spinal ependymoma. By and large for an intramedullary lesion in the cord of a young adult the differential diagnosis is between an Ependymoma and an Astrocytoma. There are a few features which separate them. Ependymomas are far and away the most common intramedullary spinal cord tumour though.

Astrocytoma

Spinal astrocytomas are the second most common intramedullary spinal tumour in adults.There is overlap of many of the features of astrocytomas and ependymomas. Eccentricity within the axial slice of the cord is a strong pointer to it being an astrocytoma as opposed to an Ependymoma (although the latter hasn’t been given as an alternative).Ependymomas tend to show avid contrast enhancement whereas what has been described here is less severe than that.

Haemangioblastoma

The classic description for haemangioblastomas is of a cyst with an enhancing nodule. This occurs far less commonly in spinal haemangioblastomas than it does for posterior fossa ones. Cystic components are still extremely common for spinal haemangioblastomas however. On MRI spinal haemangioblastomas are iso or high on T1 and high on T2. Sometimes they can cause polycythaemia due to erythropoietin production.

Epidermoid

These tumours are usually extramedullary and there is a strong association with vertebral anomalies. The imaging feature usually tested is that they restrict diffusion.

PNET(primitive neuroectoderm tumour)

The age range for intracranial PNET is quoted as < 5 years. Spinal PNETs have been reported in the literature as case reports but are very rare.

Ganglioglioma

Spinal gangliomas are a reasonable differential diagnosis for intramedullary cord lesions however are more prevalent in the paediatric cohort and still far less common than ependymomas. They tend to show heterogeneity on T1.

stem: A 22-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of lower back pain. She has also noticed pain in her left sternoclavicular joint. She undergoes x-rays of her shoulder which shows that the joint space is well preserved but there is bony expansion and ankylosis. A subsequent MRI scan is reported as showing new bone formation with oedema and synovitis at the sternoclavicular joint. There is no discernible collection. She goes on to have a nuclear medicine scan which shows uptake in both sternoclavicular joints. Old x-rays of her pelvis show left sided sclerosis of the sacroiliac joint.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
SAPHO (Synovitis, acne, palmoplantar pustulosis, hyperostosis, osteitis)

This disease is thought to be a variant of psoriatic arthropathy. The cutaneous manifestations may not be apparent at diagnosis (like psoriatic arthropathy) but hyperostosis and osteolysis and ankylosis of the sternoclavicular joint is absolutely typical. On a nuclear medicine bone scan, bilateral uptake in the sternoclavicular joints and manubrium is called a ‘bull’s head’ sign. About a third of patients also have spinal disease with paravertebral ossifications and osteosclerosis. Unilateral sacroiliitis may also occur. Appearances can be quite striking on CT. In the knees, ankles and small joints of the hands there may be inflammation of the joints with juxta-articular osteoporosis.

stem: A 13-year-old girl with Turner syndrome complains of pain in her wrist following a fall. An x-ray reveals no fractures but the carpal angle is markedly decreased to around 110 degrees and the proximal carpus is V-shaped. Additionally the distal radio-ulnar joint is dorsally subluxed.
prompt: What is the name of this abnormality?
explanation:
The patient has a Madelung deformity. This arises due to a problem with the development of the ulnar side of the distal end of the radius. The distal radioulnar joint subluxes and the ulna displaces dorsally. Owing to growth failure of the distal radius, by comparison the ulna appears lengthened (Positive ulnar variance). The carpal bones become altered in shape from the norm, in particular the lunate appears triangular. The overall appearance is of a V-shape to the radioulnarcarpal joint with angles of <120o considered characteristic.

The Madelung deformity has a number of different aetiologies (Mnemonic = DIGIT):

D = Dysplastic - Ollier disease, osteochondromatosis, achondroplasia, mucopolysaccharidoses, diaphyseal aclasis

I = Idiopathic

G = Genetic - Autosomal dominant.

50% of patients have bilateral deformities. Most common association is Turner syndrome

I = Infection

T = Post-Traumatic

Diaphyseal aclasis can be associated with a Madelung deformity but patients may have a reverse-Madelung (or pseudo-Madelung) deformity instead. Here there is negative ulnar variance due to excessive overgrowth and bowing of the radius with consequential ulnar deviation at the wrist.

Ulnar variance

Description

Associations

Positive

The ulna is unusually long

Ulnar impaction syndrome

Negative

The ulna is unusually short

Kienboch disease

stem: You are reviewing the x-ray of a 38-year-old man's lumbar spine. There are concavities to the posterior surface of the vertebral bodies affecting L3 and L4.
prompt: Which of the following is NOT a cause of this finding? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Please note that the question asks which answer is NOT a cause.

Posterior vertebral scalloping

There are a number of specific differential diagnoses which can lead to this finding. In each case the image should be interrogated carefully to look for further clues as to the underlying diagnosis. Scalloping is a chronic process whereby mechanical pressure on the bone causes remodelling. In many cases the mechanism of posterior vertebral scalloping is secondary to dural ectasia.

stem: You are reviewing the cervical spine x-rays of a 30-year-old man. There is fusion of C5/6 and in the corner of the film you notice the left scapula is small and elevated above the clavicle.
prompt: Which of the following is NOT associated with this condition? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Please note that the question asks which feature is NOT associated with this condition.

Klippel-Feil syndrome

Klippel-Feil syndrome is predominantly a segmentation anomaly which arises during foetal development and leads to cervical fusion of two or more vertebral bodies. C2-3 are most commonly involved, accounting for around half of cases. Thereafter C5-6 accounts for a further third and the remainder are made up from fusions at other levels. There are a multitude of associated features, the predominant ones of which include:

GU abnormalities (of which a third have unilateral renal agenesis) (66%)

Scoliosis > 20 degrees (50%)

Sprengel shoulder (33%)

Deafness (sensorineural) (33%)

Cervial ribs (20%)

Yet further features of this condition, all present in under 20% of cases include:

Odontoid dysplasia

Hemivertebrae / butterfly vertebrae

Syringomyelia / diastomatomyelia

Ear anomalies (microtia, deformed ossicles etc)

Congenital heart disease (ASD or coarctation)

Sprengel shoulder

This condition can occur in isolation as well as part of Klippel-Feil syndrome. It is (like Klippel-Feil syndrome) also often associated with renal anomalies. Sprengel shoulder is a congenital abnormality where the scapula (usually, but not exclusively, unilateral) is attached to the cervical vertebra either by a fibrous or osseous connection, and therefore fails to descend into the normal position. The result is elevation and medial rotation of the scapula, which is usually hypoplastic. The condition can be readily appreciated on a plain film although cross-sectional imaging is useful to plan surgical correction if required. If present, the osseous connection between the scapula and the spine is termed an omovertebral bar.

Holt-Oram syndrome

This syndrome is associated with numerous skeletal and cardiac malformations. It is usually evident either antenatally or in the early neonatal period. Cardiac manifestations include either ASD or VSD, tetralogy of Fallot and coarctation. Perhaps most strikingly the condition is often associated with radial ray hypoplasia often meaning the absence of one or both thumbs. An x-ray may show absence or hypoplasia of one or both radii.

stem: You are reviewing the radiographs of a 30-year-old marathon runner who has been experiencing worsening hip pains over the last few months. There is a roundness to the superior aspect of the left femoral neck and you suspect he has cam-type femoroacetabular impingement.
prompt: Which of the following is most likely to be seen with this abnormality? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Femoroacetabular impingement (FAI)

Mixed type - >80% of patients have components of both cam-type and pincer-type FAI.

Cam type - a cam is an engineering term for an oval/egg shaped component with a hole through the middle of the wider end. In cam type FAI the femoral head takes on a 'cam' shaped appearance due to bony overgrowth at the superior aspect of the femoral neck. This abnormal bony contour impinges against the anterosuperior aspect of the acetabulum during movement. The condition occurs more frequently in men and tends to affect men in their 30s. Certain conditions can predispose to cam-type FAI, including SUFE, DDH and Perthes disease. Some patients with cam-type FAI exhibit femoral retroversion.

Pincer type - here bony protuberance of the anterosuperior acetabulum causes over-coverage of the femoral head and impingement against the femoral neck. Protrusio acetabuli predisposes to pincer-type FAI. The relationship of the overgrown anterior acetabular rim to the posterior acetabular rim in pincer-type FAI is called acetabular retroversion since it causes the femoral neck to twist posteriorly. Patients usually stand with their toes pointing outwards as a consequence. The condition is more common in women and a patient is typically aged around 40.

Cyanosis

stem: A 60-year-old man is being investigated for left sided leg weakness. On his MRI scan there is a well-defined cystic area with high T2 signal in the right S2 lateral recess. The S2 neural canal is expanded with bony scalloping. Along the wall of the cyst there are nerve roots visible. The facet joints appear normal.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
A Tarlov cyst

A tarlov cyst is the name given to dilatation of the posterior nerve root sheath. They follow CSF on all sequences and can cause significant bony scalloping.

A synovial cyst

Synovial cysts relate to the joint rather than the nerve. They tend to be seen in cases where the facet joints are already degenerate.

Sacral Chordoma

Chordomas are aggressive lesions although they can be extremely large at the time of diagnosis. They often exhibit high T2 signal.

Giant cell tumour

These are bony tumours arising from within bone. They can cause bony expansion from within but not bony scalloping from without.

Dural ectasia

This is an interesting alternative diagnosis however usually occurs over more than one vertebral level. It can be associated with tarlov cysts.

stem: A 45-year-old man with back pain is seen by an orthopaedic surgeon who requests x-rays. The x-rays show a number of findings which lead you to suspect he has ochronosis.
prompt: Which of the following is NOT a feature of ochronosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Please note that the question asks which answer is NOT a feature.

Alkaptonuria (also known as ochronosis)

This condition is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. It is caused by excessive circulating levels of homogentisic acid (HGA) when the enzyme which would usually degrade it is deficient. HGA has an affinity for collagen and accumulates in the connective tissues throughout the body. In visible light HGA has a blackish colour and thus the disease can be diagnosed in infancy when a baby’s nappies are stained black by the presence of HGA in the urine. By the time patients reach their 20s pigmentation may be visible in their skin, particularly the ears. This is initially a dark yellow colour (hence the term ochronosis, from ‘Ochre’ in Greek meaning a dark yellow colour) but can progress to blue-grey and black.

In imaging chondrocalcinosis is the most prominent feature, with calcification and destruction of the intervertebral discs. Premature osteoarthritic changes to the hands, feet, shoulders, hips and knees will also develop as the collagen deteriorates. Deposition in the heart and kidneys too leads to cardiac and renal failure.

stem: A 34-year-old man presents to his GP with worsening back pain and stiffness. Plain radiographs show some slight sclerosis of the sacroiliac joints bilaterally with small vertebral syndesmophytes in the lumbar spine. He is referred to an orthopaedic consultant who is concerned he may have ankylosing spondylitis and requests an MRI scan.
prompt: Regarding MRI in ankylosing spondylitis, which of the following is NOT correct? Select ONE answer only.
options: Axial spine - to evaluate disc herniation
STIR - useful for bone marrow abnormalities
Sagittal SIJs - best sequence for the SIJs
Sagittal spine - to evaluate facet joints
explanation:
Please note this question asks which answer is NOT correct.

T1 fat sat - useful for visualisation of bony erosions and new bone formation

T1 fat sat post contrast - useful for detecting bone marrow abnormalities (but so is STIR, so contrast is not an absolute requirement for imaging ankylosing spondylitis).

STIR - useful for detecting bone marrow abnormalities in the SIJs and spine

T2 fat sat - useful for detecting oedema

Coronal SIJ - ideally this should be taken parallel to the long axis of the sacrum, the better to view the SIJs, both SIJs can be seen on each image for comparison.

Axial SIJ - ideally this should be at 90 degrees to the modified coronal plane and is used to evaluate the ligamentous portion of the SIJs.

Axial spine - useful if co-existing disc herniation present but not ordinarily included otherwise

Sagittal spine - useful to evaluate facet and costovertebral joints

Ankylosing spondylitis

This disease usually presents in early adulthood with gradual onset of back pain. There is a male preponderance, though it can affect women too. The vast majority (>90%) of patients are HLA-B27 positive. Radiologically the late features are classical with:

Bilateral symmetrical sacroiliitis

Enthesopathy - calcified tendon insertion sites

Bamboo spine - vertebral syndesmophytes, particularly in the thoracolumbar spine

Dagger sign - spinous process fusion

Erosion, then fusion at the symphysis pubis, costochondral, costovertebral and sternoclavicular joints

Thoracic manifestations: upper lobe pulmonary fibrosis, pericarditis, aortic root dilatation

Early features are far more subtle and require a higher index of suspicion

Enthesopathy - high signal on MRI at tendon insertion sites

Romanus lesions - triangular shaped oedema at the corners of vertebral bodies

Andersson lesions - bony oedema in the vertebral bodies adjacent to the disks.

Oedema in the sacroiliac joints.

Patients with advanced ankylosing spondylitis are at increased risk of pathological fractures due to fusion. These can be pelvic fractures following a simple fall, or chance fractures of the spine (involving all three columns - in ankylosing spondylitis, these fractures are also sometimes termed chalk-stick or carrot fractures).
