stem: You are reviewing the radiographs of a 40-year-old marathon runner who has been experiencing worsening hip pains over the last few months. There is a roundness to the superior aspect of the left femoral neck.
prompt: Which of the following regarding femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) is correct?
options: Acetebular retroversion is seen with cam-type FAI
More patients have mixed type FAI than either cam or pincer-type
Patients with cam-type FAI are usually older than those with pincer-type FAI
Protrusio acetabuli predisposes to cam-type FAI
explanation:
Femoroacetabular impingement (FAI)

Mixed type - >80% of patients have components of both cam-type and pincer-type FAI.

Cam type - a cam is an engineering term for an oval/egg shaped component with a hole through the middle of the wider end. In cam type FAI the femoral head takes on a 'cam' shaped appearance due to bony overgrowth at the superior aspect of the femoral neck. This abnormal bony contour impinges against the anterosuperior aspect of the acetabulum during movement. The condition occurs more frequently in men and tends to affect men in their 30s. Certain conditions can predispose to cam-type FAI, including SUFE, DDH and Perthes disease. Some patients with cam-type FAI exhibit femoral retroversion.

Pincer type - here bony protruberance of the anterosuperior acetabulum causes overcoverage of the femoral head and impingement against the femoral neck. Protrusio acetabuli predisposes to pincer-type FAI. The relationship of the overgrown anterior acetabular rim to the posterior acetabular rim in pincer-type FAI is called acetabular retroversion since it causes the femoral neck to twist posteriorly. Patients usually stand with their toes pointing outwards as a consequence. The condition is more common in women and a patient is typically aged around 40.

stem: A 70-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis presents with pain, numbness, and tingling, in the thumb, index finger, middle finger, and ring finger of her left hand. You are reviewing her MRI scan and suspect that she has a diagnosis of carpal tunnel syndrome.
prompt: Which muscle group will atrophy as a consequence of carpal tunnel syndrome? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Carpal tunnel syndrome is an entrapment neuropathy of the median nerve. It causes weakness and parasthesia in the distribution of the median nerve.

The median nerve innervates the thenar eminence and the lateral two lumbricals. The thenar eminence consists of the following three muscles:

Abductor pollicis brevis

Flexor pollicis brevis

Opponens pollicis

stem: You are reviewing the cervical spine x-ray of a patient with neck pain. The atlantodental interval is increased.
prompt: Which of the following is a cause of increased atlantodental interval? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
The atlantodental interval is measured from the posterior aspect of the anterior arch of C1 to the anterior aspect of the dens.

Normal in adults is <3mm

Normal in children is <5mm

The gap increases due to anterior translocation of the atlas. This often simultaneously causes the posterior arch of C1 to become anterior displaced with respect to the spinolaminar line.

There are a number of non-traumatic causes of an increased atlantodental interval.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

The prevertebral space is also important to appreciate on the lateral cervical spine view. Enlargement of the prevertebral soft tissue is a secondary sign of a bony injury. Normal measurements are given below.

<7mm at C2

<5mm at C3+4

<22mm at C6 (14mm in children)

Sprengel shoulder

This condition can occur in isolation as well as part of Klippel-Feil syndrome. It is (like Klippel-Feil syndrome) also often associated with renal anomalies. Sprengel shoulder is a congenital abnormality where the scapula (usually, but not exclusively, unilateral) is attached to the cervical vertebra either by a fibrous or osseous connection, and therefore fails to descend into the normal position. The result is elevation and medial rotation of the scapula, which is usually hypoplastic. The condition can be readily appreciated on a plain film although cross-sectional imaging is useful to plan surgical correction if required. If present, the osseous connection between the scapula and the spine is termed an omovertebral bar.

Klippel-Feil syndrome(different from Klippel-Trenaunay-Weber syndrome: port-wine stains, localised hypertrophy and venous malformations)

Klippel-Feil syndrome is predominantly a segmentation anomaly which arises during foetal development and leads to cervical fusion of two or more vertebral bodies. C2-3 are most commonly involved, accounting for around half of cases. Thereafter C5-6 accounts for a further third and the remainder are made up from fusions at other levels.

stem: A 23-year-old woman is brought in by ambulance having been involved in a road traffic accident. A FAST scan is performed to check for a haemoperitoneum.
prompt: Which of the following anatomical areas is assessed as part of a standard 4 view FAST scan? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
The hypochondrium (left or right) are the upper lateral aspects of the abdomen. There is no such thing as a hyperchondrium.

A Focussed Assessment with Sonography for Trauma (FAST) scan is a point-of-care ultrasound examination performed at the time of presentation of a trauma patient.

The main aim of a FAST scan is to identify intra-abdominal free fluid (assumed to be haemoperitoneum in the context of trauma). This helps to make decisions about further management.

Sensitivity of FAST scanning is in the region of 90% and specificity of is approximately 95% for detecting intraperitoneal fluid. The sensitivity for detecting solid organ injuries is much lower. It has now largely replaced diagnostic peritoneal lavage as the preferred initial method for assessment of haemoperitoneum.

Four regions are assessed during a standard FAST scan:

Subxiphoid transverse view: assess for pericardial effusion and left lobe liver injuries

Longitudinal view of the right upper quadrant: assess for right liver injuries, right kidney injury and fluid in the hepatorenal recess (Morison’s pouch)

Longitudinal view of the left upper quadrant: assess for splenic injury and left kidney injury

Transverse and longitudinal views of the suprapubic region: assess the bladder and fluid in the pouch of Douglas

An ‘extended FAST’ or ‘eFAST’ may also be performed that looks at the left and right thoracic that helps to assess for the presence of pneumothorax and haemothorax.

stem: A 43-year-old man weight lifter presents with unilateral calf pain. When this fails to resolve with simple analgesia blood tests are taken which show an elevated creatine kinase. He undergoes an MRI scan. The MRI shows enlargement of the calf muscles with high T2 signal. The muscle fibres and architecture are preserved.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
The preservation of the muscular fibres and architecture helps confirm this diagnosis.

Hypertrophy related to exercise should be bilateral and approximately symmetrical.

The elevation of the creatinine kinase simply confirms that there is an acute muscular process going on where muscle cells are being damaged, thereby releasing their creatinine kinase into the blood.

There are a number of causes of myositis and further information would have to be provided to progress the diagnosis. One of the roles of MRI in cases where more than one muscle is involved, is to indicate the best muscle group to biopsy for diagnosis. Those with active inflammation, including enhancement post-contrast, are most likely to yield diagnostic tissue.

stem: A 23-year-old goalkeeper injures her thumb during a football match. The radiograph demonstrates an avulsion fracture of the proximal end of the proximal phalanx of the thumb.
prompt: Which fracture is described? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Gamekeeper’s thumb

This is an avulsion fracture of the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb associated with ulnar collateral ligament disruption.

Bennett fracture

This is a non-comminuted fracture which requires operative fixation due to the action of Abductor Pollicis Longus causing dorsolateral dislocation.

Rolando fracture

This descrives a comminuted fracture through the base of the thumb.

Guyon

Guyon’s canal transmits the ulnar nerve which can be injured in a Hamate hook fracture.

Stener lesion

A Stener lesion occurs when the Adductor tendon gets caught around the ulnar collateral ligament following a Game-keeper’s thumb injury. It is best appreciated on ultrasound (by an experienced MSK radiologist). This requires surgery.

stem: A 55-year-old man complains to his GP of pain in both wrists. Bilateral x-rays of the wrist are requested which show soft tissue swelling to the second and third digits with marginal erosions and periosteal new bone formation.
prompt: Which additional feature would be most likely in this case? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Psoriatic arthropathy

Around a fifth of patients with psoriasis develop arthropathy and it is also possible to suffer from psoriatic arthropathy in the absence of the typical psoriatic cutaneous plaques.

Importantly, on x-ray there are findings of both erosive changes in addition to productive changes with periosteal new bone formation. The combination of the two contrives to leave a ‘pencil-in-cup’ appearance. The joints can appear fluffy due to the exuberance of new bone formation.

The differential diagnosis for periosteal reactions in the presence of an arthropathy is relatively narrow and very specific:

Psoriatic arthropathy

Juvenile rheumatoid arthritis

Reiter syndrome

Infective arthritis

Although often classified as a distal arthropathy, preferring the DIPs to the MCPs, psoriatic arthropathy does also affect the spine and SI joints frequently. ‘Sausage digits’ is a term used to describe the diffuse soft tissue swelling which can affect the fingers and toes. Osteoporosis does occur but is a feature of later disease.

Normally metastatic deposits in the spine lead to low T1 signal and high T2 signal. There should be no signal drop out on fat saturated sequences in contrast to marrow reconversion where although red marrow will experience far less signal dropout than yellow marrow, there will still be some loss in signal owing to the fat content of both types of marrow.

Sclerotic or blastic metastases return little signal on either T1 or T2 weighted sequences. These include prostate, breast or TCC metastases among others.

Breast cancer can cause lytic or sclerotic metastases or a mixed picture.

Lytic metastases are more likely than sclerotic metastases to enhance with contrast. Similarly on DWI imaging, whereas lytic metastases will usually appear hyperintense, sclerotic metastases return little signal since they contain little water.

If there is a diffuse abnormality of the bone marrow it can be difficult to identify but normal bone marrow should not be lower in signal intensity than the muscle on T1 weighted sequences.

stem: A 35-year-old man involved in a severe road traffic accident is brought to A+E. He undergoes a trauma CT scan which shows a complex pelvic fracture with a large pelvic haematoma. The scan shows a large contrast blush around the right obturator artery tracking towards the haematoma. The patient becomes unstable after the scan.
prompt: What should the next management step be?
explanation:
A retrograde urethrogram can be performed if there is concern regarding a possible urethral or bladder injury. For optimum results this should be achieved prior to IV contrast however can still be performed after a CT scan if necessary. It is, however, somewhat futile in the case of an unstable patient with a large pelvic haematoma and will go no way towards halting further blood loss.

Target artery embolisation via endovascular techniques can be hugely successful in such cases and is associated with a far lower morbidity and mortality than surgical exploration. Pelvic fractures are associated with a high risk of vascular injury. Catheter angiography is the gold standard for identifying a bleeding point although the scan results in this case suggest a target vessel even prior to catheter angiography. Endovascular embolisation can be extremely successful in achieving haemostasis for arterial bleeding but is not useful where the haematoma is thought to derive from the bony fractures.

She undergoes x-rays of her shoulder which shows that the joint space is well preserved but there is bony expansion and ankylosis. A subsequent MRI scan is reported as showing new bone formation with oedema and synovitis at the sternoclavicular joint. There is no discernible collection.
prompt: Considering the likely aetiology, which additional finding would NOT fit with the diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Please note that the question asks which answer would NOT fit.

In SAPHO, the sacroiliitis is usually unilateral if present, not bilateral.

SAPHO

(Synovitis, acne, palmoplantar pustulosis, hyperostosis, osteitis)

This disease is thought to be a variant of psoriatic arthropathy. The cutaneous manifestations may not be apparent at diagnosis (like psoriatic arthropathy) but hyperostosis and osteolysis and ankylosis of the sternoclavicular joint is absolutely typical. On a nuclear medicine bone scan, bilateral uptake in the sternoclavicular joints and manubrium is called a ‘bull’s head’ sign. About a third of patients also have spinal disease with paravertebral ossifications and osteosclerosis. Unilateral sacroiliitis may also occur. Appearances can be quite striking on CT. In the knees, ankles and small joints of the hands there may be inflammation of the joints with juxta-articular osteoporosis.

stem: You are reviewing the scans of a patient who is being followed up in the diabetes clinic. The x-ray is markedly abnormal, and an MRI scan shows effusions and soft tissue oedema.
prompt: Which of the following is NOT a cause of Charcot Arthropathy?
explanation:
Differentiating between osteomyelitis and Charcot arthropathy

There are a number of complications of diabetes which are important to correctly diagnose, the better to guide treatment. Sometimes imaging can help although often there is overlap between the features. Osteomyelitis in a diabetic foot should definitely be suspected where there are marrow changes adjacent to an area of broken skin with soft tissue inflammatory changes in continuity with both the affected bone and the broken skin. Frank fluid collections (as opposed to either effusions or soft tissue oedema) also suggest infection over Charcot arthropathy. High T2 signal in the bone marrow is very sensitive for osteomyelitis and there should be a corresponding loss of normal high T1 signal too. If the T1 signal is normal, technically the finding may be of osteitis as opposed to osteomyelitis.

The earliest radiographic manifestation of Charcot arthropathy is juxta-articular osteoporosis however changes can be seen on MRI prior to radiographic changes becoming apparent. Effusions are a prominent feature, and may be significant in size. Soft tissue oedema is also seen. Usually Charcot arthropathy affects multiple joints at once, and has a predilection for the mid-foot joints whereas osteomyelitis is more likely to affect an isolated joint, or be contiguous in nature from the index pathogen admission point; thus, the presence of an ulcer with adjacent inflammatory changes is far more suggestive of an infective process than a neuropathic one such as Charcot arthropathy.

Charcot joint also known as neuropathic osteoarthropathy

More commonly this condition is seen in the forefoot or ankle joints in patients with advanced diabetes mellitus. Although only a small number of Charcot joints affect the shoulder most of those caused by a syrinx do. A syrinx is also a more common cause of Charcot joints than either multiple sclerosis or Hansen disease (leprosy).

Causes of Charcot joints

Diabetes mellitus

Syringomyelia

Hansen disease (leprosy)

Poliomyelitis

Neurosyphilis

Multiple sclerosis

Whatever the underlying cause, compromise to the sensory nerves supplying the relevant joint prevent the normal protective mechanisms and as such minor trauma does not have sufficient an environment to heal correctly. This is particularly pertinent to weight-bearing joints. Loss of sympathetic control of the same area is also thought to play a part.

The joints can take either an atrophic pattern, a heterotropic pattern or a mixed pattern.

stem: A 53-year-old man collides with one of the hurdles during his son’s sports day. Two months later he is still noticing a lump around the distal femur and undergoes an x-ray. There is a well defined partly calcified soft tissue mass underlying the tender area. There is cortical erosion of the underlying bone.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Malignant fibrous histiocytoma (MFH) - more recently referred to as Undifferentiated Pleomorphic Sarcoma (UPS)

A soft-tissue MFH is the most common subtype of MFHs and the most common malignant primary soft tissue tumour in the over 50s age bracket. It usually presents as a painless soft tissue mass which enlarges over a matter of months. They can be large at the time of diagnosis measuring tens of centimetres. On x-ray they appear as a partly calcified soft tissue mass. Cortical erosion of the underlying bone is an important diagnostic feature. On MRI it returns a similar signal to muscle although areas of haemorrhage can be seen as regions of high signal on both T1 and T2 weighted sequences.

Myositis ossificans

Trauma to the muscle causes local haemorrhage and necrosis of damaged muscle. The sequelae of this is calcification which can persist long-term. Large muscles are particularly prone to this and the typical patient is a young, active adolescent. Myositis ossificans appears as a calcified soft tissue mass underlying the area of clinical concern. A periosteal reaction may or may not be present but crucially there is no erosion of the underlying cortex, a fact which discriminates it from malignant fibrous histiocytoma. The string sign refers to the presence of a plane of normal tissue separating the mass from the bone and unlike a parosteal osteosarcoma, in myositis ossificans this plane will extend along the whole length of the mass completely separating it from the bone.

Tumoral calcinosis

Surprisingly for the sometimes extreme appearance of this condition, it can be completely painless. Patients are typically black and in their teens or 20s. Around a third of cases are inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion. A biochemical defect in the metabolism of phosphorus leads to accumulation of hydroxyapatite fluid around the joints causing a foreign-body type granulomatous reaction and fibrous capsule development. On imaging this appears as a progressive and calcified soft tissue mass. The skin overlying the mass can ulcerate and exude a chalky or milk like fluid. Any or all of the hips, shoulders and elbows can be affected but characteristically tumoral calcinosis does not affect the knees. Importantly the underlying bones are normal, a feature which differentiates it from gout or pseudogout.

Gout

Excess circulating urate levels leads to crystalisation of urate (monosodium urate crystals) within the joint spaces. An acute attack may be precipitated by any acute event such as trauma or surgery as well as a change in diet to include purine containing foods (liver, kidney, game meat, some seafood, alcohol). Historically chronic manifestations of this condition included the development of gouty tophi; white lumpy areas under the skin which could ulcerate and exude a chalky material. These are still seen today but far less so thanks to improved management strategies. Involvement of the first metatarsophalangeal joint is considered classical but involvement of the carpometacarpal joints of the hands is often most debilitating where it occurs. On x-ray the earliest radiological manifestation is a joint effusion. Joint erosions develop on the lateral corners of a joint but contrary to many other erosive processes the base of the ulcers has a sclerotic margin. Juxta-articular osteopenia is not often seen, a feature which acts as a good distinguisher from rheumatoid arthritis, which is thought to be because the attacks come in acute bursts during which time disuse osteopenia does not have the time to develop. Another reasonably specific feature of gouty arthritis is the preservation of the joint space itself until relatively late into the disease.

Crystals

Gout

Pseudogout

Content

Monosodium urate

Calcium pyrophosphate dehydrate

Shape

Needle

Rhomboid

Birefringence

Strongly negative

Weakly positive

Osteosarcoma

Secondary osteosarcomas

Paget disease

Bone infarct

Osteochondroma

Osteoblastoma

Radiotherapy change

These are bone forming tumours which can either be primary, or secondary. Primary osteosarcomas occur in young patients or young adults when the bones are more active during adolescence than in later life, and have a predilection for either the proximal tibia or distal femur i.e. around the knee joint. Secondary osteosarcomas occur as malignant degeneration of pre-existing bone lesions. Clinically they present as a painful mass with a fever. Pain on movement is also typical. In later disease patients may have a raised serum ALP. On x-ray they are poorly defined aggressive lesions with sunburst periosteal reaction and fluffy cloud-like osseous matrix. For staging the patient should receive an MRI of the entire of the affected bone (to rule out synchronous lesions), a nuclear medicine bone scan and a CT chest. Tissue biopsy should only be performed at tertiary referral centres where to mitigate the risk of seeding the biopsy tract, immediate tissue analysis with the option of immediate amputation can be performed.

In the case of a parosteal osteosarcoma, the attachment to the underlying bone may be thin and stalk-like but will be present. Depending on the view a radiolucent plane may seem present for some of the length of the tumour, giving rise to ‘string sign’ appearance, but an attachment to the parent bone will be present.

Some of the pertinent subtypes of osteosarcoma

Parosteal

Lower grade, older age (20-50s)

Telangiectatic

Purely lytic, poor prognosis, fluid-fluid levels

Multicentric

Ages 5-10 with very poor prognosis

stem: A 46-year-old motorcyclist has a road traffic accident. On arrival at the hospital he has a GCS of 4 and is taken to have a trauma-protocol CT scan. This is reported as showing subtle petechial haemorrhage at the grey-white matter junction. The A&E registrar rings you up to ask you for more information.
prompt: Which of the following best explains this finding?
explanation:
Cortical contusions would be the main alternative theory however these are usually located cortically since they are caused by the impact of the brain on the skull.

Cerebral amyloid angiopathy does give rise to micro-haemorrhages at the grey-white matter junction but it is usually found in a far more elderly population, is seen on MRI as opposed to CT, and would be unrelated to trauma.

Neurocisticercosis is an infection caused by taenia solium which in its fourth stage can cause widespread cerebral calcifications.

Cavernomas can be incidental findings or can present with haemorrhage. They are usually associated with calcification (classically described as popcorn calcification).

stem: A 27-year-old man suffers a hyperextension injury while playing football and has pain around the popliteal fossa. An ultrasound scan reveals a partial gastrocnemius tear.
prompt: Which SINGLE statement regarding the gastrocnemius muscle is true?
options: 15 to 30% of individuals have a sesamoid bone that lies in the lateral head of the gastrocnemius muscle
It acts to dorsiflex the foot at the ankle joint
It forms a common tendon with soleus that inserts into the anterior aspect of the calcaneus
It is innervated by the common peroneal nerve
It receives its blood supply from the fibular artery
explanation:
The gastrocnemius muscle is a large, bipennate muscle, situated in the posterior compartment of the leg. It has two heads; a lateral head that arises from the lateral condyle of the femur, and a medial head that arises from the medial condyle of the femur. The two heads combine and then form a common tendon (the Achilles tendon) with the soleus muscle, that inserts into the posterior surface of the calcaneus.

Between 15 and 30% of individuals have a sesamoid bone, called the fabella, that lies in the lateral head of the gastrocnemius muscle.

Gastrocnemius is innervated by the tibial nerve and receives its blood supply from the sural arteries.

Gastrocnemius is primarily involved in running, jumping and other ‘fast’ leg movements. It is also involved to a lesser degree, in walking and standing. Its main actions are to plantarflex the foot at the ankle joint and to flex the leg at the knee joint.

The gastrocnemius muscle (from Sobotta’s Atlas and Text-book of Human Anatomy)

stem: A 65-year-old lady complains to her GP of ongoing burning pains in her hand and wrist following a fall 6 months previously. At the time she was found to have fractured her ulnar styloid process and wore a plaster cast for 6 weeks. She is otherwise well. On examination her hand is oedematous with some dystrophic nail changes. She undergoes an x-ray which shows peri-articular patchy osteopenia and subperiosteal bone resorption but the joint spaces are well preserved. The GP suspects a diagnosis of complex regional pain syndrome.
prompt: Which of the following regarding this condition is correct? Select ONE answer only.
options: Symptoms develop following an initial URTI
The joint spaces are well preserved
X-rays show a generalised increase in bone density
explanation:
Complex regional pain syndrome also known as Sudeck dystrophy

Patients develop chronic pain in an area previously affected by an, often disproportionately mild, injury. The pain is said to be burning in nature and symptoms of allodynia (pain with stimuli which would not normally be painful) and hyperalgesia (excessive sensitivity to pain) are also usually described. By contrast, reduced sensation is not normally found. On x-ray there is juxta-articular osteopenia with sub-periosteal bone resorption but preservation of the joint spaces. Soft tissue swelling can also be seen. Nuclear medicine tests may show either increased flow with increased uptake on the delayed blood pool images or (less commonly) decreased flow with decreased uptake on the delayed blood pool images.

stem: A 23-year-old woman is brought in by ambulance having been involved in a road traffic accident. A FAST scan is performed to check for a haemoperitoneum.
prompt: Which of the following anatomical areas is assessed as part of a standard 4 view FAST scan? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
A Focussed Assessment with Sonography for Trauma (FAST) scan is a point-of-care ultrasound examination performed at the time of presentation of a trauma patient.

The main aim of a FAST scan is to identify intra-abdominal free fluid (assumed to be haemoperitoneum in the context of trauma). This helps to make decisions about further management.

Sensitivity of FAST scanning is in the region of 90% and specificity of is approximately 95% for detecting intraperitoneal fluid. The sensitivity for detecting solid organ injuries is much lower. It has now largely replaced diagnostic peritoneal lavage as the preferred initial method for assessment of haemoperitoneum.

Four regions are assessed during a standard FAST scan:

Subxiphoid transverse view: assess for pericardial effusion and left lobe liver injuries

Longitudinal view of the right upper quadrant: assess for right liver injuries, right kidney injury and fluid in the hepatorenal recess (Morison’s pouch)

Longitudinal view of the left upper quadrant: assess for splenic injury and left kidney injury

Transverse and longitudinal views of the suprapubic region: assess the bladder and fluid in the pouch of Douglas

An ‘extended FAST’ or ‘eFAST’ may also be performed that looks at the left and right thoracic that helps to assess for the presence of pneumothorax and haemothorax.

stem: A 30-year-old man injures his knee in a road traffic incident. Once life threatening injuries have been ruled out, he is examined carefully by the A+E doctor. He complains of tenderness to his left knee and undergoes x-rays of it. There is a crescentic shaped bony fragment adjacent to the head of the fibula.
prompt: By what name is this finding usually known?
explanation:
The arcuate ligament, complex and sign.

The arcuate ligament of the knee is a Y-shaped ligament arising from the fibular styloid process and splitting into a medial limb and a lateral limb. Together with the lateral collateral ligament and lateral joint capsule (different sources of literature also variably include the biceps femoris tendon and fabellofibular ligament), it forms the arcuate complex and is important in stabilising the knee joint.

The arcuate sign is the elliptical shaped avulsed bony fragment adjacent to the fibular styloid process representing an avulsion fracture of the fibular styloid.

The usual mechanism of injury is a direct blow in extension such as a traffic incident, whereby a vehicle strikes a standing pedestrian.

Associated cruciate ligament injuries are common with arcuate ligament avulsions. Some literature reports this to be particularly so for the posterior cruciate ligament injuries.

Clip injury and pivot shift injury

These two injuries are very similar. Both involve valgus stress on a flexed knee (such as a tackle to the knee during sports). A pivot shift injury also requires external rotation of the tibia. The three main structures most at risk during these injuries are:

Anterior cruciate ligament (especially in a pivot shift injury)

Medial collateral ligament (especially in a clip injury)

Medial meniscus (remember that the medial meniscus is attached to the medial collateral ligament)

If all three are present together it is referred to as the O’Donoghue triad. Since O’Donoghue defined this triad however, it has been discovered that lateral meniscal tears are actually more common with this type of injury than medial meniscus ones.

Pelligrini-Steida lesion

These are tiny fragments of calcification which have formed within the medial collateral ligament following a trauma. On an x-ray they can be seen superomedially to the medial femoral condyle.

Osgood-Schlatter disease

The typical demographic for this disease is boys aged 10-15 years. There is fragmentation at the insertion of the patella tendon to the tibial tuberosity with overlying soft tissue swelling and an infrapatella bursitis (Clergyman’s knee). Pain is particularly exacerbated by jumping or kicking manoeuvres.

Sinding-Laresn-Johannsen disease

This is very similar to Osgood-Schlatter disease but affects the other end of the patella tendon, namely the inferior pole of the patella. It also occurs primarily in boys aged 10-15 years and imaging findings are mainly centred on patellar tendon thickening and T2/STIR signal changes within the patella and patella tendon. Ossification of the patella tendon is also seen.

stem: A 40-year-old woman presents with an uncomfortable swelling at the back of her right knee. On examination you palpate a round, smooth, fluctuant mass within the popliteal fossa. An ultrasound scan confirms that she has a Baker's cyst.
prompt: Which of the following muscles forms the inferomedial border of the popliteal fossa? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
The popliteal fossa is a diamond shaped depression situated at the back of the knee joint. It acts as the main conduit for the neurovascular structures entering and leaving the leg.

The borders of the popliteal fossa are:

Superomedial border: semimembranosus

Superolateral border: biceps femoris

Inferomedial border: medial head of gastrocnemius

Inferolateral border: lateral head of gastrocnemius and plantaris

The roof of the popliteal fossa is formed by (from superficial to deep):

Skin

Superficial fascia

Deep (popliteal) fascia

The floor of the popliteal fossa is formed by:

Popliteal surface of the femur

Capsule of the knee joint

Fascia covering the popliteus muscle

The contents of the popliteal fossa (from medial to lateral) are:

Popliteal artery

Popliteal vein

Tibial nerve

Common peroneal nerve

The tibial and common peroneal nerves are the most superficial of the contents of the popliteal fossa. The deepest structure is the popliteal artery. The small saphenous vein pierces the deep fascia to enter the popliteal fossa. The popliteal lymph nodes surround the vessels.

The popliteal fossa and its contents, with the popliteal lymph nodes in blue (from Gray’s Anatomy)

stem: You are performing an ultrasound scan on a patient with only one kidney. She has attended with a sign-language interpreter who explains that she also has abnormalities of her heart, neck and left shoulder.
prompt: Which of the following is NOT a feature of Klippel-Feil syndrome?
explanation:
Please note that the question asks which is NOT a feature of Klippel-Feil syndrome.

A third of cases have sensorineural deafness but bony deformities (and thus conductive deafness) of the middle ear are present in a number of cases too.

Congenital ASD is associated with the syndrome, not VSD.

Klippel-Feil syndrome

(different from Klippel-Trenaunay-Weber syndrome: port-wine stains, localised hypertrophy and venous malformations)

Klippel-Feil syndrome is predominantly a segmentation anomaly which arises during foetal development and leads to cervical fusion of two or more vertebral bodies. C2-3 are most commonly involved, accounting for around half of cases. Thereafter C5-6 accounts for a further third and the remainder are made up from fusions at other levels. There are a multitude of associated features, the predominant ones of which include:

Main associations and frequency

Renal abnormalities (of which a third have unilateral renal agenesis)

⅔

Scoliosis >20o

½

Sprengel shoulder

⅓

Deafness (Sensorineural)

⅓

Cervical ribs

⅕

The renal anomalies seen include agenesis or dysgenesis, ectopic location, and duplication.

Yet further features of this condition, all present in under 20% of cases include:

Odontoid dysplasia

Hemivertebrae / butterfly vertebrae

Syringomyelia / diastomatomyelia

Ear anomalies (microtia, deformed ossicles etc)

Congenital heart disease (ASD or coarctation)

Sprengel shoulder

This condition can occur in isolation as well as part of Klippel-Feil syndrome. It is (like Klippel-Feil syndrome) also often associated with renal anomalies. Sprengel shoulder is a congenital abnormality where the scapula (usually, but not exclusively, unilateral) is attached to the cervical vertebra either by a fibrous or osseous connection, and therefore fails to descend into the normal position. The result is elevation and medial rotation of the scapula, which is usually hypoplastic. The condition can be readily appreciated on a plain film although cross-sectional imaging is useful to plan surgical correction if required. If present, the osseous connection between the scapula and the spine is termed an omovertebral bar.

stem: You are reviewing the images of a patient known to have an inflammatory arthritis.
prompt: Which of the following would make a diagnosis of reactive arthritis more likely than one of ankylosing spondylitis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Iritis is another term for anterior uveitis. Although anterior uveitis does occur in conjunction with ankylosing spondylitis, it is much more closely associated with CRA.

Seronegative arthritides - These are negative for Rheumatoid factor but have a strong association with HLA-B27 positivity.

Ankylosing spondylitis - 95%

Enteropathic arthropathy - 90%

Psoriatic arthritis - 80%

Chronic reactive arthritis - 70%

Ankylosing spondylitis

This disease usually presents in early adulthood with gradual onset of back pain. There is a male preponderance, though it can affect women too. The vast majority (>90%) of patients are HLA-B27 positive. Radiologically the late features are classical with:

Bilateral symmetrical sacroiliitis

Enthesopathy - calcified tendon insertion sites

Bamboo spine - vertebral syndesmophytes, particularly in the thoracolumbar spine

Dagger sign - spinous process fusion

Erosion, then fusion at the symphysis pubis, costochondral, costovertebral and sternoclavicular joints

Thoracic manifestations: upper lobe pulmonary fibrosis, pericarditis, aortic root dilatation

Early features are far more subtle and require a higher index of suspicion

Enthesopathy - high signal on MRI at tendon insertion sites

Romanus lesions - triangular shaped oedema at the corners of vertebral bodies

Andersson lesions - similar signal changes to Romanus lesions but take place centrally at the discovertebral junctions

Oedema in the sacroiliac joints

Patients with advanced ankylosing spondylitis are at increased risk of pathological fractures due to fusion. These can be pelvic fractures following a simple fall, or chance fractures of the spine (involving all three columns - in ankylosing spondylitis, these fractures are also sometimes termed chalk-stick or carrot fractures).

Chronic reactive arthritis

This disease is said to present as a triad of arthritis, conjunctivitis/uveitis and urethritis/cervicitis (Can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree) however in reality only around a third of patients present with all three symptoms. Patients are usually aged 16-60years. It has a reasonably strong male predominance but does occur in women. It can occur following infection with chlamydia, but also with gastrointestinal infections such as salmonella, shigella, campylobacter and yersinia. Most (>2/3rds) of patients are HLA-B27 positive.

Bilateral asymmetrical sacroiliitis

Paravertebral ossification - similar to syndesmophytes but in theory are seen separately from the disc, bridging around it. Most commonly in the thoracolumbar spine

Enthesopathy - particularly at achilles tendon insertion, interspinous ligaments, and pelvic ligaments

stem: Which of the following is most suggestive of a diagnosis of acromegaly.
prompt: Select one answer only.
explanation:
Acromegaly

Excess circulating growth hormone can be caused either by a pituitary adenoma (>90%) or hyperplasia of the anterior pituitary. If this occurs prior to skeletal maturation it leads to gigantism in children. Thereafter there are a number of skeletal manifestations. Some of the most widely known are prognathism and spade-like hands.

Famously, the actor Richard Kiel who played Jaws in the James Bond films ‘Moonraker’ and ‘The Spy Who Loved Me’ had acromegaly.

Other important characteristics to look for are as follows:

Enlargement of the paranasal sinuses – 75%

Posterior vertebral scalloping – 30%

Widening of the terminal tufts

Heel pad thickness >25mm

Premature osteoarthritis

Enlargement and erosion of the sella

Hyperostosis of the inner table of the skull

Normally metastatic deposits in the spine lead to low T1 signal and high T2 signal. There should be no signal drop out on fat saturated sequences in contrast to marrow reconversion where although red marrow will experience far less signal dropout than yellow marrow, there will still be some loss in signal owing to the fat content of both types of marrow.

stem: A 50- year-old man suffers an anterior dislocation of the shoulder. He visits his local A+E department where the joint is successfully reduced.
prompt: Which of the following is the most likely abnormality demonstrated on the plain films following reduction?
options: Avulsion of the lesser tuberosity alone
Indentation of the anterior humeral head alone
Indentation of the anterior humeral head with a fracture at the inferior glenoid
Indentation of the posterior humeral head and avulsion of the lesser tuberosity
Indentation of the posterior humeral head with a fracture at the inferior glenoid
explanation:
Anterior dislocation (95%)

The integrity of the shoulder joint is weakest when at extreme abduction and external rotation.

When the humeral head dislocates anteriorly with respect to the glenoid, the posterolateral aspect of the humeral head impacts on the inferior glenoid and both can suffer. The damage to the humeral head is known as a Hill-Sachs lesion and the inferior glenoid fracture is called a Bankart lesion.

Posterior dislocation (5%)

At extreme abduction with internal rotation the humeral head is forced posteriorly and can dislocate. The usual scenario is in the context of a seizure or alternatively when a patient has been electrocuted. The AP x-ray can seem normal to the untrained eye. If the humerus remains internally rotated, the greater tuberosity rotates to a more anterior position and its characteristic outline is lost, leading to the so-called ‘light-bulb’ sign of a posterior dislocation. To establish the relationship between the humeral head and the glenoid, a Y-view, where the glenoid is viewed head-on, is often performed but an axillary view, where the beam travels through the axilla, is said to be even more useful. Avulsion fractures of the lesser tuberosity (where the subscapularis muscle attaches) are commonly seen in association with posterior dislocations.

A bony defect on the anteromedial surface of the humeral head is known as reverse Hill-Sachs lesion. Similarly a tear to the posterior glenoid labrum is called a reverse Bankart lesion.

Inferior dislocation (<1%) – Also known as Luxatio erecta

The patient presents with their arm held over their head. X-rays will show the humeral head displaced downwards and caught underneath the glenoid.

stem: A 67-year-old overweight man presents with lower back pain. On examination he has weakness of ankle dorsiflexion, eversion and inversion as well as weakness of hip abduction. His GP thinks he may have a problem with an intervertebral disc protrusion.
prompt: At which level is this most likely to be?
explanation:
This is a straightforward anatomy question. In the cervical spine the nerve roots exit above their named vertebral body; thus at the level of C4/5 it is the C5 which will be exiting. This is unlike the lumbar spine where the nerve root exits below its named vertebral body and is explained by the presence of 8 cervical nerve roots with only 7 cervical vertebra.

There is also the concept of the exiting nerve root and the descending nerve root. This applies in particular to disc bulges/protrusions/extrusions and is more pertinent in the lumbar spine. The exiting nerve root at a given level will be one less than the descending nerve root. (ie at L2/3 the exiting nerve will be L2 and the descending nerve will be L3). Central disc pathology affects the descending nerve whereas paramedian or foraminal disc pathology may affect the exiting nerve.

explanation:
Please note that the question asks which is NOT a cause of block vertebra.

There is a differential diagnosis for block vertebra and although Sprengel shoulder features as a predmoninant part of Klippel-Feil syndrome, an isolated sprengel shoulder is not a cause of block vertebra.

Sprengel shoulder

This condition can occur in isolation as well as part of Klippel-Feil syndrome. It is (like Klippel-Feil syndrome) also often associated with renal anomalies. Sprengel shoulder is a congenital abnormality where the scapula (usually, but not exclusively, unilateral) is attached to the cervical vertebra either by a fibrous or osseous connection, and therefore fails to descend into the normal position. The result is elevation and medial rotation of the scapula, which is usually hypoplastic. The condition can be readily appreciated on a plain film although cross-sectional imaging is useful to plan surgical correction if required. If present, the osseous connection between the scapula and the spine is termed an omovertebral bar.

Klippel-Feil syndrome

(different from Klippel-Trenaunay-Weber syndrome: port-wine stains, localised hypertrophy and venous malformations)

Klippel-Feil syndrome is predominantly a segmentation anomaly which arises during foetal development and leads to cervical fusion of two or more vertebral bodies. C2-3 are most commonly involved, accounting for around half of cases. Thereafter C5-6 accounts for a further third and the remainder are made up from fusions at other levels. There are a multitude of associated features, the predominant ones of which include:

stem: A 43-year-old woman sustains a pelvic injury in a road traffic accident that causes damage to the lumbar plexus.

explanation:
The obturator nerve is the only nerve listed in the options that is a branch of the lumbar plexus and is therefore the most likely nerve to be affected in this case.

The lumbar plexus is a network of nerves that supplies innervation to the skin and musculature of the lower limb. It is formed by the anterior rami of the spinal nerves T12, L1, L2, L3 and L4. Additionally, the anterior rami of L4 pass communicating branches (the lumbosacral trunk), to the sacral plexus.

The lumbar plexus is formed within the psoas major muscle anterior to the transverse processes of L2-L5. Most of the larger branches run obliquely through the pelvis before leaving beneath the inguinal ligament. The exception to this is the obturator nerve, which leaves the pelvis via the obturator foramen.

prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Lipoma arborescens

This condition can affect children or adults and is thought to be a reaction to chronic inflammation of the synovium leading to extensive fatty infiltration of the synovium. It is almost always the knee which is affected. Plain radiographs will show only an effusion, which may be large, but on MRI there is frond-like or nodular synovial proliferation which returns fat-signal according to the different sequences used. The signal should be high on T1 and T2 but suppress on fat-saturated sequences. Post-contrast the synovium itself will enhance. Treatment is by synovectomy.

PVNS - Pigmented villonodular synovitis

The classic joint to be affected by PVNS is the knee but it can also occur at other large joints. Usually only one joint is affected in each patient. On x-ray the only sign may be a large joint effusion. Large subchondral cysts can also be seen. On MRI however, the appearances are characteristic. Haemorrhagic proliferation of the synovium in a frond-like villonodular fashion gives rise to the classic low signal 'feathery' sea-anemone-like finding. On susceptibility weighted sequences there is blooming artefact owing to the presence of haemosiderin. Patients are usually middle-aged and treatment is with synovectomy although there is a high rate of recurrence.

If the patient is male, the usual differential diagnosis for PVNS is of haemophilic arthropathy owing to the presence of blood products there too. PVNS appears as a differential diagnosis for subarticular lucent bone lesions due to the formation of large subchondral cysts.

Rheumatoid arthritis

A joint effusion and synovial thickening (which would avidly enhance post-contrast) is a worthy description for rheumatoid arthritis however the high-fatty signal of the synovium is not a feature of rheumatoid arthritis. As the condition develops, patients with rheumatoid arthritis exhibit erosive changes with cartilage loss, bony erosions and marrow oedema.

SAPHO (Synovitis, acne, palmoplantar pustulosis, hyperostosis, osteitis)

This disease is thought to be a variant of psoriatic arthropathy. The cutaneous manifestations may not be apparent at diagnosis (like psoriatic arthropathy) but hyperostosis and osteolysis and ankylosis of the sternocleidomastoid joint is absolutely typical. On a nuclear medicine bone scan, bilateral uptake in the sternoclavicular joints and manubrium is called a ‘bull’s head’ sign. About a third of patients also have spinal disease with paravertebral ossifications and osteosclerosis. Unilateral sacroiliitis may also occur. Appearances can be quite striking on CT. In the knees, ankles and small joints of the hands there may be inflammation of the joints with juxta-articular osteoporosis.

Haemophilic arthropathy

The larger joints are most at risk for this disease, and the knee is particularly classical. On an xray there may only be a joint effusion in early disease but erosions and subchondral cysts develop. In particular there may be widening of the intercondylar notch (for which there is a differential diagnosis of: JIA/RA, Psoriatic arthropathy, TB and haemophilia) due to pannus formation. Also classical is epiphyseal overgrowth secondary to hyperaemia.

On an MRI there may well be nodular deposits on the synovium however the presence of blood degradation products renders these very low in signal on all sequences with blooming artefact present on gradient echo sequences or similar. If a haemarthrosis is present, the signal of the fluid will change depending on the chronicity of the event.

A haemophilic pseudotumour occurs in around 1-2% of patients with haemophilia. The presence of blood degradation products leads to a wide variety of intralesional signal patterns. The lesions are usually surrounded by a low signal haemosiderin rim though. Lesions can arise within bone (intra-osseous) or in soft tissues (usually muscular). Growth and pressure effects on adjacent bone can cause scalloping.

On a nuclear medicine bone scan, bilateral uptake in the sternoclavicular joints and manubrium is called a ‘bull’s head’ sign. explanation:
Traumatic aortic rupture is a relatively common cause of sudden death following major trauma, particularly high-speed road traffic accidents (RTAs). Between 15-20% of deaths from RTAs are estimated to be due to this injury. Patients that survive the initial injury can make a full recovery if the aortic rupture is promptly recognized and treated.

Patients that survive tend to have an incomplete laceration near the ligamentum arteriosum of the aorta. Continuity is maintained by an intact adventitial layer or contained mediastinal haematoma that prevents immediate exsanguination and death.

It can be difficult to detect and may go unnoticed as many patients have no specific symptoms and other injuries may also be present clouding the picture.

Findings on chest X-ray can be helpful in making the diagnosis and include the following:

Fractures of 1st and 2nd ribs

Grossly widened mediastinum

Hazy left lung field

Obliteration of aortic knob

Deviation of trachea to the right

Presence of a pleural cap

Elevation and rightward shift of right mainstem bronchus

Depression of left mainstem bronchus

Obliteration of space between pulmonary artery and aorta

Deviation of oesophagus (or NG tube) to the right

Helical contrast enhanced CT scanning has close to 100% sensitivity and specificity for aorta rupture, however CT scanning should be reserved for patients that are haemodynamically stable.

Treatment is with either primary repair or by resection of the torn segment and replacement with an interposition graft. Endovascular repair is also now an acceptable alternative approach.

prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Melorrheostosis

This dysplasia gives a classical appearance said to resemble the dripping of solid candle wax along a bone. The name comes from greek words meaning 'flowing' and 'limb'. It can be asymptomatic but if there is encroachment on nerves or joints patients may present with pain and movement limitations. Uniquely for a dysplasia, it can cross from one bone to the next across a joint, sometimes causing fusion in the process. On imaging the affected 'dripping' areas are seen as slcerotic areas within the affected bones. It usually only affects one limb of the patient but changes can be seen in more than one bone of that limb (i.e. monomelic but polyostotic).

Osteopathia striata

This disease is more similar to osteopoikilosis than the other bony dysplasias. It is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion, but can arise sporadically too. It causes striking longitudinal striations in the metaphyseal regions of the long bones but patients are generally asymptomatic and it is usually therefore an incidental finding. The appearance is said to resemble stalks of celery.

Pyknodysostosis

This disorder is inherited in an autosomal recessive fashion and causes diffuse bony sclerosis. Patients are of short stature and often have a typical facies; there is usually frontal bossing despite delayed closure of the cranial sutures, small mandibular size and beaking of the nose. Additionally patients have short stubby fingers, the nails of which may be hypoplastic. It can be difficult to tell pyknodysostosis from osteopetrosis however the medullary cavity is still discernible in the case of pyknodysostosis. Patients with osteopetrosis also do not tend to suffer from short stature or mandibular involvement.

Osteopetrosis

This is a disease of abnormal osteoclastic activity which leads to thick, sclerotic bone throughout the skeleton. Although appearing very solid on an x-ray, the bone is very disorganised structurally and consequently very brittle. Patients may experience numerous fractures throughout their lives. There is an autosomal dominant form which does not impede life expectancy but the autosomal recessive form carries are poorer prognosis with death due to complications of bone marrow failure (infections, leukaemia or haemorrhage) before adulthood.

On x-ray there is a generalised increase in bone density and films should be carefully evaluated for the presence of a pathological fracture. A bone-within-a-bone appearance is typical of the autosomal dominant form and there may be alternating lines of sclerosis and lucency in the phalanges.

Osteopetrosis

Osteopoikilosis

This benign condition leads to multiple small oval bone islands forming around the skeleton. Purportedly, once the epiphyses have fused the number remains static. They can show mildly increased uptake on a nuclear medicine bone scan. Whereas a bone island may exist in isolation or near isolation, the finding of multiple such lesions suggests the diagnosis of osteopoikilosis.

Lymphoma

Primary lymphoma of the bone is far rarer than other types of non-Hodgkin lymphoma but has a variety of imaging features. Most commonly on x-ray there will be permeative bony destruction which can be overlooked initially. Lytic lesions with a wide zone of transition may be present but patients can also have sclerotic lesions (an ivory vertebra) or a mixed picture instead. Cortical destruction occurs late on in the disease process. On MRI the affected bone marrow will return low signal on T1 and high signal on T2. Scaphoid Non-Union Advanced collapse (SNAC)

This occurs following a scaphoid fracture. It is similar to SLAC but there is a normal scapholunate distance, with a scaphoid fracture. Like SLAC, there is radioscaphoid degenerative change, followed by proximal migration of the capitate and eventually dorsal intercalated instability.

Scaphoid-lunate advanced collapse (SLAC)

This occurs following injury to the scapholunate ligament or secondary to CPPD. It is similar to SNAC but there is scapholunate widening, rather than a scaphoid fracture. Radioscaphoid degenerative changes are an early feature, followed by proximal migration of the capitate and eventually dorsal intercalated instability.

Volar Intercalated Segment Instability (VISI)

This occurs when there is narrowing of the scapholunate angle to less than 30 degrees. DISI is described in the vignette above, not VISI.

Avascular necrosis (AVN) of the scaphoid

This is usually secondary to a proximal fracture. The most reliable sign is low T1 signal in the scaphoid.

Midcarpal dislocation

This occurs in association with triquetral fracture and is very similar to lunate dislocation.

Osteoporosis

Loss of bone mass is called osteoporosis. It can result from a variety of mechanisms detailed in the table. Serum calcium, phosphate and ALP levels may all be normal in patients with osteoporosis. Loss of bone mass causes the bones to be susceptible to fractures resulting from everyday stress (insufficiency fractures) or as a result of minor trauma. The typical fractures would be a Colles fracture of the wrist or a fractured neck of femur.

Diagnosis is by DEXA (dual energy x-ray absorpitometry) whereby images are taken usually of the spine or femoral neck. By subtracting the two, the density of the bone can be calculated. Patients are scored by comparing their bone density to either age matched normal individuals (Z-score, said to be a more reliable figure) or to young adults (T-score). A T-score of less than -2.5 is considered diagnostic.

The ‘H’ sign or Honda sign is seen on nuclear medicine bone scans. It occurs when there is increased uptake in the sacrum as a result of insufficiency fractures and is often caused by underlying osteoporosis.

Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI)

A defect on either chromosome 7 or 17 leads to abnormal type 1 collagen. Most cases are inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion. An adult with OI is most likely to have either type I or type IV. On imaging there is diffuse undermineralisation of the skeleton and (sometimes extreme) cortical thinning. Once a child with OI has become mobile the soft bones become bowed under the weight of the body. The pressure of the femoral heads on the soft acetabulae leads to acetabular protrusion. Basilar invagination results from pressure of the cervical spine on the base of the skull. Insufficiency fracture of the vertebral bodies lead to a biconcave appearance. OI is a differential diagnosis for multiple wormian bones which persist to adulthood. Patients are at risk of multiple fractures and this is often the initial presentation when not diagnosed antenatally.

Hyperparathyroidism

Parathyroid hormone acts to increase calcium levels either by promoting reabsorption in the kidneys or by acting on the osteoclasts of the bones and leads to increased bone resorption. This is seen as generalised osteopenia and cortical thinning, particularly of the subperiosteal bone.

Primary hyperparathyroidism is usually caused by an autonomous adenoma (alternatively parathyroid hyperplasia or a parathyroid carcinoma). Medullary nephrocalcinosis is most commonly caused by primary hyperparathyroidism but does also occur with secondary and tertiary hyperparathyroidism.

Secondary hyperparathyroidismis a hyperplastic response of the parathyroid glands to the high phosphate and low calcium levels which accompany renal osteodystrophy. Soft tissue calcification is very much a feature of renal osteodystrophy. Confusingly the high circulating levels of phosphate in renal osteodystrophy leads to dystrophic mineralisation of trabecular bone which is seen as sclerosis; hence renal osteodystrophy is a cause of generalised increase in bone density despite hyperparathyroidism being a cause of osteopenia.

Avascular necrosis

There are at least 25 different eponymous sites for avascular necrosis. On plain film the finding is usually of a lucent area with a sclerotic serpiginous border of granulation tissue. On MRI this serpiginous border returns low signal on T1 and a ‘double-line’ sign on T2 (high signal of granulation tissue surrounded by low signal of sclerosis). Loss of chondral integrity leads to disruption of the articular surface causing the patient pain on usage.

Presents aged 2-6. Blue sclera, joint laxity, deafness. II AR Often stillborn or perinatal death due to pulmonary hypoplasia. III AR Progressively deforming, fractures at birth in most cases. Primary hyperparathyroidism is usually caused by an autonomous adenoma (alternatively parathyroid hyperplasia or a parathyroid carcinoma). prompt: What is the most likely explanation?
explanation:
A traumatic nerve root avulsion has been described but the remainder of the question is based in simple anatomy.

In the cervical spine the nerve roots exit above their named vertebral body; thus at the level of C4/5 it is the C5 which will be exiting. This is unlike the lumbar spine where the nerve root exits below its named vertebral body and is explained by the presence of 8 cervical nerve roots with only 7 cervical vertebra.

A Tarlov cyst

A tarlov cyst is the name given to dilatation of the posterior nerve root sheath. They follow CSF on all sequences.

Neuropraxia refers to a temporary nerve injury.

Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (AIDP) is a term used to describe a subtype of Guillain-Barre syndrome which is an autoimmune mediated ascending flaccid paralysis. Most imaging will be normal in such cases, with the exception of some possible contrast enhancement and thickening to the nerve roots at the cauda equina.

Syringomyelia

A syrinx is a cavity within the spinal cord. They can be post-traumatic in nature but are more often thought of as a congenital entity. There is an association with Chiari I malformations (as well as myelomeningocoele, Chiari II, Dandy-Walker and Klippel-Feil) and a finding of either a syrinx or Chiari I should trigger a search for the other.  On MRI they are seen as a CSF signal cavity running longitudinally within the spinal cord. They are associated with symptoms such as spasticity and hyperreflexia (upper motor neurone signs) to the region affected, alongside a reduction in pain and temperature sensation due to the effect on the spinothalamic tracts.  A Charcot joint, particularly of the shoulder, can result from a syrinx within the cervical cord.

prompt: Which nerve root is most likely to be affected? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
In the cervical spine the nerve roots exit at the spinal cord without needing to traverse (as in the lumbar spine). The exiting nerve root takes the name of the vertebra BELOW the affected disc. A disc protrusion at C3/4 will affect the C4 nerve root. This allows for the extra nerve root at C8 before reaching the thoracic spine. In the thoracic spine the affected level takes its name from the vertebral body ABOVE that level.

In the lumbar spine the exiting nerve root is usually compressed in the neural foramen, whereas the traversing nerve root is compressed usually in the lateral recess. Far lateral bulges affect the exiting nerve root (takes its name from the vertebral body ABOVE that level). Paracentral bulges affect the traversing nerve root (takes its name from the vertebral body BELOW that level).

A metastatic deposit within a bone usually returns little signal on T1, in contrast to the normal high T1 fatty marrow of normal bone, and high signal on T2. The signal does not drop out on STIR sequences because the fatty marrow is replaced by tumour so there is no fat signal to suppress.

Normally metastatic deposits in the spine lead to low T1 signal and high T2 signal. There should be no signal drop out on fat saturated sequences in contrast to marrow reconversion where although red marrow will experience far less signal dropout than yellow marrow, there will still be some loss in signal owing to the fat content of both types of marrow.

Sclerotic or blastic metastases return little signal on either T1 or T2 weighted sequences. These include prostate, breast or TCC metastases among others.

Lytic metastases are more likely than sclerotic metastases to enhance with contrast. Similarly on DWI imaging, whereas lytic metastases will usually appear hyperintense, sclerotic metastases return little signal since they contain little water.

Myelofibrosis

In myelofibrosis the bone marrow is gradually replaced by fibrous tissue which contains few water molecules and thus returns little signal on T1 or T2 weighted sequences. It is a haematological condition and concurrent hepatosplenomegaly is common due to the need for extramedullary haematopoiesis. Paraspinal soft tissue masses may also be seen for the same reason. On x-rays or CT there can be a generalised increase in bone density and it is one of the causes of a superscan on nuclear medicine bone scans.

Marrow reconversion

Image © Medical Exam Prep

As children age, the red marrow with which we are born slowly converts to yellow marrow, beginning in the diaphysis and spreading to either end of the bones. By late adolescence this process is almost complete and only a few areas of the skeleton retain red marrow, these include the proximal femora and humeri as well as the flat bones. A small amount of red marrow does persist throughout adulthood but various conditions can cause a re-conversion whereby red marrow once again replaces the yellow marrow. On MRI yellow marrow, which is high in fat content, returns high signal on T1 and intermediate signal on T2. The red marrow that we are born with is isointense to skeletal muscle on all sequences but as we age the fat content of red marrow increases and so the appearance changes. Residual red marrow islands can often be found close to the growth plates. It is best appreciated on fat saturated sequences as it will experience less signal drop out than the yellow marrow.

When haematopoiesis increases the yellow marrow can reconvert back to red marrow. This can occur in a number of different scenarios:

Marrow reconversion

Chronic haemolytic anaemia

Sickle cell disease

Thalassaemia

Increased oxygen demand or decreased oxygen supply

Athletes

High altitudes

Smoking

Iatrogenic

G-CSF

Erythropoietin

On an MRI scan where you should find high T1 signal fatty yellow marrow there will be low T1 signal red marrow which remains reasonably bright on STIR or other fat saturated sequences. The pattern of marrow reconversion is the exact reverse of the initial conversion, so beginning at the ends of the long bones and spreading to the diaphysis.

In the spine in particular, it can be difficult to differentiate between marrow reconversion and metastases. Even red marrow does contain some fat cells and thus should exhibit some signal drop-out on STIR or out of phase images whereas metastatic disease will not lose any signal at all.

Vertebral haemangioma

These lesions are extremely common and should be very familiar to all candidates. They can occur anywhere but commonly arise in the vertebrae. They have a typical appearance of vertical trabeculae which give a ‘corduroy’ appearance when viewed in sagittal or coronal planes but a honeycomb or polka-dot appearance when viewed in the axial plane. On MRI they return high signal on both T1 and T2 sequences.

Lymphoma

Primary lymphoma of the bone is far rarer than other types of non-Hodgkin lymphoma but has a variety of imaging features. Most commonly on x-ray there will be permeative bony destruction which can be overlooked initially. Lytic lesions with a wide zone of transition may be present but patients can also have sclerotic lesions (an ivory vertebra) or a mixed picture instead. Cortical destruction occurs late on in the disease process. On MRI the affected bone marrow will return low signal on T1 and high signal on T2. (by contrast, normal bone marrow which is high in fat returns high signal on T1 and intermediate signal on T2).

Differential diagnosis for permeative bone destruction

Lymphoma

Ewing sarcoma

Eosinophilic granuloma

explanation:
The gastrocnemius muscle is a large, bipennate muscle, situated in the posterior compartment of the leg. It has two heads; a lateral head that arises from the lateral condyle of the femur, and a medial head that arises from the medial condyle of the femur. The two heads combine and then form a common tendon (the Achilles tendon) with the soleus muscle, that inserts into the posterior surface of the calcaneus.

Between 15 and 30% of individuals have a sesamoid bone, called the fabella, that lies in the lateral head of the gastrocnemius muscle.

Gastrocnemius is innervated by the tibial nerve and receives its blood supply from the sural arteries.

Gastrocnemius is primarily involved in running, jumping and other ‘fast’ leg movements. It is also involved to a lesser degree, in walking and standing. Its main actions are to plantarflex the foot at the ankle joint and to flex the leg at the knee joint.

There is a roundness to the superior aspect of the left femoral neck.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Femoroacetabular impingement (FAI)

Mixed type - >80% of patients have components of both cam-type and pincer-type FAI.

Cam type - a cam is an engineering term for an oval/egg shaped component with a hole through the middle of the wider end. In cam type FAI the femoral head takes on a 'cam' shaped appearance due to bony overgrowth at the superior aspect of the femoral neck. This abnormal bony contour impinges against the anterosuperior aspect of the acetabulum during movement. The condition occurs more frequently in men and tends to affect men in their 30s. Certain conditions can predispose to cam-type FAI, including SUFE, DDH and Perthes disease. Some patients with cam-type FAI exhibit femoral retroversion.

Pincer type - here bony protruberance of the anterosuperior acetabulum causes overcoverage of the femoral head and impingement against the femoral neck. Protrusio acetabuli predisposes to pincer-type FAI. The relationship of the overgrown anterior acetabular rim to the posterior acetabular rim in pincer-type FAI is called acetabular retroversion since it causes the femoral neck to twist posteriorly. Patients usually stand with their toes pointing outwards as a consequence. The condition is more common in women and a patient is typically aged around 40.

Patients with advanced ankylosing spondylitis are at increased risk of pathological fractures due to fusion. These can be pelvic fractures following a simple fall, or chance fractures of the spine (involving all three columns - in ankylosing spondylitis, these fractures are also sometimes termed chalk-stick or carrot fractures).

Chronic reactive arthritis

This occurs in a subsect of patients with inflammatory or infective bowel disease. Roughly 10-20% of patients with Crohns or ulcerative colitis suffer from enteropathic arthropathy. This condition used to be termed juvenile rheumatoid arthritis. It is a cluster of similar conditions affecting patients under the age of 16.

The affected joints show:

Erosions

Cartilage destruction

Epiphyseal overgrowth secondary to reactive hyperaemia occurs owing to the immature nature of the skeleton. Premature physeal closure can result in limb length discrepancies in adulthood.

Large joints are typically affected first and the small joints of the hands and feet are affected later on.

prompt: What is the most likely explanation?
explanation:
The road traffic collision has caused a rupture of the thoracic duct which is the entry point into the venous circulation of lymphatic drainage from the majority of the body. It crosses the midline at the level of T5/6 and then enters the venous circulation where the left subclavian vein meets the internal jugular vein.  Transections above T5/6 will cause a left sided effusion whereas those occurring inferior to the midline-crossing cause a right sided pleural effusion. The effusion consists of chyle and will therefore be high in fat.

stem: Nex The carpal tunnel You review an MRI scan of a 50-year-old patient with carpal tunnel syndrome.
prompt: The floor of the carpal tunnel is formed by which of the following? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
The carpal tunnel is a passageway on the palmar side of the wrist that connects the forearm to the middle compartment of the deep plane of the hand.

The carpal tunnel is formed by two layers, the carpal arch and the flexor retinaculum:

1. The carpal arch forms the floor of the carpal tunnel. It is concave on the palmar side and is formed laterally by the scaphoid and trapezium tubercles and medially by the hook of the hamate and the pisiform bones.

2. The flexor retinaculum forms the roof of the carpal tunnel. It is a strong, fibrous band that covers the carpal bones on the palmar side of the hand near the wrist. It is attached medially to the pisiform bone and the hook of the hamate bone. Laterally it attaches to the tubercle of the scaphoid bone, and to the medial part of the trapezium bone.

She undergoes an MRI of her cervical spine for further assessment. The C3/C4 vertebral disc is seen to extrude posteriorly and effaces the exiting nerve root.
prompt: Which nerve root is most likely to be affected? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
In the cervical spine the nerve roots exit at the spinal cord without needing to traverse (as in the lumbar spine). The exiting nerve root takes the name of the vertebra BELOW the affected disc. A disc protrusion at C3/4 will affect the C4 nerve root. This allows for the extra nerve root at C8 before reaching the thoracic spine. In the thoracic spine the affected level takes its name from the vertebral body ABOVE that level.

In the lumbar spine the exiting nerve root is usually compressed in the neural foramen, whereas the traversing nerve root is compressed usually in the lateral recess. Far lateral bulges affect the exiting nerve root (takes its name from the vertebral body ABOVE that level). Paracentral bulges affect the traversing nerve root (takes its name from the vertebral body BELOW that level).

Subchondral insufficiency fractures of the knee (SIFK). (Previously known as spontaneous osteonecrosis of the knee (SONK))

Women over the age of 55 is the typical demographic for SIFK but it does also occur in men. It is the adult equivalent to osteochondritis dessicans of the knee. Typically the medial condyle is affected and often there is an associated meniscal tear. On x-ray the appearances are of medial femoral condyle flattening with or without a subchondral radiolucent area. On MRI bone marrow oedema can be seen (high signal on STIR sequences).
